"GOD SAVE IRELAND 'God stye Ireland from enemies outside her borders,and from enemies within, God save Ireland trom cruel men of whatever c'ass. be ti ev—and I trust there are very f :w—arasp.ng Laid- lords and rack-renti rg 13.ndlords, or be they di,honest tenants or midni4ht marauders. God save Ireland from the pestilence that walketh at Loon and the terror nat stealeth at night: and I believe that God will save Irelard. for with all her faults there is that amount of virtue among the irsh people, there is that love of their country, tiat love and devotion of men to their families. that widingness to sacrifice for them, which are abiding and homely virtues that (to much to save a toantry and to enable God's laws to be respected, and wi, h the earne,t de- sire that God may save Leland, I thank you for having heard ins."—W. E. Forster at Tullamore. He stood erect and fearless mid a crowd Steeped to the lips in treason, demoralized By agitation, who hated him and hate.l England. Not a tremor sh, ok his daunt' ess And though a any moment death mi.. ht. lay him low, His cheek blanched not, 12r quailed his iron heart. He had work d long and tv.:ll. ;or Erin. No need of praise Was hg, but he foul tongue of calumny Had pierced him with its thousand darts, And painted Erin's truest friend a Ite. Be heeded rot, but with a high resolve, And hero-heart worked on. And nowhe stands Unarmed amid the men he'd laboured for, :But who alas ! no gratitude displayed, And met him whit dark scowls and words of hate. In burning tones he told them of the sins That stained their land; rebuked their cowardice, Which sheltered vihany and made the felon safe, And branded murder and dishonesty With their own dark brand.

Next he spoke Of brighter days to come, of love to Erin, Of Albion's widr to ease her rankling wounds, While fearlessly suppressing crime. And the crowd, Awed by the presence of an Engiishman Who knew no fear, listened and were numb. Then with a fervor that aw,:ke responsive cheers He cried " God save Ireland !" and went, his way. Brave Forster's gone! but we to-day would cry "God save Ireland !" And surely Erin needs salvation: Her laws have now been purged and purified. Ani Albion longs to live in peace with Erin. Whom she dear,y Ives. Yet still she has to grieve O'er Erin's waywardne;s, and the cruel spurns She (Item Albion's earnest outstretched hand. That hand is outstretched still, and though in pain, The hand that bears the raoiant flag of peace, Bears also j us; !ea's sword, she will loves Erin, And work, and fro: es, and prays tor her. Ay ! "God save Ireland ! cry all English hearts, Teach her sons the curse the assassin brings Upon their isle. Bid her wealthier ones be merciful, Aid bid her humbler children pay their dues. From midnight nia•sacres good Lorh deliver them; From every evil bile them with Thy shield. From famme's wolfish eyes, from pestilence May they be free. May disaffectAon die And treasol hide its hideous head in sham. Let Ei in's s ,ns obey the law and what they deem unkind in it Will die when crime des. Then in the coming day Shall Erin r se from out lic,r wretchedness. Her children's virtues, that in darkness shone Like stars conspicuous, their love of home. Devott m to their faint les—the fires of patriotism Which naught can quench, shall even brighter glow, And loving hearts and hands shall weave for Erin A golden destiny. I. he and her sister Albion Shs,ll meet in mutual embrace—the kiss of peace Shall bind two nations, henceforth only one. In bonds unbreakable.
God save Ireland!

A MAY IDYL. 0, Nature, be kind unto May, And give her the blossoms which render lizr gay; For May should be gu,en when the birds are a-winc, Allured by the sprays of her sweet fashioning. Demean her apparel, you rob her of charms Which yield more delight than the clasp of her arms. For what is Maid May to the rovers of song, Who wait for her coming in amorous throng, If radiant bloom be an abs,ntee grace, And winterly frowns chase the love from her face? The beauty of Spring is familiar in &fay ; And who is not charmed with the innocent trait Mit, breathes an endearment from every b:aigh, When May o'er the hedges her mantle doth throw ? She makes 0. the branches rare presents of buds, Who hang up her gifts in the lanes and the woods, Pf 'lumina the air with the odorous gems. That cling to the skirts of the road, and its hems. 6he kisses the bushes refre,hiuglv young As lover-like Fps in their passion have einna', And droops like a lily when smitten with death, Ere June is potential wirh summer-drawn breath. Ah! May fsa g od and a b tuntitul maid, Whose garments are pure in the lixt.t. in the shade. Whose character gladdens the earth with its wealth Of floral perfection and blossoming health. So Nature, dear Natu:e, be kind unto May, And give her the blossoms which make her so gay. May 2nd, 1882. BENJ. BAWDON, Warrington.

A cynical hid bachelor, who believes that a woman has something to say on all subjects, recently asked a friend, "Well, madam, what do you hold on this question of suffrage ?" THE AMERICAN Biaman.—A Washington paper has autho- rity for the following, which is written concerning a mem- ber of the United States Senate :—" Senator is some- wh it given to profanity. At times he makes the Senatorial wUkin ring with his expletives. He has also a pleasant fashion of wearing his hat during debate, and of standing up when he is ordered to sit down. To bullyrag the chairman and sergeant-at-arms into a state of frantic desperation is another of his favourite diversions. But under the re- st ijustiess, influence of a cocktail or two, Mr. always wales e t the next morning, and nothieg can exceed Qr resist the Chesterfieldian grace, with which he makes the amends apologetique.—Harper's Weekly. SLEEPERS IN CHURCH.—As I returned through the -churchyard I was greeted very respectfully by a person whose dress seemed to indicate that he was a functionary of :he church. I heard that he was the sexton, but that he also discharges another very useful office, which, as far as I know, is peculiar to Kerry (Montgomeryshire). It appears that it is by ancient custom a part of his duty to perambu- late the church during service time with a bell in his band, to look carefully iato every pew, and whenever he finds anyone dozing to ring the bell. He discharges this duty, it is said, with great vigilance, istrepedity, and impartiality, and consequently with the happiest effect upon the congre- gation ; for, as everybody is certain that if he or she gives 'way to drowsiness the fact will forthwith be made known through the whole church by a peal which will direct all eyes to the sleeper, the fear of such a visitation is almost always sufficient to keep every one on the alert.—Bishop Thirlwall's Letters. TRAP:DOOI liIPIDETLS.—A considerable number of species, chiefly inhabiting the Old World, live in burrows, which i they excavate n the ground and line with a tube of silk. They generally close their habitations with a regular' closely' fitting door, attached to on, side of the aperture bya silken hinge, and, from the peculiar construction of their domicile, they are known commonly as "Trapdoor Spiders." The trap-door is composed of earthly particles, firmly held to. gether with layera of silk, and, although sometimes it con- sists of a mere flap falling down over the aperture, it is in most cases a regular stopper, accurately fitting into the ori. lice of the burrow. In some Instances the spider snows still more ingenuity in fitting up its abode as a place of refuge. After making the main nest, it works through at one side, and there digs both upwards and downwards obliquely, so as to produce a side chamber into which it can retreat should some enemy succeed in opening the trap-door; and the lateral chamber is cut off from the main burrow by a silky curtain-like door, which hangs before it, and thus apparently completes the inner lining of the tube.—Cassell's (aural History. div.head: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.
div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

Lieutenant Danenhaner, of the Jeanette, and his corn. panions arrived at Moscow on Saturday. Mr. Melville re- mains on the shores of the Lena, to carry on the search for Lieutenant De Long. At the recent matriculation examination of the Calcutta University eight women passed successfully, of whom six I are natives of India; and at Bambay seven women were I successful, including four from the city of Poonah. At the First Arts examination at Calcutta a female candidate ob. tained a scholarship of the first grade. MM. Becket and Schlagdenhausen brought before the Academy of Sciences at the Séance of March 20th a paper on the kola nut (seeds of Sterculia acuminata). They show that this nut contains in a free state more caffeine than the finest coffees, a considerable quantity of theobromine ard much glucose, three times the starch of theobroma, little fatty matter, and some tannin. M. Henri Giffard, the French engineer, is dead. He will be best known in England by his "injector." Giffard de. voted a large part of his time and mach money to experi- ments in aerostation. Especially he invented a balloon, ellipsoidal in form, and with an helix attached which was used as an instrument of propulsion. M. l'Abbe Moigno, in ' Les Hondes for April 22nd, devotes several pages to a memoir of his friend.

Les Mondes in a paper "On the Illumination of Conser- vatories by the Electric Light," states that the naked rays were found to be injurious to the plants, but the light having passed through glass globes did not appear to affect them. Nocturnal illumination is not fatal to plants, bat there is no proof that it is beneficial. Upon the whole, M. l'Abbe Moigno says, the results obtained at the Palace of Industry were not favourable.

The University of Michigan is described by the Nation as now holding, in point of numbers, "the leading position among the higher political institutions of the country." The total of students for the current year is 1,534, of whom 180 are women. Less than one-half belong to the State of• Michigan. A school of political science has recently been organised; and in the arts department a wide, though not unlimited, choice of studies is allowed, the principle being to require a certain degree of proficiency in one or inure specified branches of knowledge. ANoreteen Secompaity BA,TTERY.—The secondary battery question, so far as patents are concerned, appears to be compli- cated by a paper by J. B. Oeter, which appeared in a German serial in 1881. He covered a sheet of lead with a coating of peroxide, wrapped it flannel, soldered on an anode of copper, rolled the whole tightly into a cylinder ; sheet lead was then put round, and the whole introduced into a porous pot, containing dilute sulphuric acid. That was placed in a glass cell containing a similar solution, with amalgamated zinc plates. The author found it to be a powerful and con- stant voltaic cell, which he now proposes to modify and convert into an accumulator.—Eaylish Mechanic. DEFENCE OF THE CHANNEL TUNNEL.—Dr_ Siemens has, by request, presented to the Military Committee, on the subject of the Channel Tunnel, an ingenious and novel plan for defending the tunnel, if constructed, from hostile inva- sion. He proposes that immediitely above the lateral drain- age tunnel there should be a drift-way or tube, terminating on the tunnel side in a double arch, with numeroas perfora- tions into the tunnel, and on the land side in several cham- bers of wrought-iron sunk into the ground. These cham- bers he proposes to fill with lumps of common chalk, and to connect each of them by means of a pipe with a large cis- tern filled with muriatic acid. Upon opening the comma nication Vale acid would fie er into the upper portion of one of the chambers, where it would be distribated by perforated pipes over the entire area. The result of such an inflow would be a 7owerful chemical reaction, giving rise to a generation of carbonic acid gas, which would for half a mile or more form an insuperable barrier to the passage of human beings through the tunnel. The va'yes by which the acid gas was turned upon the chalk might be worked from a site distance by electricity. The scheme thus brieflyl sketched is recommended by Dr. Siemens as being compara- tively cheap and easy of adoption, while leaving the tunnel intact and fit for use after a reasonable interval for proper measures to clear it from the carbonic acid gas. A NEW INSULATING MATEUIAL.—The immense strides which have been made in electrical discovery, particularly in practical applications, have compelled electricians to seek for new and cheaper insulating materials than those alreedy in use. Hitherto they hive been limited to glass, porcelain, s tone ware, gutta-percha, indiarubber, and ebonite. Owing to the greatly increased demand, the price of the last three named has risen very much, and is likely to rise still more, and, while the quality has deteriorated, it is impossible for the existing sources to supply what is needed, not only for telegraph and telephone work, but for the immense field opening in electric light work. The public require, before everything, safety in the use of electricity, and there is a corresponding demand for a cheap insulating material, the supply of which shall be equal to the demand likely to arise. This has now been met by the invention of a material called insulite. A method has been discovered by which wood, sawdust, cotton waste, paper pulp, and other fibrous materials cm n be converted into a material perfectly imper- vious to moisture and acids, easily moulded under pressure into any shape, and capable of being worked or cut into any form. This material is an excellent non-conductor of elec- tricity, and can be used for all forms of battery-cells, tele- graph insulators, supports for electric light leads, and tele- phone work. It affords the means of securing perfect insu- lation at a very much less cost than ebonite or gutta-percha. As it is perfectly impervious to moisture, articles made of it cannot shrink or warp. It supplies exactly what is wanted in practical work, in which ordinary wood cannot be used because it absorbs moisture, and ebonite is inhibited on ac- count of its cost.—Times.

GRANNY.--Fifty-tbree years ago, Sir John Da!mil gathered a well-grown matronly specimen of the common smooth sea anemone from the rocks of North Berwick, and transplanted her to a suitable aquarium. There she out- lived her patron, and at his death was bequeathed to the care of Professor John Fleming; afterwards to Dr. James Mcßain, who, when he found hi a end approaching, sought another guardian, and after the trust had been declined by some to whom he offered it, found at last a willing and worthy successor in Mr. Sadler, the curator of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Edinburgh. Last year the venerable actinia mesembrNanthenzum, whose personal name, "Granny," is more distinctive and pronounceable, was alive and "as well as might be expected," seeing that she had brought forth twenty•seven bala77 actinim, all alive and well, during the previous summer. In 1857, when Sir John Dalzell was still her nurse, she gave birth to 240 in one night. Not haring heard any bad news, I sunpoe that she is still alive, an;i having survived unchanged for so many years, there is fair prOtlpt'et Of nut- on!living many more generations of e human curators. In t4he coLitia Of a very ::.. number of - s:perirnmts in compounding an artificial inclEatinn of tea 1 water, I have used these animals as my tests, and have die- covered V,at the first symptom of serious illness has been the ejection of a multitude of little =Unite, with a single I ring of tentacles. If this continue, the parent shrivels and I then gradually di-ea—so gradually that one portion may be quite putrid while the other still lingers on alive. The young are ejected from the month of the parent, and soon , fix themselvss to any convenient rock, but I have never been able to rear them in an aquarium. They somehow disappear. They vary from about -4- th to ith of an inch in diameter across the circle of the tentacles. They may be , seen living and growing inside the parent of the greenish and more transparent varieties. I have never earlan anthea thus produce young, bnt have had cases of increase by sub- diviaion ; a single animal splitting into as many as six in less than a week. This splitting is a curious process, the complete animal being a stomach surrounded by tentacles which proceed from a circular wail and base of flesh divided into compartments corresponding to the tentacles. Each half has, therefore, to complete itself by uniting its severed walls and forming a camplete stomach of its own. In the case above mentioned, five of the six fragments did this, but the sixth failed, the tentacles rotting one by one, the last retaining its vital movements until decomposed. This re- markable vitality of detached tentacles of the anthea has often surprised me. I have watched them for days, wonder- ing how they could survive without the central stomach which forms so important an element of the anatomy of the normal animal.—The Gentleman's Magazine,

One morning lat2ly a valna'Dle milch cow belonging to Mrs. Booton, of Bromyard Downs, was found dead. On opening the stomach, there was found a considerable quan- tity of lead, and it is supposed that lead poisoning was the cause of death. The metal was not unlike portions of rifle bullets, which the animal may have eaten while grazing, the Rifle Corps range being on the Downs. Among the other contents were pins and tin tacks, which were fastened in the coat of the stomach, sprigs, bits of glass • and wire, small stones, dzc., altogether a very remarkable assortment. SCOTTISH EXPORTS OF CATTLE.-1 very large and vain- able let of polled Aberdeen or Angus cattle, purchased by Mr. William Findlay, auctioneer, Peterhead, for several clients in America, has left Aberdeen for Glasgow. The lot includes 67 yearling heifers and 14 yearling bulls, making a total of 81, selected from among a number of the leading herds in the north and south of Scotland. This is the third consignment that Mr. Findlay has sent to America within a short period, and the fact that some of his old clients have renewed their orders shows that the polled breed is taking a *strong hold on "the other side of the pond." The demand is not likely to fall off for a long time at any rate. gr. Wilke!), Waterside of Forbes, than whom no one has a retire accurate knowledge of the state of the American demand for polled cattle, stated the other day that at this moment 'he could send 500 of them to that country provided he coidd get them at last year's prices. Conotta OF CATTLE.—Every one who travels in this country, and has agricultural proclivities, cannot fail to note the distinctive colour of the various herds of cattle. Each division of the kingdom has its favourite or especial breed of stock, more or less intermixed with others. To take a broad view of the five most prominent breeds, it will be found the South have the reds, Wales and Scotland the blacks, and the Midlands the whites and roans. The rees take in the Sussex, Devons, and the Herefords. Scarcely any other colour than black can be found in Wales. The heavy blacks, or Galloway, and the small Byloes, shale with the yellow and dun he greater part of Scotland ; while the great central counties from Durham, through York, and the Midlands produce the only white cattle found in England. Shorthorns are white or roaLs—all red of course abound. The great Holderness cows are roans, or red and white speckled—an invented breed, produced sue- cessively from stock selected with judgment from Holland, Scotland and Yorkshire. Dutch cows are not remarkable for long horns, and when these are cros.%ed with the Gallo- way or polled Scots a breed of shorthorn cattle is almost

Some curious effects are produced by the short- horn breeder in selecting, as he thinks, sires that will bring the stronger colour red into his herd, and displace the more delicate constitutions of the white. Red bulls to red cows would be supposed to produce a red calf, but an instance is known where the produce was white continuously. White Is the predominant colour of Swiss and Charlerois breeds, whilst the Holstein and Jutland stock have the dun colour mixed with white. The Dutch cows have a white sheet over a black body, presenting a pleasing effect to the eye. Although the Jerseys and Alderneys are g-merally of a deli- cate yellow, the Duke of Richmond has a grand herd of them at Goodwood, all black and snaoliy colour. These cows of the Duke's seem to have grown about twenty stone bigger than any, other known Alderney breed.—Land and Water.

_ WHAT IS LARD CHEESE ?—The following is the answer given in the Ohio Farmer :—lu York State not a.little atten- tion is given to the manufacturing of lard cheese, under the Freeman patent. The cream is all taken out of the milk and lard substituted. The "cream" that restores this milk back to its original quality is made by mixing two parts milk and one of lard. This is done by means of a rapidly revolving upright cylinder about 6 inches in diameter and 20 in height. The inside surface of this cylinder is thickly set with minute points, which by the rapid motion cat through the lard and divide and subdivide until it has lost its adhesiveness, and becomes so separated that the milk has formed an artificial covering which prevents them from re- uniting. The milk and lard are each heated to 130 degrees before being turned into the machine, and when it is ex- pelled by the centrifugal motion it reappears in the form of a thin cream, so natural that it is well calculated to "deceive the very elect." Meanwhile the milk in the vats has been warmed no to 90 degrees, and this cream is then added at the rate of 11 lb. of lard to each 100 lb. of milk, and after thoroughly stirring to incorporate the cream, extract of rem - net is pat in at the rate of about 4 oz. to the 1,000 lb. of milk. The process after this is not essentially different from any cheesemaking. The cooking of the curd usually t tkes about one hour and a half, and the curds are salted at , the 2h lb. rate. The reports of those who handle these lard cheeses upon the market and those who do not are somewhat conflicting. Yet these cheeses seem to have come to stay. When from 100 lb. of new milk 4 15. of butter can be taken, and then, by putting back the buttermilk 14 per cent. and adding 11 lb. of lard, 9 lb. of full stock cheese can be pro- duced, there will be no lack of adventurous cheesemakers willing to become millionaires by making lard cheese. _ _

DAR-BY'S STEAM DIGGOR AT BARRINGTON HALL.-Mr. G. A. Lowndes, of Barrington Hall, Hatfield Broad Oak, having had two of his farms thrown upon his bands, has had the courage to turn farmer himself instead of suffering the land to lie dormant and grow rank with weeds, to its own injury and its proprietor's loss. A few days ago, Mr. Lowndes invited a large party of his friends to witness the perform- ance upon his farms of the now celebrated implement known as "Darby's Patent Broadside Steam Digger." Among those present were the Hon. C. H. Strutt and Sir Henry Se'win- Ibbetson, Bart., M.P., and Lady Ibbetson. As soon as the digger commenced work a great many of the agriculturists assembled, and were much a-tonished at the ease and regu- larity with which the strong clay laud was turned com- pletely over, or rather placed at such an angle as to be in the best position to absorb the largest amount of the fertilis- ing nitrogen so abundantly and gratuitously supplied by the all-pervading atmosphere. Toe fields were very irregular in shape, but this presented no difficulty to the almost übiqui- tous digger, which could travel anywhere at the bidding of its driver, and leave no headlands to be dealt with afterwards. The admirable condition in which the subsoil is left, offering the most generous welcome to the enriching air, was especi- ally admired by all present. It is claimed for this mode of breaking up land that the surface of soil exposed by it for aeration is at least four times as much as when the land is ploughed in the ordinary way, and no subsoil having been compressed, the absorbing tendency of the clay is allowed its full power of extracting ammonia from the air. Since the above meeting, Mr. Lowndes invited the Board of Guardians of the Darunow Union, of which he is an active ex officio member, to luncheon, and afterwards to inspect the opera- tions of what may be called the "Steam Spade." The digger was on this occasion working in a large field on a hill side, and it was steered and turned with the greatest ac- curacy.• After inspecting the work previously done in seve- ral other fields (one of which had been crossed to prove that the digger is equally at home on stirred and loose as well as on solid land), the party adjourned to the homestead on Little Barrington Hall, which is a fine specimen of what a homestead should be. On arriving at the farmhouse they were entertained by Mr. H. S. King, the steward, and Mrs. King. at a capital luncheon provided by Mr. Lowndes. After the meal, a discussion was kept up, while the subject of it could be seen in the distance steadily plodding away at its work. Mr. Darby expressed himself satisfied, as the re- sult of four years' experience, that a great saving of horse and manual labour can be effected by the adoption of steam digging, and that better crops are obtained with a very much less outlay of capital. If he can succeed in establishing this fact, he will have done a great service to the agricul- tural community.

EXAMPLES OF THE LAW OF Dtsnexss.—Last week in the county court at Ross the case of liolder v. Caddick was , heard. The facts are:—The tenant, Mr. Holder, who is a ; well-known man far beyond the confines of his county, oc- ' cuoied a farm of 720 acres for seven years, at a rental of £6OO. He very greatly improved his holding, but after seven years' experience he felt compelled to apply for a re- duction of rent, failing which he gave notice that he must leave the farm. In doing so no compensation for the im- provement in its cultivation was allowed, but under the terms of his agreemect he had covenanted to pay the last , half year's rent before it was due, and that was enforced, despite the valuable stock he had upon the farm, and the fact that the value of his 51 acres of offgoing wheat crop was in Itself ample security for the half year's rent when it became due. Under the agreement he was to be paid by valuation for the clover seeds. Arbitrators were appointed, and an umpire called in, whose award was made, but not al- lowed by the landlord, who demanded the full amount of rent to be paid, thus leaving no Other resource than an ac- tion in the county court to recover the sum of £2O, the amount of the award. Up to that point the provisions of the agreement were rigidly enforced, but now mark the con- trast. In the court the agreement is called for by the land- lord, who, being a lawyer, and one who prepared his own agreement, well knew that it was in his own hands, and not tbat of his tenant, but who, when called upon to produce, raised the plea., "It is not stamped," and non-suited the tenant.—Another case is that of three years' claim for rent and arrears, the seizare and sale of a terlant's stock and affects, which realised upwards of £1,300. The whole of the rent had to be paid, and, after the expenses were de- ducted, a balance of £ll 163. is handel to other creditors, to meet their demands, amounting to £2,069,

His friend, to induce him to take greater notice of what was going on, told him how extremely difficult it was. "Diffi- cult, do you call it, sir 2" replied the doctor; "I wish it were impeseible." THE ANTI4UITY or FGYPT.—We look with a sense of strained or imperfect perfection at many of the old ecclesi- astical and other buildings in our own land. They seem to us hoary with age. But what is a duration of, say, some 800 years, compared with that of the Great Pyramid, built, according to the least ancient computation of its date, 4,2.510 years ago ? There are grave authorities which determine it to be much older. It is impossible for the mind to gra%) and realise such a space of time. When, however, we think of the witness to still more distant ages revealed by the con- struction of the Pyramid itself; when we discover by the marks of the workmen upon its materials that they were acquainted with the decimal notation; when we find enor- ' tnous blocks of stone in its interior fitted with a nicety which almost defies the search for a joint; and when we peer further into the dim past, and try to apprehend the song growth of civilisation which must have taken place before ! such finished perfection of worlizaanghip could have been reached, our nimble thought is checked. We are fairly aghast at the attempt to realise the antiquity of Egypt. It was civilised, its chronicles were kept, its kings carried on wars with armies of imported negroes, its priests conducted an elaborate ritual in gorgeous temples, its rich men em- ployed skilled painters and engravers to decorate the walls of their tombs, its courtiers—in notes which might have been penned yesterday—recorded their gratification at proofs of royal confidence, its life was full of the minutiae and eti- quette of civilisation in government, religion, science, and art, ages before what many had considered to be the dawn of history, before a word bad been written of the oldest books known to European scholars.—The Rev. Harry Jones, in "Good Words" for May. As INDIAN FOP.—Under the name of Antis are com- prised a variety of tribes, who find their home in the val- leys, and along the river-courses of the Bolivian Alps. M. " Marcoy," who visited these people, describes them as being stout in person, though less bulky than some of the Peru- vian tribes, lightish in complexion, and rather effeminate in the face. Not, however, content with the complexion which Nature has given to them, they paint the cheeks and the circle round the eyes red, and the other parts of the body exposed to the air black, the colours being in both cases de- rived from the juices of plants. They dress in a loose shirt- like garment, and are assiduous—beyond aboriginal wont— in combing their hair, which they cut short in front, and wear in long tresses on either cheek, and down their back. The Antis Indian is moreover somewhat of a fop. His toilet requisites he never parts with, but carries in a bag slung over his back. Here is an inventory of them :—A comb made of the thorns of the chonta palm; the paste (rocou) with which he paints his dusky cheeks; half of a gempa apple which supplies the dark pigment for his limbs; a tit of loOking-glass ; a ball of thread; a little bit of wax; two mussel-shells, which he uses as pincers to extract any un- ruly sign of beard or whiskers which makes its appearance (like all Indians, he looks upon facial hair as a disfigure- ment) ; his snuff-box, composed of a snail's shell; an ap- paratus for taking the snuff, made of the ends of reeds, or two of the arm-bones of a monkey, fastened together with black wax at an acute angle; with a few other trifles, pro- bably of European manufacture, rmch as scissors, knife. needles, &c. A silver coin suspended through the septum of the nose, a necklace of beads or berries, the skins of bright-plumaged birds, the claws of birds or wild animals, and such like, go to make up the Antis Indian 'a personal ornamentation. They are savages of the ordinary American type—hunters and fishers—living in open sheds in the enm- mere and in closed huts, almost hid by vegetation, and buil on the banks of streams, in the winter. Both kinds of houses are equally filthy, and, when the air cannot circulate through them, smell like the dens of wild beasts.—" The Peoples of the World."

the 26th of July, 1813. On the day following O'Connell I rose to speak for the defence. His manner at all times was bold and defiant. But when he knew the Judges were pre- determined, and the jury well and truly paceed, he was even more fierce and contemptuous. On such occasions he did not stop to argue points of law, but launched out into de- nunciation of the whole system of law and government in Ireland. It was so on this occasion. He knew that he could not save his client, and so he took all Ireland for his clients and made the Judge and the jury feel that they were the real criminals on trial. Throwing Ireland into the air, under the name of Portugal he put the Portuguese Roman Catholics in the place of the Irish Protestants, and the Portuguese Protestants in the place of the Irish Roman Catholics, and bade the jury suppose thetnselves to be Portu- guese Protestants assailed by dominant Portuguese Papists. On the canvas thus provided he drew a picture of the state of things under actual Protestant ascendancy in Ireland. He pat in vivid sketches of the chief functionaries—the Viceroy. "one of those men who imagine they govern the nations, while in reality they are but the instruments upon which the crafty play with safety and with profit ;" the Accountant-General, "some being more canine than human, who not having talents to sell, buys of the market of bigotry his impudence ;" the favourite Privy Counsellor, " some learned doctor, half lawyer, half divine, entire brute." Every man in the Court, and the Court was densely crowded, was familiar with the events which O'Connell thus described or caricatured. He had not, however, reached his climax. With the eyes of the Attorney-General glaring on him, and his own looking into the faces of the jury, those "saints" and "Members of the Society for the Suppression of Vice," he dashed with the quick fierce stroke of a Rubens into his picture a group of the men before him, with central portrait of the Attorney-General, who was prosecuting, making him figure as Chief Inquisitor in the Popish and persecuting Portugal. Magee, it so happened, was a Protes- tant, and of coarse being a Protestant in the real Ireland, he was a Papist in the imaginary Portugal. Of this circum- stance O'Connell availed himself in putting the final touches to his picture. "Gentlemen," said he, addressing the pious men in the jury box, "put yourselves as Protestants under such a persecution; behold before you this Chief Inquisitor, with his prejudiced tribunal—this gambler with a loaded die —and now say what are your feelings, what are your sensa- tions of disgust, abhorrence, affright ? But if at such a moment Some ardent and enthusiastic Papist, regardless of his interests and roused by the crimes that were thus com- mitted against you, should describe, in measured, and cau- tious, anl cold language, scenes of oppression and iniquity; If he were to describe them, not as I have done, but in feeble and mild language, and simply state the facts for your bene- fit and the instruction of the public,—if this liberal Papist for this were dragged to the Inquisition as for a crime, and menaced with a dungeon for years, good and gracious God! how would you revolt at and abominate the men who could consign him to that dungeon! With what an eye of con- tempt, and hatred, and despair, would you not look at the pecked and profligate tribunal which could direct punish- ment against him who deserved rewards! What pity would you rot feel for the Advocate who heavily and without bops laboured in his defence; and with what agonised and fren- zied despair would you not look to the future destinies of a land in which perjury was organised, and from which humanity and justice had been for ever banished. With this picture of yourselves in Portugal come home to us in Ireland. Say is that a crime when applied to Protestants which is a virtue and a merit when applied to Papists? Behold how we suffer here; and then reflect that it is peas- , cipally by reason of your prejudices against us that the Attorney-General hopes for your verdict." It may be doutatd whether a more audaci4sus passage was ever uttered in a Court of law. His pleading for the unfortunate editor, however, proved ineffectual. The liberal Protestant was , subject to fine and imprisonment. But in spite sof this con- viction and sentence, the victory in the whole contest, viewed broadly, remained with O'Connell. His speech was , not only a glowing impassioned vindication of a persecuted creed and a trampled race, but it was a terrible impeachment, a burning scathing denunciation of all their tyrannous 1 oppressions and wrongdoing of the Government. Corrup- tion, bigotry, intolerance, faction, power, trembled and quivered under the invectives of his "rough and rasping tongue." The downtrodden and persecuted took heart and hope, and from the day when he concluded that wonderful harangue until he threw his profession into the background, and devoted his energies without reserve to political agita- tion, O'Connell was the Saul among the Irish barristers, towering head and shoulders above his fellows of the gown.

BY VVILLIAINI FRANCIS. No. XIX.—DANIEL O'CONNELL. But not to Erin's coarser chief deny, Large if his faults. Time's large apology, Child of a land that ne'er had known repose, Our rights and blessings, Ireland's wrongs and woes; Hate at St. Omer's into caution drilled, In Dublin law courts subtilised and skilled, Hate in the man, whatever else appear Fickle or false, was stedfast and sincere. But with that hate a noble passion dwelt— To hate the Saxon was to love the Celt. Had that fierce railer sprung from English sires, His creed a Protestant's, his birth a Squire's No blander Pollio whom our bar affords Had graced a Woolsack or cajoled my lords. Lord Lytton. The name of Daniel O'Connell is written in very large type in the annals of his native land. The idol of one party and the ogre of another, there was never, perhaps, a man at once so hated and so loved—more madly worshipped or more fiercely denounced. While in Ireland he was regarded as "Our Patriot," as "Kerry's pride," and " Munster's glory," here in England he was familiarly known as the "Big Beggarman," who was enriching himself at the ex- pense of the poor and foolish people carried away by his clap trap. Mr. Fagan, in his Biography of O'Connell, pro- nounced him to be "the greatest man this or any other country produced ;" while the Sage of Chelsea declared him to be "one of the ugliest quacks of recent times." But time, Whose gentle influence makes a calf an ox, And brings all natural events to pass, removes us far beyond the dust and din of the battle field on which the dauntless warriors contended, and as the smoke clears away we are able to perceive how extreme and erro- neous are the decisions of contemporary writers. Somewhere between Mr. Fagan's supreme hear and Mr. Carlyle's ugliest quack ;—somewhere between the deity of one party and tire demon of the other, rests the true O'Connell. I This Illustrious Irishman was born in the year 1775—the year in which the illustrious Grattan, Ireland's most splen- did orator, and perhaps her greatest patriot, took his seat in the Irish House of Commons and commenced his glorious career of patriotism—the year in which the American Colo- nists rose in their might to shake off the dominion of the mother country. The place of his birth was called Carhan, beside the small post town of Caherciveen, in the county of Kerry. Long after, when our hero was at the summit of his power, The Times commissioner visiting the town wrote home that "there wasn't a pane of glass in the whole town." O'Connell humorously remarked that "if the Commissioner had as many pains in his belly his tongue would be more veracious, and his wanderings less erratic." Whatever the little town lacked in architectural grandeur was amply made up to O'Connell in the wealth of loveliness of his native county. Kerry, so remarkable for the richness and sublimity of its scenery, must have been a divine revelation to him. In his orations we can see with what enthusiasm he gloried in the majesty of external nature. "In his mountain home" he was, as Shell says, "encompassed with the loftiest images liberty on every side." There he could hearken to the voice of the mighty Atlantic, and watch the wild billows which, he tells us, in one of his speeches, he imagined "to roll across from the shores of Labrador as they burst in foam and spray upon our rockguarded shores." As a boy he was genial and rollicking, "of a bustling in- trepid nature, fond of physical exercises and full of pranks and playfulness." It was during this period that he narrowly escaped losing his life in an encounter with an in- furiated bull. Like his mighty namesake in after times this bull was seized with a great desire to annihilate poor Dan. He ran at him, and Dan's retreat was cat off by a high ditch. The career of the future Liberator seemed- about to be prematurely cat short. But Dan faced the taurine monster much in the same way as he was wont to face other difficulties, and he escaped. What a difference it would have made to Ireland and the Irish if that mad bull had succeeded in carrying out his wicked will, and had tossed young Dan on his horns and out of existence. When well in his teens, having received his early educa- tion in Ireland, he proceeded to the Jesuit College of St. Orner'e, in France. Here he so distinguished himself that the President, Dr. Sta.pylton, declared that "he was destined to make a remarkable figure in society." From St. ()meets he removed to Donav College, where he only stayed a few months. It is not difficult to perceive the influence which these colleges had upon his after life. Through his whole career he showed himself a devout son of the Church of Rome, and enjoyed in return the unlimited confidence of her priests. In the years 1792 and 1793 Pitt made several concessions I -- to the Catholics. One of these had a most important influ- I At the Manchester City Police Court, on Tuesday, before ence on the destiny and renown of O'Connell. Admission: Mr- C. H. Richards and Mr. P. Ferguson, A. OPKenzie, J. to the Bar was at last conceded to the Catholics. But for H. Shakespear, J. S. Rogers, and W. div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

An Omagh correspondent telegraphs that on Saturday night three shots were tired into the bedroo.n of the Rev. John Gilmore, a Presbyterian clergyman residing near Omagh. He had disputes with his tenants. The reverend gentleman was not injured. _ _

Among the parliamentary papers issued on Tuesday is a return of arrests under the Coercion Act up to March 31. The total number is 872. One of the suspects, Patrick Gordon, has since been sentenced to twelve months' impri- sonment for inciting to murder. An isquest on the body of Thomas Brady, who was shot dead on Sunday night, April 23, at Crolahemy, county Longford, was concluded on Tuesday evening' wbel the jury found that the deceased was wilfully and feloniously shot by Patrick M'Cormick, and tL,at the prisoner's brother was an accessory to his death.

Mr. Clifford Lloyd, it is reported, has received informa- tion from official sources in America that it is the intention of the Irish-American politicians to assassinate him, and that seven persons are now on their way to Ireland to carry out the threat.

Placards are posted about Dublin announcing the advent of the National Association of Ireland, which will have for its object the restoration of the ancient legislative indepen- dence of Ireland, and calling a meeting on the 15th to enrol members. The placard contains hostile referencea to the Castle officials and the present form of Government. A return issued on Wednesday, dated May 3rd, shows the number of suspects still detained in custody to be 386. Six of these, however, are temporarily released on parole. Another Parliamentary paper gives the number of nrigina- ting notices and agreements lodged in the Irish Land Com- mission and in the Civil Bill Courts respectively up to the end of March. The number lodged in the former waz 77,326, and in the latter 4,492. The Court of Queen's Bench in Dublin on Wednesday refused to interfere with the decisions of the magistrates, by which the Rey. Mr. Fehan, a R )man Catholic curate, and Mrs. Moore, a lady Land Leaguer, are imprisoned in con- nection with the agitation. The court deferred their decl- sion in an application to quash the conviction of Captain Dugmore, who is also in prison. A. lamentable affray between police and populace occurred at Ballina the other. night. The constabulary interfered with a demonstration in honour of the released prisoners, and the people attacked them with stones. At length the police tired on the crowd, and a number of persons, in- cluding several children, are reported to have been seriously wounded. The coroner's inquest on the body of the unlucky old soldier who attempted to shoot a Mayo landlord, but who was himself shot dead by his intended victim, has resulted in the following verdict :—" We tied that Patrick Jennings met his death by a bullet wound discharged from a rifle by Mr. M`Gloin, at Blackpatch, in the county Mayo, on 4tt May, 1882." Twelve of the jurors, it is stated, agreed that Mr. M`Gloin was not justified in shooting the man, two that he was.

The mail car convoying mails between Cork and Queens- town was attacked on Sunday morning at four o'clock by four men who wore crapes over their faces and carried arms. The car left Cork on .the arrival of the mail train from Dublin about half-past two, and it had reached a point of the read baween Fota, the residence of Mr. Smith Barry, and Slatty, three miles from Queenstown, when the four men, who were evidently lying in wait, came out on the road and called on the driver to halt, one of the men at the same time seizing the horse by the head. The driver was asked if he carried arms. A search was made of the car and of his person, but no weapons being found, the party retired. There was no attempt made to interfere with the mails.

BIGGAR ON FIGHTING FOR ENGIAND.—The following appears in St. James's Ga.:ette:—" Sir,—At this moment, when the attention of the world is directed to Ireland, I need add no words of mine in forwarding to you the accompany- ing letter from Mr. Joseph G. Biggar, M.P., to a discharged soldier of the Ist battalion of my regiment, who had written to the member for Cavan to bring his case—a complaint of some kind, but not connected with his regiment—before Parliament.—! am, Ivo., MARK KERR, General, Colonel The Prince Albert's Light Infantry. May 8."—" House of Com- mons, London, 7th March, 1882. Mr. John A. Henry. Sir,— Your letter of yesterday to hand. Any one who fights for England deserves to be treated as you have baen. —I am, sir yours faithfully, JosEpa G. BIGGAR." RELEASE OF MICIIAEL

Michael Davitt, the founder of the Land League was re- leased from Portland Prison on Saturday, and was met by Messrs. Parnell, Dillon, and O'Kelly, the lately incarcerated members of Parliament. Davitt is described as looking in good health, and he himself has no complaint whatever to make of his treatment in gaol. His release came upon him as a thorough surprise, as he had no recent communication whatever with the outside world. In an interview with a correspondent yesterday he said that of course his imprison- ment has not altered his views respecting Irish questions, but as regards the present situation Davitt had nothing to say, as he has had no means of knowing what has taken place. He himself fully expected another two years' incar- ceration. At the same time, he complains strongly of being released on a ticket-of-leave, the conditions attached to which are extremely irksome and onerous, including one that he is not to be out of doors after ten o'clock at night. In an interview with a reporter Davitt asserted his deter- mination not to feel himself in any way fettered by the conditions of his license. RECEPTION OF THE IVEW VICEROY AND SECRETARY.
