div.head: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

The French Divorce Bill has been read in the Chamber of Deputies a first time by a majority of 334 against 124. Great rejoicings have taken place in Germany in con- sequence of the birth of a son to Prince William, the first heir born to the Modern German Empire. The Bacchante, with the Royal Princes on board, has arrived safely in the port of Athens, in Greece, and his Majesty the King has received them with all due honour. A terrible colliery accident occured at Bochum, in Prussia, on Thursday morning, the result of an explosion of fire- damp. Fifty-six bodies have already been recovered, but the extent of the fatality is not yet ascertained. 1 Berlin correspondent hears on good authority that the coronation of the Czar in Moscow is definitely given up, as the authorities are unable to guarantee the safety of the Emperor. The Governor-General of Turkestan reports that 8,000 Chinese troops, armed with weapons of European make and led by able commanders, have occupied the Kuldja territory recently evacuated by the Russians. It is reported that the English Minister at the Court of Morocco has been stoned by a large number of Moors while he was taking a stroll along the high street of the capital. The Sultan has in consequence imprisoned, it is said, 600 men.

The Supreme Court of the United States has found that the court-martial has full power to try Sergeant Mason, the man who shot at Guiteau while he was in prison. The court accordingly refused the petition of habeas corpus made in Mason's behalf, and discharged the rule to show cause. The other day the King of Greece turned the first sod of the new canal to be constructed through the Isthmus of Corinth, in presence of about 5,000 of his subjects. The event was celebrated with manifestations of great rejoicing throughout the kingdom. The fittings of the magnificent stables which were built in Paris during the reign of the late Emperor Napoleon, were sold at the Louvre last Friday, and the stables themselves have been converted into storehouses for the statutes and marbles for wkich room cannot be found in the galleries of the Louvre.

Dr. Newald, the ex-Burgomaster of 'Vienna, has been ac- quitted of the charges brought against him in connection with the conflagration of the Ring Theatre. After enduring a vast amount of obloquy, he had the satisfaction of hearing the Public Prosecutor admit that on the evidence no charge against him could be sustained. Reports from Catalonia represent that cotrplete tranquility reigns throughout the province, notwithstancing the reports which had been industriously circulated to the effect that disturbances might be apprehended after the approval by the Cortes of the Franco-Spanish commercial treaty. Anti-Jewish riots have taken place at Alexandria, in the government of Cherson, where a mob of several hundred people wrecked some houses belonging to Jews. An attack has also been made on the Jewish inhabitants, some 3,000 in number, of the Russo-Polish town of Yombin, in the same way as their co-religionists in Belts. A panic is re- ported to exist among the Jewish inhabitants of Baits. According to a telegram received from Cronstadt, the equipment of war vessels for the Pacific is being carried on with increased activity. It is stated that in the course of the next six months fourteen ships, capable of carrying al- together 8,000 troops, will be stationed in the Russian Paci- fic ports. The agitation which exists in Zululand is said to be largely owing to a message, purporting to come from Cete• wayo, stating that he would socn be re-instated at Ulundi, and that the chiefs must prepare to meet him at Maritzburg. This message, says the correspondent of the Daily Nees, is explicitly stated to have come from Colenso. John Dunn, says the same authority, has returned hastily to Zululand, and is "threatening vengeance against the chiefs who com- plained of hirn."___

div.head: BURMESE EMBASSY.
div.p: THE BURMESE EMBASSY.

A telegram from Calcutta states that Mahommrd Afzul, the Indian officer who has been selected for the post to which Major Cavagnari was appointed, left Simla for Cabul on Thursday. The Burmese Embassy at Simla has had a cool reception at Simla. The Times correspondent says : It is reported that the Embassy are anxious to cement friendly relations; but in view of the recent reports of, wholesale executions at Mandalay, the Indian Government will necessarily be very slow to enter into treaty negotia- tions until these reports are negatived." There is a rumour, telegraphed from Rangoon, to the effect that, together with certain Armenians, some British subjects have been seized and illtreated, among others the wife of the commander of a flotilla steamer; but this report requires official confirma- tion. Our present diplomatic relations with Mandalay, says the correspondent, are certainly embarrassing on both sides. The Government are believed to be desirous to entertain proposals, if they be feasible, for the reopening of the ques- tion of a British Agency at Mandalay. THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION.

The Khedive has signed a decree commuting into simple exile the sentence of the court-martial upon the Circassian officers and their accomplices. It is added that with regard to the Circassian officets the Sultan, not knowing whether their guilt had been fully proven, demanded communica- tions of the whole of the documents submitted to the court- martial.

Intelligence has reached Cairo that the "Propket" Mabdi, who recently defeated the Egyptian troops in the Soudan, has been killed and his troops dispersed. A belief is expressed at Cairo that the Egyptian Govern- ment has ordered troops from the Abyssinian frontier to march west, and that there are already 35,000 soldiers in the Soudan. .

Latest accounts show that the position of affairs at Cairo is very critical, and in a short time we shall see whether Ourah'i Pasha or the Khedive is the head of the State. The Ministry complained strongly to the Khedive of his decree commuting the sentences on the Circassians who had, as it was alleged, conspired against Ourabi Pasha. The foreign Consuls were summoned to the Palace on Tuesday, and the Khedive informed them that the Premier had used insulting language towards him, and had let fall threatening hints with regard to the European community in Egypt. The Premier, en being interrogated by the Consuls, repudiated the interpretation which had been put upon his language, and said he was about to resign. There is a report that the Ministry are about to ask the Chamber of Notables to depose the Khedive if he should refuse to accept Ourabi Pasha as President of the Council of Ministers. The aspect of affairs is so serious that we are inclined to credit the report that some of the Consuls have requested their Governments to send iron-clads to Alexandria. The Snitan has a strong desire to intervene; and he has "sounded" the Ger-

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 13, 1852.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 13, 1852.

' man Foreign Office, but has been advised to come to an ar- rangement with England and France. The crisis in Egypt has suddenly ly-Totne acute. The Ministry, acting in direct violation of the organic law which they nersuadtd the Khedive some months ago to sign, have summoned a meeting of the Chamber of Notables without having obtained the sanction of the Khedive, and they make no secret of their intention to dismiss His Highness. They have assured the Foreign Consuls that the person of the Khedive is sacred, but little teliance can be placed on assurances given at the beginning of a struggle. There has been no outbreak either at Cairo or Alexandria. The situa- tion was the subject of an interpellation in the French Chamber on Thursday. M. de Freycinet stated that the Cabinet were fully prepared to act up to their responsibili- ties in the matter. It might be that the complications which were arising would affect European interests, and in that case it would be necessary to consult the Powers, who, however, recognised the preponderent influence of England and France at Cairo.
A large schooner capsized on the Thames, on Wednesday, and one of her crew was drowned.

The Hon, F. Hanbury Tracy, M.P., who has been suffer- ing from an attack of smallpox, is now recovering. Mr. J. G. Holyoake has received a grant of £lOO from the Premier in order to visit America to report on co-operation. At a meeting of the Salford School Board, on Wednesday, it was resolved to estabish a day and industrial school in the barough_if.suitable premises could be found.

In view of the recent events, the Conservative party have reprinted and are widely circulating the memorable letter on the Irish question which the late Lord Beaconsfield addressed to the Duke of Marlborough on the eve of the general election in 1880._ _

In the Queen's Bench Division. Westminster, on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Field, a special jury gave damages, £3OO, against The Referee newspaper for a libel accusing the pro- prietor of the Pavilion Music Hall of having permitted in- decent_songs to be sung in his establishment.

In the tipper House of Convocation, on Tuesday, the Archbishop of Canterbury stated that after conferring with the Archbishop of York it hadben decided to submit a short Act of Parliament to effect the release of the Rev. S. F. Green, now imprisoned under a writ of de contumace eapiendo. On Tuesday morning a destructive fire occurred at the Woodside Mill, Great Leaver, belonging to Messrs. J. Har- wood and Son. It originated in the cotton-mixing room, and spread to the room above, in which 100 bales of cotton were stored. The damage is estimated at £l,OOO, which is covered by insurance. Mr. Dugdale, of Merevale Hall, and Mr. Pogmore, solicitor, two of the gallant " explorers " who attempted to save the men entombed in the Baxterley pit, have died from the injuries they received. The number of dead among the exploring party now exceeds that of the men who were lost in the first explosion. The death is announced of the Rev. Dr. Steane, who for very many years was associated as a leading spirit with several of the chief religious organi-ations of the day. Dr. Steane was a Baptist. He was officially connected with the Baptist Union, but as the founder in 1845 and since as a principal supporter of the Evangelical Alliance he was most widely known and generally esteemed. On Wednesday morning, Redland House, Glasgow, the residence of ex-Lord Dean of Guild Minces, was totally destroyed by fire. It has not been ascertained how the fire originated, but it spread with such fearful rapidity that in about an hour the house was completely gutted, and only a portion of the furniture was saved. The damage is esti- mated at about £15,000, and is partly insured. The Daily Telecpapli says it is understood that the Gov- ernment has now definitively decided to refrain from ' attempting to pass the closure by a bare majority, and that it will accept Mr. Gibson's amendment to the First Rule of Procedure, which provides that no debate shall close until the evident sense of two-thirds of the House shall be in favour of its ending. On Wednesday night a crowded meeting was held in St. James's Hall, London, to protest against the continued ex- clusion of Mr. Bradlaugh from the House of Commons. Mr. Bradlaugh said the ckance of his case being determined this session had no relation to his duty and his determination to take his seat when his constituents gave him their mandate. In spite of opposition' he meant to fight the question in eve y way, and his friends had made up their minds he should not be made bankrupt. Resolutions in support were passed. INTIMIDATION BY APPRENTICES.-At the Glasgow Police Court, on Tuesday, 18 apprentice lads, in the employment of the Caledonian Railway Company at their engine works, I were charged with a breach of the peace and intimidation. The majority of the men are out on strike, but a few re- turned to work. The prisoners entered the premises and created a disturbance, and carried the men out in the street. IFour of the prisoners were fined two guineas each, and the others wore dismissed.

COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN SOUTH WALBS.—A Pontypridd correspondent reports a serious explosion of gas which oc- curred on Tuesday afternoon at the Crown Level Colliery, Neweby, Rhondda Valley. Mr. S. W. Kelly, of Cardiff, the owner, and Mr. Harris, manager at the colliery, and .three men were in the workings, the two former making explora- tions in a disused section, when suddenly an accumulation of gas ignited. Both Mr. Kelly and Mr. Harris were very badly hurt, but no others were injured. The Coroner for North Stafford held an inquest at Hanley on Tuesday on Joseph Griffiths, butty at Berry Hill Col- liery, who met with his death by falling down the pit shaft. On Monday the deceased was being drawn up the pit at a rapid rate, when he overbalanced himself and fell out of the cage, dropping a distance of over 100 yards. He was killed instantaneously. This is the third fatal accident in pit shafts in the district during the last fortnight. Verdict, "Acci- dental death."

TRE PRESS ASSOCIATION—The annual meeting of the Press Association, Limited, was held on Tuesday, presided over by Mr. John Feeney, of the Birmingham Daily Post. The annual report and balance sheet were unanimously adopted, on the motion of the chairman; and Mr. W. W. Hargrove. of the York Herald, was elected a member of the commit- tee of m inagement in place of Mr. Spark, of the Leeds Ex- press, who retired by rotation. Mr. Spark was chosen a member of the consultative board, vice Mr. Leng, of the .Thindee Advertiser. The proceedings concluded with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

NORTH-WEST RIDING ELECTION.—Both parties are ac- tively engaged in preparing for the forthcoming contest. The Liberal candidate is Mr. I. Holden, and the Conserva- tive candidate is Mr. Gathorne Hardy. The contest is expected to he a severe one. At a meeting of the leaders of the Conservative party on Wednesday, it was decided not to employ paid eanvasnrs, but to Make an effort to enlist volunteers in the work. The Conservative party will hold an aggregate meeting in St. George's Hall on Monday night, and the Liberal party on Tuesday night. It is stated that the claims of the candidates will be advocated by pro- minent members of the opposite parties from other districts of the county. COMPULSORY ATTENDANCE AT BOARD SCHOOLS.—On Wednesday afternoon the chairman and several leading members of the London school Board and other boards had an interview with Mr. Alundella at the Education Depart- ment. The deputation stated that the Summary Jurisdic- tion Act had worked very mysteriously so far as the enforce- ment of compulsory attendance wasconcerned. They desired a return to the old and successful system in which impri- sonment followed non-payment of the fine, and under which ' not more than one or two per cent, of defendants accepted that alternative for even a portion of the time to which they ' were committed. Mr. Mundella said that what the deputa- tion had told him was merely an echo of what he was hear- ing every day in that department. He believed that on the whole summary procedure had worked exceedingly well for the purpose for which it was mainly intended. He felt quite as strongly as the deputation the necessity for re- verting to the former state of things as administered under the Small Penalties Act, or that a measure should be intro- duced which would allow the school attendance to be enforced in a much more summary manner. He would not fail to give the matter the best attention in his power, and to represent it in the proper quarter. SUICIDE IN GAOL: A SAD CASE.—On Monday evening an inquest was held in Preston Gaol, by Mr. Gilbertson, coroner, on the body of William Clegg, aged 40 years, who had been committed flom Accrington on the 27th April for an aggravated assault on his wife. On Saturday morning last the deceased was accused of idleness, and the governor of the gaol found that he bad done no work (picking cotton) since his admission. He therefore sent him to be confined to his cell for one day on bread and water. Shortly bAore , six o'clock, however, he was found by William Kitchen, a , warder, banging from the bell handle behind the door, being suspended with a handkerchief and towel. His knees were bent, and were only about four inches from the floor. Alice ' Clegg, widow of the deceased, said he had been seven or eight weeks out of work, and was very low spirited in con- sequence. She had had some lotion from Blackburn In- firmary, and had tried several times to drink it. He had told her her "dove were numbered," and it was becaused he tried to strangle her that he was sent to gaol. The jury returned a verdict of "Temporary insanity.'

FOUR TRIALS FOR ATTEMPTED MURDERS.—At Warwick Assizes, on Tuesday, Mr. Justice Stephen disposed of four attempted murders. Herbert Allen, 25, was indicted for shooting at Rose Hatton, parlour maid, at Lellington Manor, Leamington. The prisoner visited the prosecutrix whom he had courted four years. Suddenly he seized her by the throat, and placed a revolver at her heart. The prosecutrix diverted the barrel, and whilst struggling the pistol exploded. The bullet struck a wall. Assistance arrived, and the pri- soner was disarmed. The jury acquitted the accused, who pleaded guilty to a common assault, and was sentenced to twelve months imprisonment, the heaviest punishment the judge could inflict.—George Tidman was similarly indicted for attempting to kill his sweetheart at Walsbrove-on-Sow, Coventry. The prisoner threw the prosecutris upon the floor, and was drawing a knife across her throat, when her mother providentially entered and placed upon her daughters neck her hand, which was badly injured. The prisoner re- gretted that the wound was not on the prosecutor's throat. His Lordship sentenced the prisoner to 20 years' penal ser- vitude.—Clara Humphries, recently cook at Illington Vicarage, was rentenced to five years' penal servitude for attempting to murder her illegitimate infant. She tied a broad piece of tape tightly round its neck, and the child was nearly strangled when discovered in her box.—Annie Burger, 24, was acquitted of attempting to poison her two children at Birmingham with bichromate of potash.

The TOTE DOCTRINE OF RECENT POSSESSION.—T doctrine of " recent possession," on which men have often been con- victed in the courts of law, received a rude shock at Liver- pool the other day. A man was placed on his trial for steal- ing jewellery from a house. There was no proof that ho had committed the burglary, but a few days after the robbery he was found endeavouring to pawn some of the stolen property. His defence was that it had been given to him by a man who could not be produced. The prisoner had shown some "nervousness " about the matter by send- ing another man into the pawnbroker's shop to arrange as to the ph- dge. Mr. Justice Cave thought that the evidence was insufficient, and the jury acquitted the prisoner, who could scarcely have believed in his good fortune. The three men charged with the jewellery robbery in Hulme were tried before the same learned Judge. Two of thorn, who had been seen to come out of a place in which a large quantity of the stolen property was found immediately afterwards, were acquitted by direction of the Judge, who held that there was no evidence of minty knowledge. Nobody bad seen the prisoners place the property where it was found. The result of the cast recalls the famous decision—which we do not believe will be found in any law book—of a" lay" magistrate in the case of a man who was charged with stealing. "Six witnesses," said the prisoner's counsel, " have sworn that they saw my client steal the watch. I can bring one hundred and fifty who will swear that they did not see him steal it." "In that case," the magistrate is alleged to have said, "lot him be discharged at once."

The Pennsylvania Republicans have nominated Mr. James A. Beaver as the candidate for the Governorship of the tate A return of the Irish agrarian outrages during April gives the number as 462. This includes two cases of murder and 1701 firing into dwellings.
The lloY-al Mines Commissioners resumed experiments at Rhondda Valley on Thursday morning. It has been ascer- tained that South Wales gas is less explosive than that of the Lancashire coal fields.

As the result of the Board of Trade Inquiry in Liverpool respecting the loss of the steamship City of London, the court found there was no evidence to lead to any conclusion on the cause of the disaster.

The hearing of the action brought by Mr. Victor Emanuel St3vens, "diplomatist in private life," against Madame Patti for services rendered in " mitigating" tradesmen's bills, re- sulted on Thursday in a verdict for the defendant. On Thursday afternoon, Mr. J. C. Mooreville, of Smith's- lane, King-street West, Manchester, was walking along Roebuck-lane, Sale, when he suddenly fell down uncon- scious. He was taken to a neighbouring house, where he shortly afterwards expired. Death is supposed to have re- sulted from apoplexy. The Press Association learns that Mr. Parnell has applied to the Home secretary for, and has obtained police protec- tion, his friends feeling, in consequence of the rumours that are current and the threatening letters received, that he is a marked man.

Two more deaths have been added to the. long death list from the recent disastrous explosion at the' Baxterley Col- liery, Amos Ball and Joseph Ball, two of the ill-fated exploring party, having succumbed during Wednesday night. This brings up the total, inclusive of the nine unfortunate men still entombed in the workings, to 27 deaths. Many others are in a dying state.

Among the i'ariiamentary papers issued on Thursday morning is a copy of the document sent to the Speaker in the action by Mr. Guerney, of Northampton, against Mr. B,adlaugh for illegally sitting and voting. In acknow- ledging receipt of the pleadings, the Speaker says that he sees no reason for interfering with the proceedings now pending.

It was reported on Thursday morning to the Glasgow police, on Wednesday night, Rose:Ann Mackie, or Hart, aged 56, residing in Coatbridge, was burned to death in the house of her son, in Glaagow. Whilst the son's wife was absent, the old woman approached too near the fire. Her clothes ignited, and she was at once enveloped in flames. When the daughter-in-law returned she threw water upon her,but the 01l woman immediately died. The nomination for the Border Burghs has been fixed for Wednesday next, and the polling, if any, for the following Monday. It is expected, however, that Mr. Trevelyan, whose appointment as Chief secretary • for Ireland in suc- cession to Lord F. Cavendish has everywhere been so well received, will be re-elected without opposition. At the general election Mr. Trevelyan polled 3,518 votes against his opponent's 553. _

. . CITY OF GLASGOW BAN.—A crowded meeting of the shareholders of the City of Glasgow Bank was held on Thursday in Glasgow. It was unanimously agreed to form an assets company, whose main object is to close the liqui- dation, pay the remaining liabilities of the bank, and also save the assets from forcible realisation. Mr. James Boyd, who presided, said many shareholders had suffered from the failure of the bank, some being dead, some in lunatic asy- lums, and many impoverished. _ _

MR. GLADSTONE AND LOW. TAX&TION.—At Lewisham District Board of Works, on Thursday, the following reply was read from Mr. Gladstone to a memorial on the subject of local taxation :—" Sir,—Mr. Gladstone has received the memorial addressed to him by the Board of Workz for Lewis- ham district. and I am to request that you will point out to that board that reference to the speeches from the Throne will show that Her Majesty's Government were anxious, but for delays in public business which have unhappily occurred, to legislate comprehensively in connection with this question daring the present session." TRIAL OF TIIE SKYE CROFTERS —1 he trial of the Sky e crofters took place at Inverness, on Thursday. On the in- terference of counsel they were tried for assault only. Sheriff Blain, the presiding judge, found all five guilty, but in dif- ferent degree. Donald Nicholson and Alexander Finlayson ' were sentenced to pay 50s. each, or a month's imprison- meat; James Nicholson, Malcolm Finlayson, and Peter Macdonald 205., or fourteen days. A cheque was handed in by sympathisers of the prisonera, and paid under protest, so as to keep the case open for appeal to the High Court of Justiciary if deemed expedient. William Bradburn, coke-burner, Farnworth, was charged at Bolton, on Thursday, with murdering Phcebe Hardy, 17, his step-daughter, and *Peter Bradburn, 9, his son, by cutting their throats while asleep in bed. Prisoner was in a weak c ,ndition and accommodated with a seat. Shortly after the proceedings commenced he was seized with a fit. His hands were pinioned to prevent him tearing the bandages from the wounds he had inflicted in his throat. The evidence was the same as at the inquest. The prisoner was committed for trial.

Shortly after noon on Thursday, as a cigboat belonging to Seacombe, and the property of John Henry, was crossing the river from the Birkenhead Great Float, it caught the bow of the City of Rome, lying anchored in mid-stream, and outward bound. The boat "shouldered," and a man named Gallagher, being thrown out, was drowned. His companion bated the water out, and made his way to the Waterloo steps, where he landed.

Aaron Leedham, grinder, Sheffield, is in custody on a charge of assaulting his wife. The latter states that last Jou her husband confessed to her that in October, 185 G, he, with his father (since dead) and an Attercliffe man, whom he named, helped to murder John Whittaker, a cattle dealer, of Maryburg, near Rotherham. Whittaker, on returning from York market, was attacked near his own farm and savagely beaten by three men. He crawled home but died. The police have traced a watch supposed to be decea.sed's to a relative of the prisoner. Prisoner's wife states that Leed- ham has been very uneasy since his confession. DEATH OF A WELL-KNOWN AUTHOR.-Dr. John Brown, author of " Rab and his Friends," died at his residence, Rutland-street, Edinburgh, on Thursday, in the 71st year of his age. Dr. Brown was going about till last Saturday, when he was seized with inflammation of the lungs. Nothing serious was anticipated till Wednesday, when the deceased rapidly sank, and expired about half-past six on Thursday morning. Within the past few years he published two volumes, one entitled "John Leech and other Papers," and the other " Locke Sydenhan and other Papers," Thdl former is already in its third edition.

DEATH OF THE PREMIER BARONET OF ENGLAND.— The death is announced as having taken place on Monday, at the age of 56, of Sir Edwin Hare Dashwood, of West Wycombe, Bucks, the premier Baronet of England. The deceased was born in September, 1823, and served for some time in the army, retiring from.the service with the rank of captain. He succeeded to the baronetcy, as seventh baronet, on the death of his uncle, in 1863, having married, in 1853, Roberta Henrietta, fourth daughter of Sir Robert Aber- cromby, of Birkenborg, fifth baronet. He :eaves issue, and is succeeded in the title by his eldest son, Edward Aber- cromby Dashwood, who was born at Nelson, New Zealand, in October, 1854. Mr. Pollard, the solicitor for the Treasury, has advised that the whole of the prisoners at present in custody for conspiring to defraud by carrying on the next-of-kin agency in various towns throughout the kingdom should be tried together at Manchester, where four of them are already in custody. In accordance with this an application was on Thursday made to the Birmingham stipendiary to remand to that city the Birmingham manager, Edward Beeton, who was arrested three weeks ago. The solicitor for the prosecu- tion stated that this was the result of an interview he had had with Mr. Pollarl on Monday last. The prisoner asked that the Birmingham charge should be withdrawn ; but the stiptndiary ordered that he should be remanded until the arrival of the warrant from Manchester. MR. JUSTICE NORTH AND HIS DECISIONS.—Mr. Justice North has been pretty severely handled by the Judges of Appeal for a decision given by him in the case of Cowen a. Hulton. It was sought on the part of the plaintiff, who is owner of the Newcastle Chronicle, to prevent the sale in that town of a newspaper called the Sporting Chronicle, on the ground of infringement of title. The latter print, which is a mere record of racing and other sporting events, is issued in ieveral towns in the kingdom, including Liverpool, Man- chester, Leeds, and Newcastle. Mr. Justice Field North granted an injunction stopping its sale, but the decision has ben overruled by the Lord Justices, with expressions of sur- prise as to how such a judgment could ever have been given. The two papers are entirely dissimilar in form, make- up, time of publication, in character, and in their contents, and, in fact, as the Master of the Rolls said, it was simply impossible to see how anyone who did not deserve the name of an idiot could be induced to purchase the one paper for the other. Lord Justice biker capped this by remarking that an injunction might as well have been applied for restrain- ing the defendant from using any of the letters of the alphabet. There was not the shadow of an attempt to show that the owners of the sporting paper had ever sought to deceive the public by the use of the word" Chronicle," and under these circumstances the injunction was dissolved. DR. MACFADTEN ON DISESTABLISHMENT.—In his address to the Congregational Union, on Tuesday, the President (the Rev. Dr. Macfadyen, of Manchester) said their Churches disputed the title of no Church to exist; they only denied the right of any sect to attempt the life of its fellows. They regarded disestablishment as a "consummation devoutly to be wished ;" yet they were not battling for relief from per- sonal disabilities, but for the first principles of the kingdom of Christ. Their Churches were an attempt to express the yearnings of the heart of man for that kingdom and to realise that in outward form. What the Romanist claimed for his Church Congregationalists claimed for their ChurcheS; they accepted his affirmation, but applied them differently. It was only by proving practically to England that their Churches could do the nation's work that they could persuade her to accept their ideal ; she was at this moment hesitating about disestablishment because she was not convinced that the free Churches of the country were competent to supply the religious needs of the people. He did not see that they could blame for not accepting their own ideal men who did not profess to hold spiritual views of the nature of the kingdom of Ohrist, and he was not sure that they ought to ask these persons to do so until they justify their faith by their works. The rev. gentle- man proceeded to argue that Cangregationalism could do national work, and said they were now addressing them- selves—late, but Not, he trusted, too late—by united effort to bring the Gospel and its blessed influence to the homes of their countrymen. They heard much to the effect that Eng- land was Ephraim, and that the promises made to Ephraim applied to England. Would that they heard more of the denunciations addressed to Ephraim being applicable to Eng- land. They were living in a fool's paradise if they did not lay the warnings to heart. England was worth saving, and "saving her we help to save mankind."

MRS, RIPPON ON THE "DRESS OF THE PERIOD." The following as a continuation of Mrs. Rippon's article on the "Dress of the period."—Apropos of our subject is a passage from a story of Charles Reade's, entitled " A Simpleton," where a sensible doctor is called in to attend the heroine, with whom he is in love :—The examination was concluded. Dr. Staines looked at Rosa, and then at her father. The agony in that aged face, and the love that agony implied, won him, and it was to the parent he turned to give the verdict. "The hemorrhage is from the lungs." Lusignan interrupted him. "From the lungs ? " cried he in dismay. " Yes a slight congestion of the lungs." "But not incurable? 01! not incurable, doctor ? " " Heaven ' forbid ! It is curable—easily—by removing the cause." "And what is the cause?" "The cause---" he hesitated, and looked rather uneasy; "Well, the cause, sir, is—tight stays." The tranquility of the meeting was instantly tils- turbed. "Tight stays! me ! " cried Rosa. "Why I am the loosest girl in England. Look, papa! " And, without any apparent effort, she drew herself in, and poked her little fist between her sash and her gown. " There ! " Dr. Staines smiled sadly and a little sarcastically: he was evidently shy of encountering the lady in this argument; but he was more at his ease with her father; so he turned towards him and lectured him freely. "That is wonderful, sir ; and the first four or five female patients that favoured me with it, made me disbelieve my other senses; but Miss Lusignan is now about the thirtieth who has shown me that marvellous feat, with a calm countenance that belies the Herculean effort. Nature has her every-day miracles; a boa-constructor, diameter seventeen inches, can swallow a buffalo; a woman with her stays bisecting her almost, and lacerating her skin can yet for one moment make herself seem slack, to deceive, a juvenile physician. The snake is the miracle of ex- pansion; the woman is the prodigy of contraction." "Highly grateful for the comparison ! " said Rosa. "Women and snakes ! " Dr. Staines blushed, and looked un- comfortable. "I did not mean to be offensive; it certainly was a very clumsy comparison." "What does that matter ?" said Mr. Luaignan, impatiently. "Be quiet, Rosa, and let Dr. Staines and me talk sense. "Oh ! then lam nobody in the business ! "said this wise young lady. "You are everybody," said Dr. Staines, soothingly. "But," suggested he, obsequiously, "if you don't mind, I would rather explain my views to your father—on this one subject." "And a pretty subject it is." Dr. Staines then invited Mr. Lusignan to his lodgings, and promised to explain the matter anatomi- cally. "Meantime," said he, "would you be good enough to put your hands to my waist, as I did to the patient's." Mr. Lusignan complied, and the patient began to titter - directly, to put them out of countenance. "Please observe what takes place when I draw a full breath. Now apply the same test to the patient. Breathe your best, please, Miss Lusignan." The patient put on a face full of saucy mutiny. "To oblige us both." "Oh, how tiresome !" "I am aware it is rather laborious," said Staines, a little dryly; "but to oblige your father." "Oh, anything to oblige papa," said she, spitefully. "There !—and Ido hope it will be the last— Is! no; I don't hope that neither." Dr. Staines politely ignored her little attempts to interrupt the argument. " You found, sir, that the muscles of my waist, and my intercostal ribs themselves, rose and fell with each inhalation and exhalation of air by the the lungs." " I did; but my daughter's waist was like dead wood, and so were her lower ribs." At this volunteer statement Rosa coloured to her temples. "Thanks, papa. Pack me off to London, and sell me for a big doll!' "In other words," said the lecturer, mild and pertinacious, "with us the lungs have room to blow, and the whole bony frame expands elastic with them, like the woodwork of a black- smith's bellows; but with this patient and many of her sex, that noble and divinely-framed bellows is crippled and con- fined by a powerful machine of human construction so it works lamely and feebly. Consequently, too little air, and, of course, too little oxygen, passes through that spongy organ whose very life is air. Now mark the special result in this case. Being otherwise healthy and vigorous, our patient's system sends into the lungs more blood than that crippled organ can deal with ; a small quantity becomes ex- travasated at odd times; it accumulates, and would become dangerous; then nature, strengthened by sleep and by some hours' relief from the diabolical engine, makes an effort, and flings it off; that is why the hemorrhage comes in the morn- ing, and why she is the better for it, feeling neither faint nor sick, but relieved of a weight. This, sir, is the rationale of the complaint, and it is to you I Must look for the cure. To judge from my other female patients, and from the few words Miss Lusignan has let fall, I fear we must not count on very hearty co-operation from her. But you are her father, and have great authority. I conjure you to use it to the full, as you once used it—to my sorrow—in this very room. lam forgetting my character. I was asked here only as her physician. Good evening." As he seemed in no hurry to repeat his visit, Mr. Lusignan called on him and said, politely, lie had hoped to receive another call ere this. "Personally," said he, "I was mach struck with your obser- vations; but my daughter is afraid she will catch cold if she leaves off her corset, and that you know, might be very serious." Dr. Staines groaned, and, when he had groaned, be lectured. " Female patients are wonderfully monotonous in this matter; they have a pro- gramme of evasions ; and whether the patient is a lady or a housemaid, she seldom varies from that programme. You find her breathing life's air with half a bellows, and you tell her so. "‘ Oh, no,' says she; and does the gigantic feat of contraction we witnessed that evening at your house. But, on inquiry, you learn there is a raw red line marked in her flesh caused by cruel stays. What is that ? ' you ask, and flatter yourself you have caught her. Not a bit. 'That was the last pair. I changed them because they hurt me.' Driven out of that, they say, 'lf I leave them off I should catch my death of cold, which is equivalent to saying there is no flannel in the shops, no common sense nor needles at home." He then laid before him some large French plates, showing the organs of the human trunk, and bade him ob- serve in how short a space, and with what skill, the Creator has packed so many large yet delicate organs, so that they shall be free and secure from friction, though so close to each other. He showed him the liver, an organ weighing four pounds, and of large circumference; the lungs, a very large organ suspended in the chest and impatient in pressure; the heart, the stomach, the spleen—all of them too closely and art- fully packed to bear further compression. Having thus taken him by the eye, be took him by the mind. "Is it a small thing for the creature to say to her Creator, can pack all this egg-china better than you can,' and thereupon to jam all those vital organs close, by a powerful, a very powerful and ingenious machine? In short, he delivered so many true and pointed things on this trite subject, that the old gentleman was convinced, and begged him to come over that evening and convince Rosa. Dr. Staines shook his head dolefully, and all his fire died out of him at having to face the fair. "Reason will be wasted; authority is the only weapon. My profession and my reading have both taught me that the whole character of her sex undergoes a change the moment a man interferes with their dress. From Chaucer's day to our own, neither public satire nor private remonstrance has ever shaken any of their monstrous fashions. Easy, obliging, pliable, and weaker of will than men in other things, do but touch their dress, however objectionable, and rock is not harder, iron is not more stubborn, than these soft and yield- ing creatures. It is no earthly use my coming." . . . . We cannot give the whole of the story, but for the benefit of interested readers we may say that Rosa gave up her corsets, sewed on flannel linings," and was "seen walking miles from home and blooming as a Hebe." Having stated my objections to the dress of the period, I purpose in my next paper to describe the reform dress.

There is nothing more nourishing and warming in cold weather than a cup of really good Cocoa, but the difficulty has been to obtain it pure. This may be secured at a cost of one I.alfpenny for a large breakfast cup by using Cadbury's Cocoa Es,ence, which goes three times as far as the adulterated irsti tareby compounds ordinarily sold, the smallest pa3ket making foarteen breakfast cups of strong Cocoa.—Advt.

div.head: M lUELLANEOUS.
div.p: M lUELLANEOUS.

The proprietors of The Christian offer prizes amounting to a hundred guineas for articles on the pregent condition of the churches in relation to erangeliytic wot k. Albert Young, the Mexborough telegraph clerk, was com- mitted for trial on Saturday on the charge of writing a letter to Sir H. Ponsonby in which he threatened to assassi- nate the Queen.

At the Leeds assizes on Saturday the seven prisoners charged with being concerned in a poaching affray on the estate of Lord Middleton, at Wharram-le-Street, in which two gamekeepers were wounded, were acgaitted. The Queen visited Epping Forest on Saturday for the purpose of formally dedicating the forest to the use and en- joyment of the people for ever. An immense concourse of Londoners assembled and greeted Her Majesty with enthusiasm:-

According to the quarterly returns of the Registrar- General, the resident population of th. United Kingdom in the middle of 1882 is estimated at 35.280,299 persons; that of England and Wales at 26,406,820, of Scotland at 3,785,400, and of Ireland at 5,088,079. Edward Parker, a Farnworth bricklayer, and his wife were on Tuesday committed for trial by the Coroner for the manslaughter of their infant son. The child had died of starvation, notwithstanding the fact that the father had been in receipt of good wages. Both the accused are said to be drunkards.

Seventeen boys were on Tuesday brought before Sheriff Thomson at Aberdeen and committed for trial on a charge of having set fire to the Old Mill Reformatoty, of which they had been inmates. A series of outbreaks amongst the boys culminated on Monday in the building being set fire to. Damage to the extent of about £2,000 was done. Mr. Thomas Ivory, a well-known Scotch advocate, com- mitted suicide early on Saturday morning by leaping over Dean Bridge into the Water of Leith, a height of 120 feet. Deceased was seen to take the leap by a constable. Mr. Ivory was the son of the late Lord Ivory, one of the Lords of Session. He was a social reformer and Dissenter of some- what advanced type, and a great philanthropist. PATENTS —A parliamentary return issued on Saturday g.ives a classification of the whole receipts from the Patent Office for the financial year 1881-2, including stamps. From this it appears that of the total of £210,534, £111,060 was received in the initial stages, £29,520 of which being on petitions for letters patent, £21,500 on notices to proceed, £19.955 on warrants, £10,945 on letters patent, and £18,393 on final specifications. The Sultan has at last given his consent to the Convention with Russia for •the payment, by instalments, of the war indemnity to Russia, but the important question remains to ,be settled as to what districts shall be set apart in order that their revenue may be appropriated to the payment of the yearly sum, which is fixed at upwards of £300,000. There have been some new appointments to the Ministry, and Server Pasha is sent as Ambassador to Vienna.

Two MEN BURIED ALIVE—Two men, engaged in the unstruction of a culvert at Northampton, were on Saturday buried alive. They were working some distance from the surface when the sides burst in. One man was dragged out by- means of a rope, not much the worse for his entombment, but his companion, upon whom two to three tons of earth had fallen, died before he could be rescued. Great excite- ment prevailed in the neighbourhood whilst searching for the body of the deceased, and the police had difficulty in keeping the crowd back.

ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE AT LEEDS —A few days ago, Mr. George Polack, draper and hosier, of Upper- head-row and Briggate, discharged one of his apprentices, a lad named Lawrence Crossley, 18 years of age, for miscon- duct. This seems to have greatly disturbed the lad's peace of mind, and shortly before eleven o'clock the other morn- ing he went into the establishment and fired two shots from a pistol at Mr. Black, both taking effect. He then fired at himself. inflicting a serious wound.

LONGEVITY.—the obituary of the Times of the 6th inst. contained some noteworthy illustrations of prolonged existence in six persons, viz, four ladies and two gentlemen, whose united ages amounted to 519 years, giving an average of 86 years and six months to each. The oldest, as usual, was a lady, who had reachei the great age of 89, the youngest of the same sex being 84. The gentlemen were 88 and 82 respectively. The septuagenarians in the same obituary averaged 74 years and nine months each. Charles Balhachet (16), son of a timber merchant, Ply- mouth, who had been accustomed to practice gymnastic exercises, on Tuesday was missed by his father, who found him in a loft hanging from a beam. Apparently the deceased, being able to hang on a trapeze by his chin, was thus engaged when the rope slipped, and pressing on the windpipe produced stupefaction and ultimately death. De- ceased was of a cheerful and religious disposition. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned by the coroner's jury on Tuesday evening. THE FEARNEAUX FRAUDS.—At the Warwick Assizes, on Monday, Mary Jane Fearne.ux, aged 42, and Jas. Gething, aged 49, were charged with having obtained by false pre- tences from Edward Benyon divers sums of money to the amount of £2OO, with intent to defraud. They were further charged in conspiring to obtain the money with intention to cheat and defraud, with forging and uttering a warrant or order for payment for £5OO with intent to defraud. Lord Chief Justice Coleridge was one of the witnesses. The facts have already been published in detail. The jury returned a verdict of "Not guilty " against Gething. Fearneaux was convicted and received a sentence of seven years for the forgery and five years for misdemeanour, the sentences to run concurrently. REPORTED PLOT TO DESTROY A MANCHESTER WA'RE. ROUSE.—Th 3 Manchester city police have, within the last day or two, received information that an attempt was about to be made to destroy the warehouse of Messrs. A. and S. Henry and Co., Portland-street. They deemed the infor- mation to be so trustworthy that the Mayor communicated with Messrs. Henry, and special precautions have been taken to ensure the safety of the warehouse. Two constables in addition to the watchmen employed by the firm have been placed on duty in the immediate vicinity of the pro- perty. The reported explanation of the intended outrage is that Mr. Mitchell Henry, M.P., has by his political action incurred the displeasure of the Fenian section of the Irish party.—Manchester Guardian.

ATTEMPT TO MURDER A CHIEF CONSTAHLE.-011 MOH- day, at the Macclesfield Police Court, a shoemaker named Joseph Potts was charged with attempting to murder Mr. Sheasby, the chiEf constable of the borough. On the morn-, ing of the 27th ult. Mr. Sheasby left his house in Great King-street. He was met by Potts, who, after stating that a deceased publican was a relative of his and should have left him some money, stabbed him in the neck with a shoe- maker's knife. Potts was taken into custody. The medica: evidence showed that had the wound been a little deeper it must have proved fatal. Potts admitted that he meant to "do" for the chief constable, and said that bad be had money he would have bought a revolver and shot him. He is sub- j.ct to delusions, and is looked upon as a lunatic. The bench committed him for trial at the assizes. THE FINCHLEY MIIRDER.—The trial of John Baker, a pro- fessional thief and burglar, for the murder of a companion named Clarke in Finchley Wood, which occupied the Cen- tral Criminal Court for two days, concluded on Monday. The two men went out together on the 2nd of March for the purpose of committing a burglary, and two or three days afterwards Clarke's dead body, bearing a number of wounds, was found in a wood, near ths place where a burglary had been committed. The prisoner pleaded guilty to the charge of burglary, but denied any knowledge of the murder. The jury, after hearing the evidence, found a verdict of guilty of wilful murder without premeditation. Mr. Justice Hawkins said that amounted to a verdict of manslaughter, and sentenced the prisoner to penal servitude for the rest of his life.

IMPUDENT THEFT or £l4o.—At the Manchester City Police Court, on Monday, John Whalen, labourer, was charged on remand with stealhag, on the 19th April, four cheques of the value of £BO Bs. 11d. and £6O in gold, a bank book, and a bag the propetty of Hr. T. L. Murgatroyd, skirt and costume manufacturer, Tongue-street, Greek-street, Chorlton-on-Medlock. Detective-inspector Slater stated that he received information of the robbery about twelve o'clock on the morning of the robbery, and went in search of the prisoner. He did that in consequence of the prisoner having been employed at Mr. Murgatroyd's shop and having left his work hurriedly. He afterwards traced prisoner to Ballinasloe, and then to Queenstown. Evidence having been given in support of this statement, the prisoner was committed for trial at the sessions. When apprehended, con- tract tickets were found in his possession for the conveyance of himself and family to New York for Philadelphia, by the Inman steamer City of Berlin. DESPERATB ENCOUNTER WITH A BURGLAR.—On Mon- day, at the Leigh petty sessions, Thomas Reddington, labourer, was charged with stealing a brush on the 25th of April. About one a.m. on the day named police-constable Jordan encountered the prisoner at Lodge Farm, Atherton. Finding that the policeman was about to enter the room in which be was, the prisoner struck him on the helmet with a broom handle and seized his throat. The two men then struggled on the ground, first one and then the other being undermost, and fully a quarter of an hour elapsed before the policeman was able to blow his whistle, the prisoner being a very powerful man. At length the prisoner opened the blade of his pocketknife and with an oath threatened to stab the officer, who, having his handcuffs in his band, dealt the prisoner a terrible blow in the face with them, which rendered him unconscious, and in this state he was removed to the police station at Tyldesley and attended by a doctor, under whose advice he was taken to the workhouse. The effect of the blow was such as to cause the accused to lose the sight of his left eye. Fourteen years ago the prisoner was tried and sentenced for biting a man's nose off. The Bench sentenced him to three months' imprisonment, with hard labour.

MAJOR BOND AND MR. JESSE COLLING, M.P.—The award of the Attorney-General in the action for libel by Major Bond against Mr. Jesse Collings was published on .Saturday. On the 9th of February, Mr. Collings, in the House of Commons, gave notice of his intention to ask Mr. Forster whether his attention had been called to the resolu- tions of the Birmingham magistrates and of the Watch Committee and the Town Council, which led to Major Bond's resignation. The question was asked on the 10th of February, and Mr. Forster's answer not being satisfactory to Mr. Collings, and the rules of the House not allowing a further discussion, Mr. Collings wrote to the Times an explanatory letter, which contained the alleged libel. After the action bad been commenced it was agreed to submit the matter in dispute to the arbitration of the Attorney-General, who has found that the letter was a privileged commnnica- lion. At the same time the Attorney-General states that ho saw no ground for suggesting that Major Bend had any intention to convey a wrong impression to the Court of Quarter Sessions, the dispute in connection with which had led to his resignation,

div.p: WIGAN.

Stncrnr.—The Wigan borough coroner held an inquest on Wedn,day, .11 the body of Josq.ll Walsh, a well-known butcher in the town. The deceased left his shop to g, t shaved, but being absent some time a search was made, and he was shortly afterwards found in his own slaughter-house, suspended by a rope from the roof. It appeared that the deceased had been ill, and this had affected his mind. A verdict of "Suicide whilst in a temporary state of insanity" was returned.

TAKING A PIPE IN-TO—A- -D-ANGE-R-O-PS MINE.—John Hat. ton, a collier, pleaded guilty at Newton, on Saturday, to haying had in his possession in a mine where naked lights were prohibited, a tobacco pipe, thereby committing an offence against the Colliery Act.—Mr. Swift, who appeared for Messrs. Evans and Co., said that the pipe had been found in a pocket of defendant's coat while he was in the 'Florida" mine, at Haydock, a mine which he reminded them was the scene of a most disastrous explosion some time ago, and ono where the greatest care was required.—A fine of 20s. and ccFts was inflicted.

Cunnah.—Extensioa of the churchyard: The vicar re- ported that a letter had been received from the solicitors to the Marquis of Chohnondeley, approving of arrangement for conveyance of land required for extension of the church- yard, but in consequence of the illness of Mr. J. Ashton, the necessary documents had not been completed. After some conversation, it was resolved that a committee, consisting of the vicar, Dr. Robinson and Mr. C. E. Linaker, be appointed to take the necessary steps for completion of conveyance of land for extension of the churchyard, and report to an ad- journed meeting to be fixed by the vicar and churchwardens. —Cheshire's charity: The accounts relating to the Frod- sham and Stocklvm or Cheshire's charity were produced by Mr. Henry Linaker, from which it appeared that the sum of £l2 had been received and disbursed during the p ist year. —Lay representatives: Mr. John Ashton and Dr. Robinson were appointed lay representatives at the ruri-decanal con. ference.

A RAMBLE IN THE VICINITY OF EAR LESTOWN. [BY A ROVING CORRESPONDENT.] To enjoy the fine Spring weather on Saturday, we took a stroll by the river SAnkey, crossing its inky waters by the footbridge at the entrance to the dell. Here the wird hyacinth grows in profusion, and a few weeks hence the air will be fragrant with oerfume and.the scent of the hawthorn blossom. 'Just now the throstle is making melody, a lark is soaring and singing, a swallow skims along, and the caw of a crow is heard, and a confused twittering of birds. The Sankey paper mills, lockhouse, coal wharfs, sugar and wazon works, and the nine arches are h,fore us. Rifle shooting on Parr Moss and the thud of the steam hammer at the Viaduct are heard mingled with the chirping of sparrows. Taking the field path at the head of the lane, we cannot but be struck by the good ploughing and even sowing of the grow- ing corn on each side of the pathway and high hedge. Standing at the turning of the path to look at a passing train on the Viaduct, of which there is a picture some fifty years old in a friend's house, the cuckoo suddenly flew past, and within a very few yards of us, uttering its peculiar cry by which it is known (and its onomatopoetic) in all lands and languages; and it seemed as much startled by our ap- pearance as we were surprised by it, for this harbinger of summer is a shy bird, often heard, but seldom seen. And it had had something to do with the confused sounds heard in the plantation from which it was making its way to the next in Burtonwood, for it is by no means an acceptable friend to other birds, having an evil propensity for lay- ing its eggs in other birds' nests, and which has given birth to the very English word cuckold, which requires no further explanation. Discussions often rise as to the form and coleur of the cuckoo. To us it seemed a long-tailed, reddish-grey bird, like a pigeon, as indeed it belongs to that order, and it was alone, unless the bird far-a- field was another, but we think that was a plover, for we heard its pee-weep as we continued our walk. The earliest mention of the cuckoo to be found in English literature is in a Harleian MSS. of date 1240. It is a pastorale,and,although we cannot give the music to which it is set, here we may give a verbal translation of the early English in which it is written, from A. J. Eliss's learned work en that sub- ject : " Bummer has come In, loudly sing, cuckoo! Grows seed and blossoms mead, alid springs the wood now sing cuckoo! Ewe bleats after lamb lows after (its) calf (the) cow, Bullock leaps, buck ve:•ts (seeks the green) merrily s'ng cuckoo! Cock o, cuckoo! Well singost thou, cuckoo! Cease thou not :.ever now. Fing cuckoo, now! Sing cuclico Sing cuckoo! Sing cuckoo, now." The song is for a tenor, and the musical interval of the cry is a descending minor third (first descending and then ascending), the notes being f, doe. There is a popular belief, or free, that in whatever direction one may be look- ing when first he hears the cuckoo, he will, before summer is over, travel in that direction. As we were looking North- east at the new railway bridge in E irlestown,now approach- ing completion, and of which there is a fine view, it may be true as we hope te return there h a few hours, put if furEher, then we have some hopes of seeirig a braw-tra* town in the far far north. After gazing at Bil tinge Hill, of which, owing to the clarity of the atmosphere after the storm, there is a very fine view, we turn right about face and walk onward to Bradley, the Most House of the Leghs of Lyme, and original home of the yeomen of that name, who won lands and honours under the Black Prince at Crecy. However that may be, we ourselves, have heard the very last owner of these lands of that name speak of the glories of Agincourt with the fire and fervour of youth, when speaking to the Newton Volunteers at Lyme Hall, in Cheshire, where the present representative lives, and when the spirit which caused his grandfather to raise a regiment for the Government in Peninsular war tinle' seemed to possess him, although then, and for many years, devoted to the cervice of the church ; and he would jocularly remark to us, when asking why we did not don the new red coat, that in him a good soldier had been spoiled and an indifferent parson made. But this was not our estimate of his worth, for Newton hardly ever had a kinder hearted preacher or teacher, for he was the first to gather a Sunday school to- gether in the Assembly Rooms. And perhaps, his last pub- lic act was to preach a serinon to the volunteers after the flags of the Wigan Local Militia were given to the Newton Volunteers at Miss Claughton's,Winavick, and hung as trophies in Newton Church. And the legend of his family was descrip- tive of his life "En Dieu eat ma Foy," in God is my trust. He was a sturdy knight, and in him the race had not degenera- ted in pith or prowess from the time when the manuals of English History, written for the feudal gentry, narrate that: "In the yere of oure Lord (1323) King Edward the 111 after the conquest, was crowned at Westminster, and in the fifth yere of his reigns, Edward Baliole, right heir to the kingdom of Scotland, corn and clayme it. Tnen drewe to him divers lordes and gentlimen which had title to divers landes there; either by theymself or by their wyfes. And the said Baleen and they went into Scotland by the see, and landed to King- borne with 4 thousand Englishmenne, and there they discom- fitted 10 thousand Scottes, and slew 700; and then they went furth to Dunfermelyn, whereas the Scottes assembled against them 40 thousand; and in the lest of Saint Laurens at a place called Gastvmore, otherwise called Crladmore, were Blayne on the Scottish partie 5 erlis, 13 barons, 140 knyghtes, 2,000 men of armes, and many othre, so that fewe of theym escaped. And on the English partie were slayne but 14 per- sones." Truly a marvel of valour, if only the history be veracious. But like many other writings these rolls were manufactured to suit the palates of the readers of those days just as is the case in our own times. The fine old English gentleman of feudal times had need of such rolls to refresh his memory, and for the instruction of his children. In the Baronial Hall, after dinner, songs, such as the cuckoo song, were sung and historical and romantic poetry were recited by the family minstrel to the guests, and political and social movements noted in these records, and any important event omitted, was written on the back of the vellum' or, as we say, endorsed. Many of them furnish the facts of history as they were received in medi- revel times, and, which is quite as important, they give us ! the amount of knowledge relating to the history of his !country, which it was considered that an English baron or ! gentleman of the feudal period ought to possess, as well as !its special colour and character. They are peculiar to Eng- ! land, and are nearly all written in (Norman) French—a ! sort of Goldsmith's History of England, beautifully written, but baseless fabrications in many instances. But enough to show that the dwellers in these moat houses were stout fellows, and could give a good account of themselves. The many othre reerred to were the villeins or followers of the men-at-arms, and of these he must bring at least a dozen to entitle him to this rank, and he again formed one of the , retinue of a baron and so on up the ladder of social import- ance. Perhaps he was fortunate in having by his prowess won to wife one of those wards in Scotland, or in France, as in later days brought to them the heritage of Haydock, rich lin mineral wealth, it poor in pasture. But to return nothing I remains of the house but a gateway, as we think, in the ! Tuder style, and this only a fragment six feet wide at the entrance, with two embrasures and loop holes, with two arches on the right hand intact to key of arches, of I windows, and 13 yards of masonry, and on the left 9 yards; the chamber being five yards long, the whole of local red sandstone' faced with a grey sandstone of a harder material. Three old trees grow around this remnatn, and the ivy has overgrown the whole, and will ultimately destroy it. A kitten is peering at us while taking stock of this relic, and our dog nearly has an experience of aerial navigation, for one of the score of cows in the outer enclosure, or second moat, is tossing her fodder like a young bull. The moat is some dozen yards wide, and encloses about GO square yards of land, upon which stands the modern farm house and , garden, andjwhich but to preserve this remnant of anCquity , might as well be filled up. But, tortunately or unfortunately, there it is like Bald Old Hall, to which our walk extended, to teach a lesson to this generation not to think too lightly of the many advantages they enjoy beyond their forefathers. We reserve the remainder of our six hours' walk for another occasion.

nOAL AND CANNEL.—The Lymm Local Board are prepared to receive TENDERS for the supply of such quantities of Coal and Cannel, to be delivered at their Gasworks in Lymm during the year ending 30th June, 1893, as may be required. The probable quantit'es required are about 500 tons of coal and 300 tons of cannel, but the Board reserve the right of increasing or decreasing the quantities mentioned. The person whose tender is accepted will be required to ' enter into a contract, form of which can be seen at the Board office any Tuesday or Friday afternoons. div.head: TTTE EXAMINER.
div.p: TTTE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, MAY 13, 1882.

ONE of the foulest crimes which have darkened the pages of Irish history was committed in tbe Phoenix Park, Dublin, on Saturday evening, when the new Chief Secretary to the Lord-Lieutenant, Lord F. Cavendish, and the Under Secretary, Mr. Burke, were completely hacked to death. In another portion of the paper we give ample details of the horrible crime, which surpasses in its cruelty anything that has been known in modern times, either in Ireland or any- where else. It almost compasses belief that in the twilight of a summer evening, in one of the most frequented parts, probably, of Dublin, in presence of a number of persons who were carelessly looking on but who were unaware of the black deed which was being committed, and in full view of the highest offi- cial in Ireland, two of the Queen's most faithful ser- vants should have been butchered to death, yet such is the case. It is still more incredible that with rill the boasted efreeiency of our police and detective force the assassins should even for a short period hfee-e escaped capture. These facts, however, only serve to show that the ghastly work, unprecedented for 'its audacity, has been that of no 'prentice hand, and that the murders .must have been as skilfully plannel as they were• swiftly and surely executed. The deepest sympathy for the bereaved, and disgust and indigna- tion at the perpetrators of the foul murders are the feelings which operate in every breast at the present moment, and with one or two notable exceptions-these have found expression in one form or another in•every portion of -the civilised world. If, therefore, it be any comfort to 'the sorrowing relatives of the victims to know that their grief is shared by the highest to the lowest in the land, and by none more se than by the Irish people themselves, then this comfort has-been extended to them in an unexampled degree. tit is usual when a crime of this nature, or, indeed, of any other, has been committed to inquire into the motives of the criminals, hut we must confess that in the,pre- sent instance, unless it arose from sheer bloodthirsti- ness, or, as Mr. Gla4stone has suggested, "to rouse indignant passions and embitter the relations between Great Britain and Ireland " we fail to 'discover any motive whatever. The nobleman whose life has been sacrificed had entered the country but a few hours before; it wae generally believed he, along with the Lord Lieutenant, hal brought in his hand the olive branch of peace ; it is *a fact that the last official act of his life was to make arrangementc for the release of a very large number of suspects on an early date; and it was expected in every quarter that this, together with remedial measures of legislation which were to follow, would: inaugurate a no w and more promising era in the history of the country. Mr. Burke occupied a differ- ent position. He had been the permanent Under Secretary for a period of nearly twenty years, and beyond being upright, diligent, and conscientious iu the discharge of the duties entrusted to him—by this means securing the confidence of those whom circum- stances placed over him no matter to what shade of politics they belonged, and commanding the respect and esteem of his subordinates—he does not appear to have made an enemy of anybody. Presumably. therefore, there could be no grudge against the in- dividuals, but notwithstanding this one or koth officials had evidently been marked out for the assassin's knife. Some political motive must have been at the root of the conspiracy. The public veld readily acquit the active members of the Land League of any complicity or even knowledgie of such a dark deed. They have already plenty to answer for without having murder laid at their door, and they are sufficiently alive to the fact that at the present time, above all others, it is necessary they should be on their best behaviour. Mr. Parnell and his friends may at least he credited with having the interests of Ireland at heart, they more than any-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 13, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 13, 1882.

body else are interested in seeing its people contented and prosperous; but amongst the authors of the crime, who will in all likelihood be found to be American Fenians, there is no such community of feeling. They know that were Ireland pacified, were its tenant farmers made the owners of the soil they cultivate, the labourers more comfortably housed, and fed, and some of its bad landlords expatriated, heir occupation which feeds on excitement would be gone, hence they resort to these demonaical actions in order to "embitter," as has been very properly said, "the relations between Great Britain and Ireland." The crime, the most appalling of our time, is enough o make every Irishman blush for very shame, it has naturally called forth the strongest feelings of repug- nance everywhere, alike from the pulpit and the Press, and no event in the present century has created so profound a sensation in this country. The Parnel- lites have been prompt to disavow the murders, and they have done all in their power to render aid to the police in discovering the assassins. It is a significant fact, however, that O'Donovan Roses, unlike many of his friends across the Atlantic, refuses to stultify himself by denouncing the assassinations, and by many his reticence will be construed as a guilty knowledge of all that has taken place. Time alone will disclose whether the erirniulla are the emissaries of tia6 tiecret socieEies of which he eems to be the guiding spirit ; but it is to be hoped that whoever the assassins are they may be specdily discovered anti brought to justice. It is a satisfaction to us to find that even with such a pardonable excuse as now presents itself for the government refusing to pro- ceed in the path which they had marked out for themselves, they are not to be deterred from doing their duty to Ireland. Although we can never hope, for some time at least, to escape the awful result of secret conspiracies planned and executed by the enemies of Ireland, a conciliatory policy such as that which has been announced cannot fail to have a tranquilising effect, and the sooner that policy is carried into action the better. On Thursday the Government bill for the better administration of justice in Ireland and the suppression of secret societies there, was introduced, and is likely to meet with the support of all sections in the House of Commons. So soon as this has been disposed of the arrears question will be dealt with, and subsequently the Bright clauses of the Land Act will be expanded. That these may be of such a nature as to finally dispose of the Irish land question is the earnest prayer of all true Liberals and of all interested in the welfare of the country.
RUNCORN MILL BROW WESLEYAN SUNDAY ScsooL. --The anniversary sermons on behalf of this school, were Preached on Sunday, by the Rev. J. Nettleton, and collec- tions made amounting to upwards of £2O.

RuNcoux BURIAL BOARD. - The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. Coleburn occupied the chair, and there were also present Messrs. James Hand- ley, Wm. Littler, Peter Briscoe, and W. F. Sallield (secre- tary). The usual returns as to interments were laid upon the table, and a number of accounts were pissed. A precept for £2OO to be payable on the 10th prox., was issued on the overseers. No discussion arose, and the proceedings were of a purely routine character. RUNCORN BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. —The weekly meeting was held on Wednesday evening when the principal part should have been taken by Mr. Bis- brown, but that gentleman was unable to be present, owing to a family affliction. Mr. Timothy Sirnistcr, the president, occupied the chair; and the proceedings were of a general character.

ACCIDENT AT A WIDNES -...ViTORKS. —Oa Saturday as Patrick Baxter, a man employed at Messrs. Muspratt's chemical works, was carrying a number of pipes up a plank the plank split in two, and he fell a distance of 20 feet to the ground, sustaining such injuries that he had to be carried to the Widnes Hospital.

PRESBYTERIAN BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN. - The closing tea party for the season, of this Band of Hope, took place on Wednesday. The Rev. E. Williams (pastor), pre- sided, and addresses were given by Mr. Wilson, Mr. R. Har- rop, and Mr. J. Warburton. Recitations were given by Eliz, Level]; M. A. liavps, A. Nem:lion, W. Kennion. F, Leach, and Mitry Goy. Two prizes were awarded to Miss Elizabeth Leach and Miss Mary Guy, for the best replies to the question "Why abstain from drink ?" _

ALLEGED THEFT OF BOOTS.—At the Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. F. H. Gcssage, three boys named Thomas Randle, Samuel Mercer, and Thomas McGreevey, were remanded until the next Petty Sessions on a charge of stealing two pairs of boots, the property of Mr. 11. Syred, pawnbroker, Waterloo-road. The articles, which it is supposed had been obtained by loosening a brick in the wall of the warehouse where they were kept, had been pawned at Mr. Imison's. FARNWORTH CHITRCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—The last public meeting of the season was held in the Farnworth girls' schoolroom, on Monday evening. The Rev. Joseph Holden, curate, occupied the chair, and the Rev. George Bond and Mr. J. W. Davies took part in the proceedings. During the evening, the Rev. T. Storey Bates, M.A., diocesan secretary, of Liverpool, gave an in- teresting address on temperance topics. Selections, recita- tions, dialogues, and amusing sketches were given, as well as two farces, the first being entitled " Lawyer Charjum and his clients," and " Caught at last." A collection was made at the close on behalf of the society. NARROW ESCAPE OF A. BOY FROM DROWNING, AT RUNCORN.—On Sunday, a lad named Edward Smith fell off the boundary wall of the Bridgewater canal, in Halton-road, Runcorn, into the water. His cries for help were heard by John Davies, a man living at Stone Croft, who happened to be near the spot, and he at once took off his coat and vest, and rescued the poor fellow, who appeared to be lifeless. Smith was, however, carried to the Bull's Head public- house, where he was attended by Dr. McDougall, and after much labour restored to consciousness. This is a case which deserves the attention of some of the Runcorn gentle- men who have influence with the Board of the society which rewards such noble acts of heroism.

RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. - On Wednesday, Mr. Driffield held an inquest at the Waterloo-road vaults, Widnes, on the body of Ellen Baguley, a widow, 61 years of age, who formerly lived in Hutchinson-street. Mr. Ferrand, from the solicitors' department, Lime-street, appeared on behalf ef the Coi On the 8:11 ul, decr..ased went to the station to meet the 5-7 p.m. epress, but she, in mistake, got into the slow train which immediately follows the other. The latter train was shunted on to the St. Helens line, and whilst there Mrs. Baguley, probably imagining that she was in the wrong train, jumped out, caught her leg in the wires connected with the line, and fell backwards. Her right leg and back were badly hurt by the fall, and her system re- ceived a severe shock. Henry Ward, who was acting as station master at the time, had the poor woman removed home in a chair. She was attended by Dr. McDonnell, but died on the 8.11 inst. The jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dental death."
