div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

The branch of the Blue Ribbon Army which has been established in Runcorn bids fair to prove a successful or- ganisation. The last meeting held by Mr. Murphy and his coadjutors was densely crowded, and passed off with the greatest enthusiasm. The racy anecdotes and genial man- ner of the advocate won him many warm friends. It is a matter for regret that there appears to have been a misun- derstanding between Mr. Murphy and the gentlemen who formed the deputation who waited upon him to request he! would visit the town. Some of the deputation came back ' under the impression tbat admission to the hall was to be charged at the rate of is. 6d., is., and ed., au the entire re- ceipts would go into the pockets of the American friends. This naturally caused considerable surprise amongst many who were prepared to welcome the party, and the feeling was not by any means improved when the rumour was cir- culated that a collection would have to be made in order to defray the expenses attendant upon engaging the hall, the printing, and the advertising. At the first meeting the at- tendance was only poor, and it was made known that all which Mr. Murphy had desired was that a charge should be made for a few reserved seats. At the last meeting the ad- vocate dwelt at considerable length upon the annoyance Ile had felt at so much misapprehension having existed as to his intention. He observed that he was not at all surprised at people objecting to pay to attend meetings where total abstinence was to form the leading theme. Mr. Murphy also expressed his deep regret that such a report had been circulated in the town; and at the close Mr. Wilson stepped forward, and was greeted with enthusiastic applause when he intimated his determination to undertake the payment incidental to the visit to _Runcorn. In all my connection with public life, I never remember to have been a witness to such a manly and straightforward course of proceeding, which reflects the greatest credit upon Mr. Murphy's party. At the last meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners, Mr. Robert Shaw spoke with somewhat extreme warmth in respect to an alleged wilful misrepresentation of himself by your reporter ; and also delivered his soul as to the criticisms which appeared a few weeks age concerning the same Board, under the head " Flaccus." I propose to make a few remarks upon both matters. As to the report of Mr. Shaw's words, which appeared in ne Examiner, I have not been able to ascertain that in the past that gentleman has made any observations condemnatory of the style in which his speeches have been given in your journal. Under these circumstances, I attribute the language which he used to a tittle soreness concerning the way in which his action on the Free Library question Irscs been spoken of in the colt:mu to which. I have the honour of contributing my quota. In the first place, he says that the resolution stated to have been moved by him ,concerning the vice-chairman- ship of the Library Committee, was not even proposed! This is certainly a singular blunder on the part of your reporter. Of course, representatives of the fourth estate do not claim infallibility.; and it is quite within the bounds of possibility that a- blander has been committed. It, however, seems scarcely fair that Mr. Shaw should have gone so far as to call the report a concocted one, and to have actually insinuated that your representative coolly manufactured a bogus resolution, in order that tt Flaccus'" might hang a peg upon it. But is reasonable to suppose that any gentleman who bad the slightest regard for 'his•professional reputation, or his stand- ing with the large number of leading ratepayers of which the Board is composed, would take such a courses which would infallibly have the result of bringing him into ,con- tempt as a person utterly unworthy of confidence? I think I need not enlarge uporr the fate which would await ouch action on the part of the representative of any respectable paper in this countr7, where journalism is cooducted net purer lines than in any other land on the face of the globe. And now one word -ca behalf of " Flaccus," who Appears to have come in for no small share of censure. In the article referred to by Mr. Shaw, the following occurs:—" Mr. Shaw, still in a patronising vein, said that the minutes of the committee were not intelligible, and the oard,had.a right to expect that they should have clear records placed before them. I believe the Rev. Canon Barclay presided over the meeting of the Library Committee, and matters have arrived at a pretty pitch if •Mr. Robert Shaw thas to pet a scholar like the vizar of the parish right as to the drawing , up a minute." Nov', lam exceedingly astonished to find that Mr. Skaw has entirely misapprehended the meaning-cf these two sentences, for he proceeds to deliver a high eulo- gium upon the Rev. Canon Barclay, an!' to strongly con- demn the reference-which was made to that gentleman, who; it will be seen, was-spoken of asa scholarly marl, and, therefore., in a complimentary tone. Under these circumstances, R.'s somewhat questionable whether the strong language of Mr. Shaw, as to the resolution, must not be takecum wrano=s-aE-s. In conclusion, I may add that your readers musc be well aware that" Flaccuo" has very frequently spoken in high terms of this gentleman's conduct in town's matters. L .4LCCUE.

ENTERTADAMEN r T WIDNES.—OiI Monday -evening,' the St. Patrick Amateurs gave an entertainment in the Volun- teer Hall, on behalf Acf the new Catholic schools at New- town. There was a-fair attendance, and the musical part of the programme was by Mr. Powell's string band. SHOCKING D 'ZANE CT' A CHILD AT FARN WORTH. a Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Driflleld held an inquest at Farn- worth; near Widnes, tacching the death of Cyril Whitesit:e, the sun of Mr. Richard Whiteside, income-tax collectorlind estate agent, Victoria-road, Widnes, and residing in Derby- road, Farnworth, who was killed on Saturday afternoon .under shocking circumstances. Mr. Ferrand, from the soli- itors' department, Limefetreet, watched the case on behalf 41 the London and North-Western Railway Company, and. Mr. Sampson, of Liverpool, appeared for the parents of de- ceased. It appeared from the evidence that stuartly after ' three o'clock in the afternectr, deceased, in company with hie brother and sister, went to the Farnworth station to meet' his mother, who had gone to St. Helens. Deceased stood atfi the ate of the level crossing, and put his head in the aper-'1 tore between the heel of the,rate and the gate post. The! 3-10 train from St. Helens was allowed to pass, after which. shandry, driven by a man cauted Ducker, of Farnworth, approae,hed the gate, and, ha teaponse to his signal, the crossing keeper began to open the gates. When they were partly 4,,•pen a woman called out that the deceased's head was fast between the gatepost and the gate, but the crossing keener appeared not to have heard until Ducker called out . to him, when he at ence reversed the gate, and the child dropped down dead. Mr. Ferrand stated that there had been no complaints about the gate, which was of the usual kind. It was given in evidence that at the Lugsdale and Waterloo- toad crossings in Widnes the aperture between the heel of the gate and the gate post was covered by a plate to prevent accidents of this nature.—The Coroner expressed a hope that the railway company would place a plate of this descrip- tion at the Far nworth gates.—Mr. Ferranti doubted if they could do so.—The Coroner remarked that unless he under- took to do this the imi,ueet would have to be adjourned.— Mr. Ferranti, after some further conversation, intimated that he would draw up a report, and forward it to the company's 2 .•?, chief engineer at Mancbee.t,--Trie jury retu= verdict of "Acciflental death,"

div.head: Ecttero to the Uitor.
div.p: Ecttero to the Uitor.
WALKING DAY.

Sir,-Kindly allow me a small space in your next issue to say a word or two in defence of those who took part in the meeting called by the Mayor, on the 4th inst., relative to appointing the most suitable day for the children's anniver- sary. In your last issue a letter appeared from some anonymous scribbler, signing himself " St. Elphins,"—a worthy name surely—attempting to describe that meeting and what took placa. I venture to say that he is totally wrong in nearly every particular. In the first place the meeting was not crowded with Dail= forge men. There were men present from all the forges, and they attended for a special purpose, viz, not to have Walking Day fixed in Whit week. Why? Because the ironworkers of Warrington have decided to hold their sports conjointly on Whit Monday, and the proceeds are to be given to the funds of the In- firmary. Has "St. Elphins " ever been engaged in such an object ? But "St. Elphins " questions whether we had any locus staiuli in that meeting. Are the Sunday school 1 teachers and the manufacturers going to arrogate to them- , selves the right to think, speak, and act for the whole body •of workingmen in the town? If so, then I think it is high time that the workingmen should speak out boldly, and without fear or favour, on matters relative both to the in- terests of themselves and the town. But a word as regards the most suitable day for the anniversary. I contend that Newton Race Friday is the most suitable day, inasmuch as the workingmen have always regarded t hat day as a holiday ; and the school teachers of years gone by determined to cause a counter attraction to the races and the children's anniversary was established. Why do the pi esent school teachers want to discontinue it? Depend ugon it, sir, there are many workingmen who will have Newton races for their holiday, whether or no, and I think it would be policy on all sides if the interesis of tim arealest number were taken into consideration as well as school teachers and manufac- turers. If the working men of the town generally abstain from sending their children to take part in the demonstra- tion, Walking. Day must be a failure; and the school teachers will be dissappointed, and the manufacturers jubi- lant in having succeeded in robbing the workingman of his annual holiday.—l am, yours, &c...
JOHN SHUFFLEBOTHAM.

Sir,—l have seen a letter in your issue of May 6, signed "St. Eiphim," in which he makes certain charges against the ironworkers of Dallatn and Bewsey forges, which are not correct. In the first place, he says the ironworkers came from the above forges in great numbers to obtain Newton Race Friday as Walking Day, not to benefit the Sunday Schools,, but to obtain a holiday to attend the races. Now, sir, there were present ironworkers from all the \yolks in the district, and bat a small number from Dallam and Bewsey forges. He must have a very poor opinion of the iron workers indeed if he thinks they only want a holiday to attend the races. There are a great number of ironworkers who never think of such a thing as the races, but want a holiday to recruit themselves for their labour in the ensuing week. Their work is very laborious and hard, and they need a rest now and again. "St. Elphins " seems to think that the ironworker i have no interest in the Sunday school. This is a sad mistake on his part, as every working man has an interest in the schoola either directly or indirectly. " S. Elphins " feels hurt at being defeated by the majority of votes which were taken at the meeting. Now, sir, the majority rules. everywhere, and why should not the minority be ruled in this CASC by the majority according to the usual custom ? He also implies that because the representatives of Dallam forge vanted Newton Race Friday the men must vote in their favour whether or not. I do not think any man went to that meeting who did not iii a free and inde- pendent spirit as a worki.ig, man should do. Aed then your correspondent contends the working men hod no right at the meeting. Now, sir, it was a nubile meeting convened by the Mayor to fix a date for Walking Day ; and I would like to know who has more right to chose a general holiday than the working men themselves. I contend that they had the most right to vote on the question, as it is not a simple school question, but a general one, to fix a time for a general holiday. He closes his letter by asserting the schools in- tend to carry the day ; but I would like to know what "St. Elphins" would do if the working men go against him, and have it on Newton Race Friday, which point they could carry in opposition to "St. Dphins" if they choose. Warrington, May 12,1882. IRONWORKER.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Sir,—The present time seems appropriate to call public attention to the existence of a secret society in this country —an order of men whose presence bodes evils Fprci who hays been cast out of nearly every natiOn for tired' iiisklious and treasonable practices—l mean the Jesuits. Since their last expulsion from France we have witnessed a large influx of them Into this country. Though they have formerly been expelled from England for their intrigues, and the law exists which denies them entrance, there appears to be no effort made to put that law into execution. The fa•ct of their having been expelled from nearly every *country as disturbers of the public peace and plotters against the weal of kingdoms, is surely a good reason why we should he chary about giving them entrance here. Where could the • Jesuits find a titter field for their operations than Ireland, or another people among whom their machinations would , prove more disastrous than the inhabitants of our sister isle? Some plume themselves upon the liberty enjoyed in Ci:eat Britain; but to give opportunity to that sect which has proved itself so prejudicial to good government (as every student of history knows), and who are amenable to no principle, is not consistent with liberty.—Yours, Warrington, May 10. RADICES AGERE.

Sir,—lreland's worst eaemies have triumphs], if concen- trating public attention upon the Irish qoestion by a deed, the foulness of which draws the opprobrium of the whole civilized world upon its perpetrators, Can he esteemed a triumph. They have revived the Irish question with a vengance ! Not that it needed reviving, for the Govern- ment were deeply engrossed with it at the ve,y miment when theseconsuaniate "gentlemen of the dagger perseasion' thought proper to record their opinions in the blood of Lord Cavendish and Mr. Burke. The menace which we are led to believe Mrs been frequently repeated by them has had a terrible ratification. We scannot conceive of a more atrocious execution of threatened serime. Horror at its daring cruelty has blanched every English, and we would fain hope, every Irish face. The time ,feir expressing indignation at the out- rage, little short of an assault upon the Crown, is however merging into that wir:ch should be almost wholly absorbed le the eigai.facance of the assassination, and the evolving of pilicy suitable to the anarchical condition of Ireland at this moment. Sympathy on behalf of the relatives of the mutilated victim-s, of worse than Nihilistic fury, is world- wide in its expresnioa. A heart without grief at such an bour-as this •innst be a rarity, or Eneland ha e causeete mourneever subjects unworthy of their country's patron:semi°. ' How is this momentous Irish question to be met l The crises that have periodically arisen in Irish history, seem to be fot,gizing in one grand crisis, the intensity of which-is fearful to contemplate when we realise what is so difficralt to realise, namely, that the highest estFicers et tt:e crown are butchered in day-light into public thoroughfare of a great and infloential, not to say enlightenedeciey ike Dublin. We have had constant occasion to feel alarm in .connection wiLla Ireland for some time past. The shedding •of'blood, is,ii is needless to repeat, no new thing. From Whatever source terrorism has emanated, it is heavy -wk,h the blood of its mangled victims. And, sorrowful to rotate, the ilia of murdera. has rapidly lengthened of late,; and now it is blurred with the crimson from the oreins of innocent men, one of whom was newly Arrived in Ireland with a ineeeiage full of conciliation and peace. It makes the -mat:el-gill-the more repugnant when we recollect,that Lord Cavendish was not permitted to even initiate the new policy fie.was about to introduce as the successor to Mr. Forster; it almost 'creates a panic of despair at ever :solving the problem eat Irish discontent. We are told by some that these .cowardlyearutalities represent the Nemesis overtaking us for the wreugs inflicted upon Ireland in the past. "Two' blacks do not •make one white," however. Wrong -endured is no justification for wrong doing; and unless wecan persuade the agitators 'for a redress of Irish grievances to • conduct the agitation on the principles of moral suasion,alistinctly free 1-from-the imputation of blood-guiltnees, how is it possible to. ,arriveoet a basis of just and conjollet procedtre'? It is im- possible. In the course of time the peremptory outcome will'be military force ; for no Minister of the-Gro-wn will be ,1 obtainable self-sacrificing enough to oblige his •chief by immolating himself upon the altar of duty. We desire, ie'. the sake of law and °Mgr, not to my of national pride, . that the mecessity for escorts to protect the Crown officers cduring"their "walks abroad" will be removed by Ireland awakening to a sense of the shame attached to such a pain- , ful relic- of barbarism ; by purging herself upon these traf- ,<fickers In blood, whose existence and 246cloc,,operandi iu •presumed.association with the Irish agitation is a dishearten- eng tblot upon Irish character and national honour. The ri.shr question is undoubtedly linked with the admit- redly unsatisfactory status of the-Irish people. Whatever anequalitiae they may be that are borne by the honest, hard- working classes of Ireland, in c munori justice those inequali- tics should-be removed, and removed at once. Lovers of . rectitude in government have no alternative be to demand Was, the best:proof of our desire to make Ireland what she ought to be, -a happy and prosperous country. With the Pheenix Pat::-tragedy appalling our senses with its emphasis of detailed ghastLiness, it is not easy to repress a feeling of antipathy towards offending Erin. As a man expreesed himself this morning, he felt when he met an Irishman as if . he could " clout " him. But t h is is exactly the kind of ,feeling which every true Englishman 1 will quench. -Coolness in critical contretemps is a trait possessed by the average Englishman; his bitterest foes admit thie. We have no right, however much the perfidy of the crime may incense us, to permit our passions and prejudices to govern us at a moment when the merest sign of unwisdona in our political attitude towards Ireland, may let leose the -demons of war and bathe Ireland in blood. It therefore behoves all who feel the slightest resentfulness to smother the disposition to deal malignantly, at least, retaliatively, with Ireland. On the other band, we are not sure that the assassins of the Chief and Under Secretaries of Ireland were associated with the effort of the Irish people to loosen the grip which landlordism, in its fouler phase, has upon them. There may be secret societies, whose object— plunder—would, if realised, run counter to the really righteous interests of Ireland. Such societies would, with paramount selfishness, welcome war as !he harbinger of wealth. Therefore, the creation of an exciting causes belle of beligerent action between England and Ireland would be primary subject in their councils, and a likely conterminus in the dastardly, and, alas ! successful attempt at the des- truction of Lord Cavendish and Mr. Burke. This, of course, is simply hypoti:elical. As, however, no evkience is as yet

forthcoming as to the object of the assassins in their dark work, we are left to conjure for data; and justice, since the character of a nation is at stake, asks us to take the most merciful view of the case. We are, undeniably, face to face with a grave, if not an unprecedented crisis in Irish affairs. It is politic to avoid, if possible, a rapture between the mother country and the subordinate isle. If Ireland claims the right of self-government, it appears certain that, in the teeth of her manifest incompetence, the liberty to govern herself will not be granted, although, as a by-considera- tion, perhaps if left to her own resources for a few are, ' Ireland might learn what no amount of preaching will con- vince her, that self-government is not feasible with the peculiar conditions which embarras Irish society unaltered. But •if Ireland demands what educated Irishmen so eloquently plead for, namely, an improvement in the land laws favourable to the tenant, together v-,ith such altera- tions and amendments in the general laws of the country as will place Irish on a level with English or Scotch subjects, we cannot demur if the spirit of our renowned freedom is not dead within us. Give Ireland ,justice ; it is her right and our duty to see this fait accompli. I must now conclude my already extensive remarks. Nothing but an earnestly sincere desire to behold the Irish question disposed of in a manner praiseworthy to English politics would have im- pelled use to trespass upon your columns with the fcregoince. My last words shall be : Justice to Ireland ; intolerance and bigotry—let these be scouted as unworthy the traditions of the Great Empire, one .of whose high-tone principles is, "Justice to alt." 13ENJN. SAWDON. %VA:. rington, May 9, 1852.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
THE MIST MURDERS.

Telegraphing 5 esterday, the special reporter of the Press Association at Dublin says :—There is a widespread com- plaint against the police, the general public feeling that the men ought to have been captured long ago, but the police say on the other hand that they do not want to apprehend a number of men upon suspicion, and that the evidence they have in their possession is strong enough to enable them at the proper time to put their hands upon the assassins. Meanwhile the public mind remains unappeased, and the ex- citement and indignation engendered has in no way abated. Considerable progress has undoubtedly been made in the . way ef eliciting evidence, and in quarters where doubt hitherto prevailed there is now a feeling of confidence that the whole party will yet be made amenable. Moreover, the! theory is now generally accepted that they returned to Dub- lin immediately after the murder, and that they are con- cealed in some part of the city at the present moment. Very little importance is therefore attached to the arrests made elsewhere. Detectives are closely watching all vessels leav- ing the river Liffey, and trains running from the varieus local stations, and a sleepless vigil is kept in districts of the city where the criminals are most likely to find a safe resting place and friends to sympathise with them in the hour of danger. Another telegram states :—lt has come under the notice of the authorities that within a short time in Dublin several formidable knives, with blades about ten inches tong, have been sold by ironmongers. The police have got some 'additional evidence as to the car and the men being seen in the pork. FURTHER ARRESTS.

Another arrest was made on Thursday night in Belfast in connection with the murders of the Chief and Under So.cre- taries. The prisoner gave the name of Ferret Walker, and has the appearance of an American. Blood stains were found on his clothes and pocket-handkerchief. He states that he belongs to Edinburgh. A Mallow telegram reports the arrest of a tramp named Allen, recently discharged from the army. He was sent to Cork gaol on suspicion of beig concerned in the Plicenix Park assassinations. LETTER FROM LADY FREDERICK CANENDISH. A deputation born Belfast. waited on the Lord Lieutenant at Dublin Castle yesterday. Lord Spencer read a letter he had received from Lady Cavendish, in which she said—" I should be very glad if there can be any means of letting it be known in Ireland, so as to have some good effect, that would never grudgs the sacrifice of my darling's life if only it.leads to the putting down of the frightful spirit of evil in the land. He would never have grudged it if he could have hoped that his death would do more than his life." THE STATE OF IRELAND.

div.head: ANOTHER AGRARIAN OUTRAGE IN IRELAND.
div.p: ANOTHER AGRARIAN OUTRAGE IN IRELAND.

S.)1113 excitoment has been caturd by the rews of an agrarian outrage near Bchnullet, county Mayo. Late on Wednesday night a man named Barrett, whd had taken a small farm from which the tenant had been evicted recently was shot whilst sitting in the kitchen of his house. The shot, wh'ch came through the window, was not immediately fatal, Barrett lingz.ring till Thursday. It is said,he had been warned not to take the farm, which is on the propsrty of Mr. Bingham, who was himself shot recently. One arrest , has been made. A Central News correspondent telegraphs : •—Barrett, the man shot at Doolagh, Belmullet, on Wednes- day night, has died from his wounds. The gun was fired through the window, end Barutt, who was in bed, was shot in the thigh. His Ivife was also injured. Barratt had re- ceived a warning to give up his farm. The previous tenant has been arrested..

There were very few spectators to witness the departure. rn the trounds surrov.ading the surgery of Dr. Art on, at Foleshilt, a tomtit has kr the fifth year in succession built its nest in a wooden letter bax, and' is now sitting on nine eggs. Tha low tides during the week have prevented the fish from running up, and little has been done either in the upper or le-wer waters of the Dee. The Chester fishermen have netted about 25 fish, while the trammel net men at the esteary have only secured some half a score. The tides are expected to be more favourable during next week. The flefuermen have, however, experienced the most successful spring sport for many seasons past. The committee of the North-East Lancashire Amalgama- ted Weavers' Association, in their annual report, say they are ssrry they are unable to congratulate the members up= the staple trade of this country. They had bones during the latterlraltbf iast year that ere this they would have induced the masters to advance wages, but trade has not maintained the position it held during that period. On Thursday evening a man named William Rigby Chamberlain, of Balshaw-street, Bolton, committed suicide. He had worked at Messrs. Thtelfall's foundry for 20 years, and latterly he bad complained of being over-worked, and had requested to be placed on a less laborious job. This was refused, and on Thursday night Chamberlain strangled himself with a scarf tied to the bed-post. When found by his wife he was dead, with nearly the whole of his body resting on the floor. Yesterday morning over 1,000 dyers and pressers in the employ of Sir Henry Ripley and Sons, Bowling dye works, Bradford struck work against a proposed reduction of lOper cent. The men proceeded to other large works, at which notices of a similar reduction had been given. These notices will not expire until to-night, when a general turnout is ex- pected. Serious riots took place two years ago when 3,000 dyers were on strike. The police have grave apprehensions of trouble

div.head: ATTEMPT TO cur A WIFE'S THROAT.
div.p: ATTEMPT TO cur A WIFE'S THROAT.

On Thursday afternoon, an attempt was made to cut a wife's throat at Higham, near Burnley. A man named Hobart Waite, a weaver, was proceeding across some fields with his wife, Elizabeth, when he told her several times that he should cut her head off, and when near Higher°, he pulled out a razor and attempted to draw it across her throat. She seized it with her hands, the latter being shockingly wounded, and at that time her screams attracted two men, who rescued her from her husband, and delivered the latter into the hands of a policeman. Waite is thirty years of age and had been seeking work, he having been out of employment for a month. The prisoner was intoxicated at the time. He was yesterday morning committed for trial.

div.head: DISPUTE AT CHORLEY.
div.p: THE DISPUTE AT CHORLEY.

IThis morning all the Chorley mills were opened, but the I spinners who were locked out did not return to work. Messrs. Nixon and Killick, Messrs. Lawrence, and Messrs. Smethurst started a few mules with the assistance of pieeers. At the mills of Messrs. Barton, and Messrs. Brown, neither spinners nor piecers appeared, and the works consequently were not started.
THE ALLEGED WIFE MURDER AT HYDE.

Yesterday morning, James liesford, a labourer, was brought before Mr. Charles Hi'kart, at Hyde, on a charge of having murdered his wife last right. His on gave evidence as to seeing the prisoner strike the deceased on the back with a poker, and she died shortly afterwards. Pr:sener has passed a very restless night and denies the c:lme, say- ing the deuascd fell, and her temper caused her death. The prisoner is of low stature, sallow complexion, and has a stooping gait. When charged, the prisoner said there had been a quarrel, but denies using the poker. A remand was granted. - THE COLLIERY CALAMITY IN WARWICKSHIRE.

div.head: ANOTHER DEATH.
div.p: ANOTHER DEATH.

There is Etlll another added to the heavy list of deaths from the above disaster, Thomas Besson, another of the ex- poring party, having succumbed to his injuries. The total number dead is now twenty-eight, nineteen of whom lost their lives through an heroic, though unsuccessful attempt, to rescue the men still entombed. Many others are yet in a critical state.

div.head: SINGULAR CHARGE OF MANSLAUGHrER.
div.p: SINGULAR CHARGE OF MANSLAUGHrER.

Yesterday morning, at the Stipendiary Court, Fenton, Stoke-on-Trent, Elijah "Griffiths, a hooker-on at the Duke of Sutherland's Great Fenton Colliery, was committed for trial at the Staffoid Assizes on a charge of having caused the • death of Thomas Gater, a boy employed at the same col- liery. The deceased descended the pit to his work, and on alighting from the cage stepped into the sump at the but- tone of the shaft, being drowned. The prisoner had, it is ! alleged, neglected to place the guards round the sump, ! which would have prevented such a catastrophe, and his arrest for manslaughter followed.
ATTACK ON A MAIL CART. THE ASSAILANT SHOT DEAD.

A man who was attacking a mail car between Navan and Drogheda on Wednesday night was shot dead. A short dis- tance outside Navan a strange an laid hold of the car. clinging on to it in the rear. The driver, Roche, being afraid to proceed rcturned to Navan and informed Mr. Boylan, the postmaster, who, thereupon, taking a loaded revolver,mount- ed the car himself beside the driver, and a second start was made. On the road the strange man again attempted to get on the car, and Mr. Boylan promptly shot him dead. It was not known what the object of the deceased was. Mr. Boylan returned to Navan, and having got a police esc)rt sent on the mail car a third time, in charge of a different driver, to Drogheda, where it arrived on Thursday morning several hours late.
