div.p: MURDER OF LORD FRED. CAVENDISH AND
ATE. THE NEW CHIEF SECRETARY AND UNDER•SECRETARY FOR IRELAND.
An event which has horrified Dubliu, and caused horror and consternation throughout the civilised world, occurred "
en Saturday night.
When the first rumours of it were
_ bruited abroad no one was inclined to believe it. Mr. T. H.
Burke, who had been for the last ten years Under-Secretary
for Ireland, and who was for years before that practically Under-Secretary to Sir Thomas Larcom, was, with Lord Frederick Cavendish, the new Chief Secretary for Ireland,
foully murdered. Lord F. Cavendish only arrived in Dublin at noon on Saturday to take up his new office. He drove
through the city in tile Viceregal procession on the occasion of the State entry of his Excellency Earl Spencer. The double murder took place under circumstances which
heighten the shccking character of the deed. The murderers

Were four in number, and the murder took place about ten minutes past seven o'clock, in view of His Excellency the Lord-Lieutenant and quite close to the Viceregal grounds. The evening was beautifully fine, and there was, as usual, a vast number of people in the park. A polo match which had been carried on in the park had just closed a quarter of an hour before. So rapidly was the deed perpetrated, and With such instant effect, that no one's attention was directed to the occurrence in any unusual degree. Even those who did observe the presence of six men imagined it was a friendly wrestling match on the part of roughs, and paid no attention to it. It appears that Lord F. Cavendish, after .taking part in the ceremony of the installation of the Lord- Lieutenant, and having been himself sworn in as Chief Secretary, proceeded on foot through the city and through the park, to walk to the Chief Secretary's Lodge, which is situated near the further end of the park, and to the left of the main road. The Viceregal Lodge being, to the right, and about a mile nearer to the city, Lord F. Cavendish being a man of vigorous constitution determined to walk the whole way, the walk on a fine evening being a very pleasant one. Mr. Burke, who had been engaged all day at the Castle, in Connection first with the installation and afterwards with the ordinary business of his office, drove from the Castle, which he left shortly before seven o'clock, on an outside car. When nearly opposite the Viceregnl Lodge he over- took Lord F. Cavendish, and thereupon dismissed his car, and the two walked on arm-in-arm in the direction of the Secretary's Lodge. They had only walked a short distance when they were attacked and brutally murdered. According to the statement of persons who saw the encounter from a distance of about two hundred yards, and who, as already stated, supposed that it was merely a wrest- ling match, they observed a struggle proceeding, but they beard no sounds. Immediately afterwards they saw four men leave the party and go towards an outside car, get up on it, the driver being on the driver's seat, and drive off rapidly in the direction of the Hibernian School, and further away from the city. One of the eye-witnesses of the occur- rence saw two out of the six persons who had been struggl- ing fill, but being of opinion that there was nothing serious in the matter no attention was paid to it. The true nature of the occurrence was first discovered by two gentlemen who were riding on tricycles. These were Mr. Patrick Maguire and Mr. Thomas C. Foley. They had passed Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke a few minutes before on their way out through the park, and bad in the meantime travelled to the "Pheenix," at the extreme end of the park. On their return they discovered the two bodies lying near each other, one on the grass about ten yards from the main road, and the other on the main road. There were marks of a severe struggle, and a large quantity of blood about the spot. Mr. Maguire proceeded immediately towards the park gate at the city end of the park, where there is a police station, and informed the police of the finding of the bodies, while Mr. Foley remained in charge of the bodies until the police arrived. In the meantime the guaed at the Vicsregal Lodge had been apprised that something had happened, and they brought a stretcher to the spot. The guard also turned out at the same time. Tee body of Lord Frederick Cavendish was placed on the stretcher, and conveyed to Stevens Hospital, which is near the park gate, although at a distance of more than a mile from the spot where the murders were com- mitted. The body of Mr. Burke was placed on an outside car, and conveyed to the same place. The removal of the bodies attracted great attention, and a crowd of people followed, but it was not then known, save by one or two, who the deceased were, otherwise the excitement would doubtless have been much greater. Both bodies presented 3 fearful spectacle, and hoth bore evidence of the desperate struggle which the deceased had maintained with the as- sassins. Mr. Burke had his gloves on, and, as was his oustom, was dressed in a tight-fitting frock-coat. Both his coat and his waistcoat were torn, and were covered with blood. His throat was cut so that the bead was nearly severed from the body. A large piece was cut off one of his fingers, where he had evidently caught one of the daggers, which apparently were the only weapons used. There was one stab-wound in the left ear which was of itself sufficient to have caused instant death. He was also stabbed several times through the heart and breaet. Lord F. Cavendish bad apparently made a still more violent struggle for his life. One of his arms, the right arm, was broken and lacerated severely. His throat was not cut, but he was stabbed in five or six places through the heart and lungs. A. large crowd of people assembled within a few minutes, and the greatest consternation and horror was visible an every face. His Excellency the Lord-Lieutenant bad ridden by only a short time before, accompanied by his private secretary and an aide-de-camp, also on horse-back. His Excellency was in the grounds to the south of the Viceregal Lodge, and saw a scuffle on the road, which he thought was a drunken brawl, and not much attention was paid to the matter. Two excise officers named Alfred Williams Walters and John Power reported that while they were on a seat in the park about two hundred yards away from the scene of the occurrence, they observed two gentle- men pass in the direction of the Pheeeix Monument. They saw no more of them until their bodies were found by the men on the tricycles, who informed the police that there were two gentlemen murdered on the road. Lord Frederick's body lay on the roadway in a great pool of blood. Mr. Burke's body was off the road, on the footway. The read is flat, and there are no ditches o 7 trees about. The place is within a few hundred yards of the Viceregal Lodge and within full view of it. A young man named Jacob who was bird-nesting in the park, saw the occurrence at a distance of 200 yards. He states that he saw four men drive up on an outside car, and after a scuffle drive away into the trees towards the Hibernian Military School, which lies to the south of the Viceregal Lodge and is hidden in tall trees. He lost sight of the vehicle, and did not think much of the occurrence. He says the men struck at each other as if playing. There Was no noise or cries. The carman remained on the dickey while the struggle proceeded. It did not last for more than two minutes, and then the men jumped upon the car hurriedly, but coolly, and drove off. Intelligeece of the outrage was conveyed to Stevens' Hospital, and hr. Myles and the house surgeons went in the direction of the park on a car, and met the police, who were bringing in the bodies. They accompanied the remains to the hospital, and placed them in No. 1 Ward. It was then found that both were dead, and that from the nature of the wounds death must have been instantaneous. In addition to the frightful gash in the throat of Mr. Burke, there was a wound right through the base of the heart. Lord F. Cavendish had a wound in the right lung and a wound in the neck which must have proved instantly fatal. There was at first some doubt as to who the two gentlemen were, but upon searching their pockets letters were found which established their identity. A servant of Lord F. Cavendish arrived at the hospital soon after the bodies were admitted, and identified them. There are several accounss given by people who saw the struggle on the road, and they differ only on the point whether the car was actually at the scene of the outrage waiting to convey away the murderers, or that they called it and ran to meet it. It is believed that Mr. Burke alone lona tended to be the victim, but that Lord Frederick Caven- dish being with him was slain also by the murderers for their own safety. This is believed to he the reason why Mr. Burke's throat was cut. It is also believed that the assassins had been watching Mr. Burke closely, that they were well aware of all his movements, and that they had lain in wait for him. Mr. Burke had been frequently advised to have an escort, but he firmly declined. The men who depose as to seeing the murderers get on the car were taken into cus- tody by the police, and they have each given a written ac- count of what they saw. A guard of police was put on tile blood marks at the scene of the murder, and they remained on duty until four o'clock in the morning, when an order was sent from the Castle to have the marks cleared away, which was done and the constables were withdrawn. This was done to allay excitement. Soon after the murder a telegram was received from Lord Frederick Cavendish's com- mittee at Keighley, announcing that at a meeting on Satur- day night a resolution of confidence had been passed in him, and a pledge given to use their utmost efforts to return him against all opposition on the part of the Conservatives. The news created a profound sensation when it became known through the town, alai people remained up till early morning in the vicinity of the newspaper offices eagerly seeking for the particulars of the murder. Never. was Dublin more iutensely moved. General horror was strongly apparent. In the various places of amusement throughout the city where news of the shocking occurrence became known before the performances were concluded profound sensation was created. The premrditation which character- ised the murder created a shock in the public mind as the details becanse known. Little doubt cm n be entertained that the fate of Mr. Burke had been decided by a vehmgerieht, and it is suspected that Lord Frederick Cavendish sacrificed his life in a gallant attempt to save Mr. Burke. It is a matter of general sur- prise how a crime of this kind could he committed in so public a part of the Park without attracting attention. Rumour at first was to the effect that several young men on bicycles had witnesaed the murder and feared to interfere, but the latest inquiry frees every one from such an imputa- tion.

The assassinations were condemned from nearly every pulpit in Dublin and throughout Ireland on Sunday. The momentous event entirely changed the aspect of Sunday in Dublin. Privy Councils were held t the Castle, the Muni- cipal Council sat, special editions of the daily papers were

published, and the inquest was formally opened. In ad- journing his inquiry till Monday morning, the Coroner said this was undoubtedly the most fearful crime that had stained ' the country for cent uries. Intelligence of the murders spread rapidly in London on Sunday. At first it was received with incredulity, followed by expressions of the strongest indignation. The Court Ciro;lar speaka of the "deep grief with which Her Majesty received the horrible news." 'fhe Cabinet, hastily sum- moned; met at three o'clock in the afternoon, and remained in deliberation until half-past six. Mr. Forster had called upon the Prime Minister earlier in the day, and offered his services provisionally as Chief Secretary for Ireland. Sir Stafford Northcote early in the day addressed a letter of sympathy to the Prime Minister, and, it is understood, ex- pressed a hope that both parties should if possible co-operate in dealing with the critical circumstances of the present time. Throughout the country the intelligence of the horrible crime was received with the greatest indignation, it was con- dernned from many of the pulpits, and universal sympathy was everywhere expressed for the families of the unfortunate victims. A correspondent in New York telegraphs that the news of the assassination created amazement and horror there. The almost universal exclamation was :—" This seals the fate of Ireland and decrees the downfall of Mr. Gladstone." Among the Irish leaders the news caused dismay, as well as aston- ishment. All the Irish are agreed, the correspondent adds, ' that a great calamity has befallen Ireland. The American papers comment on the deed in terms of unmeasured abhor. rence and condemnation. Special telegrams from the principal. European cities show the feeling of horror with which the news of the crime has been received on the Continent.

MANIFESTO BY THE LAND LEAGUE. The following manifesto was issued by the Land League and adopted on Sunday afternoon at an informal and hurriedly summoned conference in the Westminster Palace Hotel :—" To the people of Ireland.—On the eve of what seemed a bright future for our country that evil destiny which has apparently pursued us for centuries has struck another blow at our hopes which cannot be exaggerated in its disastrous consequences. In this hour of sorrowful gloom we venture to give an expression of our profoundest sympathy with the people of Ireland in the calamity that has befallen our cause through a horrible deed, and to those who had determined at the last hour that a policy of con- ciliation should supplant that of terrorism and national dis- trust. We earnestly hope that the attitude and action of the whole Irish people will show the world that assassina- tion, such as has startled us almost to the abandonment of hope for our country's future is deeply and religiously abhorrent to their every feeling and instinct. We appeal to you to show by every manner of expression that amidst the universal feeling of horror which this assassination has excited no people feel so intense a detestation of its atrocity, or so deep a sympathy for those whose hearts must be seared by it, as the nation upon whose prospects and reviving hopes it may entail consequences more ruinous than have fallen to the lot of unhappy Ireland during the present generation. We feel that no act has ever been perpetrated in our country during the exciting struggles for social and political rights of the past 50 years that has so stained the name of hospitable Ireland as this cowardly and unprovoked assassin- ation of a friendly stranger, and that until the murderers of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke are brought to justice that stain will sully our country's name. (Signed) CHAS. S. PARNELL. JOHN DILLON. MICHAEL DATITT." • LORD CAVENDISH.
Lord Fredotick Charles Cavendish, was the second son of .he Duke of Devonshire, and was 46 years of age. He woo

educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, where be took hon- ours, and in 1559 became Private Secretary to Earl Gran- ville on his appointment as Lord President of the Council in the second Cabinet of Lord Palmerston, holding this post up to 1864. On the allotment of two additional members to the West Riding by the Appropriation of Seats Act of 1861 he was returned at the general election of 1855 for the Northern Division, which he has since represented. In 1872 he was private secretary to Mr. Gladstone ; in August, 1873, he was made a Lord of the Treasury; and going out of Qffice with the Liberal Government in February, 1874, was nominated to the post of Financial Secretary to the Treasury two years ago. Lord F. Cavendish, at it is said the Premier's special request, very reluctantly surrendered that office for the Chief Secretaryship of Ireland on Thursday last, when a new writ was moved for the North-West Riding by Lord Kensington. He married in 1854, Lucy Caroline, second daughter of George William, fourth Lord Lyttelton, and leaves no issue

div.head: MR. BURKE.
div.p: MR. BURKE.

Mr. Thomas Henry Burke, Under-Secretary, was born in 1829, and was the second son of the late Mr. William Burke, of Knocknagen, county Galway. Mr. Burke, who was unmarried, was brother to Lieut-Colonel Theobald H. Burke, late of the 18th Royal Irish. He was heir-presumptive to the baronetcy of which Sir John Lionel Burke, of Glenik, county Galway, is the holder. THE INQUEST.

The inquest on the bodies of herd Frederick Cavendish, the Chief Secretary. and Mr. Thomas Burke, the Permanent Under Secretary for Ireland was resumed on Monday before Dr. Nicholas Whyte, the Dublin city coroner, at Steven's Hospital. Amongst those who attended were the Attorney- General for Ireland, Mr. John 4ash, Q.C., Mr. Porter (Sur- geon to the Queen in Ireland), and Chief Superintendent Mallins, of the Irish Detective Department. The Attorney- General said he had been instructed by the Lord Lieutenant to offer his assistance to the Coroner in inquiring into this painful affair. The Coroner expressed the hope that any person who had information to give would at once come for- ward. Mr. Steel, superintendent of the messengers at the Castle, gave evidence of identity, and said Lord Frederick left the Castle about half-past five, and Mr. Burke left ten minutes later. Nicholas Brabazen, carowner and driver, said Mr. Burke hired him soon after seven from Parkgate- street. He drove towards the Under Secretary's Lodge, and on passing the Gough Monument Mr. Burke got down and discharged him, and walked with a gentleman arm-in-arm. He knew no more until two young men on tricycles came down some six minutes after- wards. He saw no vehicle enter the Park after he left it. Mr. Patrick Maguire stated that he was with Mr. Foley riding a tricycle on Saturday evening. They entered the Park by the Zoological Gardens shortly after seven. They passed two gentlemen on the footpath in conversation, and returned from the Phcenix Column along the main road towards the Gough Statue. They then saw two bodies, one on the road and the other on the footpeth. They were the same two gentlemen they had passed six or seven minutes before. He called to Foley, who was following, that there had been a duel or a murder, and asked him to wait on the spot while he went for assistance. He saw two constables near the Gough Statue, and two others at the gate. He then returned to the scene of the tragedy, Foley being still there. The bodies were removed to the hospital. Samuel Watson Jacob said that about ten minutes past seven he was in the Park, and saw a small group of persona who appeared to be wrestling. A car was at a skort distance. One man ran to it. Another man seemed to strike someone on the ground. There were four men, including the driver, on the car, uhich drove away. Mr. Thomas Foley corroborated Mr. Maguire, and said the car had a number plate and red panel. Dr. Thomas Myles, resident surgeon of Stevens's Hospital, and Dr. Porter, surgeon in ordinary to the Queen, described the state of the bodies. Death in Mr. Burke's case was evidently c :used by a stab over the left shoulder, penetrating the heart. The fatal wound in Lord Caven- dish's case was over the right shoulder, severing two large arteries. Lieutenant Greatorex, of the Dragoon Guards, , 1 said he saw a scuffle end two men fall, but he thought they were only "larking." The jury, after a short deliberation, , returned a verdict of wilful murder against some persons L I unknown.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE ON THE CRIME.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE ON THE CRIME.

The following telegram was received on Monday by Mr. Gladstone's private secretary:—" Lady Ripon and I most anxious to hear how Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone bear the shock of this dreadful event. Please telegraph to say, and take opportunity to assure them of our deepest sympathy." Mr. Gladstone replied as follows :—" Many thanks; all are as well as could be hoped. The object of the black act plainly is to rouse indignant passions and embitter relations between Great Britain and Ireland." TflE, FUNERAL OF MR. BURKE.

The remains of the late Mr. Thomas Burke were interred on Tuesday in Glasuevin Cemetery, Dublin, where lie buried O'Connell and many other. distinguished Irishmen. Mr. Burke's funeral was of a private character, but the whole city was in mourning, and large numbers of the leading pro- fessional and official men in Dublin followed the remains to the grave.
THE ASSASSINS' PLOT.

The Government have received information to the effect that the assassination was a preconcerted plot, aimed not only at the Lish Government of the Liberal patty, but at the head of the party itself. Sir W. Harcourt has consequently instructed Colonel Henderson to adopt p-ecautions, and extra special constables hava been posted opposite the official and private residences of all the Cabinet Ministers in London.

div.head: SYMPATHY WITH MR. GLADSTONE.
div.p: SYMPATHY WITH MR. GLADSTONE.

The following communication has been published :—Mr. Glsdstoas has received a flood of telegrams and coFnmunica- tioss from every part of the three kingdoms. expressive of the universal horror and indignation which are felt at the atrocious crime on Saturday evening last. Among these it is just to say that none are more remarkable for fervour and evident sincerity than the very large number which proceed from all parts of Ireland. As sep irate acknowledgment of each of them has become impossible, he at once takes the liberty of requesting an early insertion of this paragraph, or its substance' in the public journals, that he may thus ex- press, in the first instance, his sense of the genuine feeling and just aims of these communications, and, in the next, his personal thanks for the abundant asiurauces of sym- pathy with himself and his family which they contain.- 10. Downing-street, May 9, 1882.
REMOVAL OF LORD FREDERICK CAVENDISH'S BODY FROM DUBLIN. -

The body of Lord Frederick Cavendish left Dublin at Liven o'clock on Monday evening, and arrived A t Holyhead at 2 a.m. on Tuesday, leavin4 there by the London and North-Western Railway Company's train for Buxton, where it was !riven into the hands of the Midland Railway officers. reached Rowsley station at 5'45 a.m., in the care of Cap- tain Lyring, who was met by Mr. Martin, agent to the Duke ' of Devonshire, and Mr. Doom, the representative of Messrs. and Co., undertakers, of London. The body was conveyed in a hearse from ChesterficAl, and placed in the private chapel at Chatsworth to await the interment. ' The

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY 13, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY 13, 1882.

body was viewed by the inhabitants of the neighbourhood from two to five o'clock, when those who knew the deceased gentleman pressed forward to see his remains. The coffin was covered with black velvet. It had brass mountings, and was lined with lead. The features of the deceased had a calm and placid expression resembling sleep rather than death. The only scar visible was a slight one across the nose. Over the body was placed a splendid cross composed of white azaleas, mignonette, forget-me-nots, tea roses, and maiden-hair ferns. His Grace the Duke of Devonshire was the first of the family to enter the chapel after the arrival of the body. He proceeded immediately after breakfast, and at the sight was completely broken down. The bereaved lady, accompanied by her two • brothers, the Hon. Neville Gerald Lyttelton and the Hon. Alfred Lytteltou, also visited the chapel. The former scarcely seemed to realise that her husband was dead, and quietly walked by the coffin. Lady Louisa Egerton was deeply affected, and sits in silence. The whole family, since the arrival of the body, have been in deep distress. THE LAST OFFICIAL ACT OF THE DECEASED
ward Cavendish were seated on each side of the

atoffin. The ladies and gentlemen of the house were seated along the sides and the body, and the servants of the Duke at the end of the chapel. The Rey. Mr. Talbot, cousin of the deceased, and Master of Keble College, officiated. After the service, Mr. Talbot administered the

sacrament to the Duke and immediate family, after which they all took a last look at the placid face of Lord Frederick's remains, and the lid of the coffin was put in its place. Dur- ir g this Lady Frederick was led from the chapel by the old Duke. It was expected that, according to the expressed wish of a great number of Parliamentary friends, the coffin would not be closed until after the arrival of the members of Parliament from town ' • but as the time was limited, the coffin had to be changed. It was thought best to close it before the arrival of the visitors. A black ebonywood coffin

replaced the hurriedly-made black velvet-covered one which held the remains during its transit from Dublin, on which was a brass plate with counter-sunic inscription, "Lord F. Cavendish, second son of the Duke_of.Devonshire, born 30th _ _ _
November, 1836; died 6th May, 1882." At one o'clock, the special train conveying invited mem- bers of both Houses of Parliament from London drew up at _ _

Rowsley, where the duke's carriages and many other vehicles hired by the duke's steward for the occasion, were in attend- ance to convey the visitors to Chatsworth, a distance of four miles. These were found to be inadequate for the hnmense numbcr who had arrived, and many of the members walked, among them being Mr. Forster. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone occupied the first carriage with Earl Granville, and on the box seat sat Inspector Denning, who had come down specially. from London so as to look after the comfort of the mem- bers of Parliament. In the next carriage sat the Speaker, _ _ .
Sir Henry Brand, Lord Northbrook. Mr:Dodson, and Mundella. The other carriages were full, and some had to . _ _

return to convey the remainder of the train's load. Mr. Gladstone's carriage dropped Inspector Denning at the large gate at the entrance to the private grounds of the house. Here, assisted by another constable from the House of Com- mons staff, Mr. Denning scrutinised all the occupants of the carriages as they alighted, to see that no intruder got in- side. The members and other invited guests were

met by Lord Hartington on the steps leading into the grand entrance, and ushered into a large room where light refresh- ment was laid out for them. The churchyard at one o'clock was crowded with people from Derbyshire, Lancashire, Leicestershire, and Warwickshire. Special trains had been running all the morning from the large towns surrounding, three trains coming from Manchester being full, and several from Derby likewise amply loaded. The police arrangements were under the supervision of Captain Parry, who had a large staff of the Duke of Devonshire's tenants told off to keep back the crowds. There was little need for this, for no crowd ever was so orderly. Not a word of anger was ex- pressed by anyone during the whole day, every man and woman seeming to settle down into their places as if they had been drilled beforehand. The sun's heat at this hour was tremendous, and the little breeze that rustled the spring leaflets upon the trees was most refreshing. Half an hour before the time stated for the cortege to start from Chatsworth House, the people, who bad been lying under the shade of the trees and congregating in good positions to get a view of the beautiful scenery, commenced to augment the already well packed roadside depth of mourners. The hearse had been seen to enter the gates, and no delay in getting the remains in being expected, everyone was on the tiptoe of expectancy, especially as the sweet- toned bell of the village church chimed out the melancholy passing bell. At a quarter to two o'clock the tenants of the duke who were picked to carry the coffin from the house to the hearse entered the wide portals of the residence. Teey were all dressed in deep black, and were the oldest tenants of the duke suited for the purpose. This was an honour greatly sought after, so the duke had three sets of carriers—one from the house to the hearse, the other from the hearse to the church, and from the latter to the grave respectively. The members of Parliament at two o'clock assembled on the grand terrace to the left of the house, four deep. They numbered over three hundred; and embraced every phase of politics. At two o'clock private carriages drove up to a side door of the house, and into the first got Lady Frederick Cavendish, draped in widow's weeds, Lady Louisa Egerton, Lady Edward Cavendish. and Mrs. Gladstone. The second was occudied by Miss Gladstone and three other ladies. These carriages went at a walking pace up the road to the chapel, and the occupants were generally recognised by the people assembled, who raised their hats and murmured their sym- pathies for the widow, who lay back in the carriage. When the carriages arrived at the church the ladies walked up the front steps leading into the chapel through the private door. In Lady Frederick's hand was her Majesty's special wreath sent down in the morning to be placed upon the coffin. It was circular in form, and was of the most rare description of flowers. In it was a white card with the words "From Queen Victoria." After the widow had knelt some time at the altar, she, with the other ladies, went to the duke's porch to wait for the arrival of the hearse. Exactly at a quarter- past two o'clock the bell of the church rang out the indica- tion of the starting of the funeral. The coffin issued' from the entrance hall down the steps while the members all un- covered. It was borne on the shoulders of twelve men, and had a cross formed by Lidy Frederick herself laid all along its length, composed of white azaleas, spirea, and having a centre of deep crimson roses, the edges being relieved in their abruptness by maiden hair ferns. The tenants deposited their burden in the hearse, which had been drawn up close to the steps. The hearse was of e most unostentatious description, without any plumes, drawn by four black horses. The procession was then formed as follows :—The hearse, immediately behind being the Duke of Devonshire, on his left the Marquis of Hartington, on his right Lord Edward Cavendish. The duke, with bowed head, leaning on his stick, struck all hearts with pity, his thin grey hairs, feeble walk, and grief-stricken face going home to the hearts of those who saw him a week since happy in the honour that had been paid his son by being delegated to a post of great consequence. The Marquis of Hartington held himself well, spite of the grief, but there were many signs apparent of the restlessness on his countenance. Lord Edward indeed looked careworn, and his eyes and face gave an impression of fre- quent weeping. Immediately tehind them came Mr. Glad- stone, Earl Granville, Sir Henry Ponsonby, and Lord Ed- ward Clinton, the latter two being her Majesty's special representatives. Mr. Gladstone looked extremely pale,and. although he walked erect, there were heavy traces of grief left upon his face. Afterwards came Colonel Kingscote, representing the Prince of Wales, and Colonel Colville, representing the Duke of Edinburgh. The mem- bers of Parliament and Cabinet Ministers followed next, four deep :—Lord Northbrook, Earl Kimberley, Lord Carlingford, Mr. Goschen, Hon. W. Egerton, Mr. Mundella, Dr. Playfair, the Speaker and Mr. Brand, jun., Lord Fitzmaurice, Colonel Stanley, Messrs. W. H. Gladstone, Wilson, Cameron, J. Dun- das, Illingworth, Middleton, Wenlock, Shaw Lefevre, and Fawcett, whose tall erect stature attracted much attention. The following are the names of the Irish members who at- tended :—Sir T. M‘Clure ; Messrs. Lyons, Brooks, W. Corbet, Smithwick, Marum, Burne, Lea, Kinnear, Dickson, D. Plunket, Given, M‘Coan, and Shaw. There were over 280 members present, and were followed by Lord Frederick's constituents frona the North Riding of Yorkshire, the Mar- quis of Hartington's constituents, and the constituents of Lord Edward Cavendish. In this order the procession marched along the avenue to the big gates, through which they passed, and around this point of sight had congregated , an immense multitude, who, with bare heads, bowed as the hearse was driven past them. The duke never raised his eyes from the ground, and seemed oppressed with a licavy weight of sorrow, which he several times relieved by heavily drawn sighs. If there was one thing wanting to touch the hearts of those present it was the sight of this old man following his son to his last resting place, with tottering steps and bent head. It went home at once to the hearts of ' those who saw it, and few there were whose eyes were not dimmed with tears. Arriving at the church gates the hearse bore round to the left to the ducal entrance to the church, which is on the summit of the hill. The deputations from various corpora- tions and reform clubs, numbering over 20, of about 500 men, had gone in front of the hearse from their standpoint outside the church gates as soon as the hearse arrived. The second batch of tenants now came forward, and taking the coffin from the hearse entered the gate, where they were met by the clergy, four in number—Archdeacon Derby, Canon Humphries' Rev. Mr. Hall, and Rev. Mr. Talbot. The latter. a relative of the deceased, read the impressive service. Immediately inside the entrance gate was the oldest tenant on the decal estate and his wife, seated upon the sward with head uncovered. This old man was a conspicuous object, sitting among the tombs. Mr. Gladstone, when the hearse arrived, left the procession and walked into the church, whence he issued bearing Lady Frederick upon his arm. They met the body half-way to the porch, and the Duke then gave his daughter-in-law his arm, Lady Louisa Cavendish taking that of the Marquis of Hartington. On the clergy entering, the chant "Lord now lettest Thy servant depart in peace," was sung by the choir of the church, the organ being played by the schoolmaster. On the left of the coffin, which was placed on the trestles as it had left the hearse, sat the Duke, Lady Frederick, and Lord Edward Cavendish. On the right was Lady Egerton, Lord Hartington, and Admiral Egerton; Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, and the nearer family mourners, sat behind, while the body of the church and aisles were filled with members of Parlia- ment. Outside were many members who could not get in. The Rev. Mr. Talbot, in a sympathetic voice laden with feeling, read the impressive service, in the mie.dle of which the sweet boyish voices of the choir, with Derby rustic accent, sang the 39th Psalm, followed after a time with the 90th Hymn commencing "Christ will gather in His own." This mosebeautiful of hymns was rendered with peculiarly impressive feeling. The little boys, sons of tenants and pensioners of the Duke in their every-day habiliments, giving expression to the simple words seldom heard. The scene at this juncture as every one stood, and the mellor-toned organ and sweet voices . flooded the Church with music, was most effective. Lady I Frederick was so overcome that she bowed her head and ' a paroxysm of tears, which the Duke tried hie utmost to ; stop. In the meantime outside the crowds which had lined the road on the Chatsworth Avenue and the road on the other side of the hill from the church, had congregated in and around the church-yard. God's Acre, with its thousands of mourners thirty deep, was glorious in the shining sun- light, as the music fell upon the ears of the multitude, among whom not a wisper was heard. After the conclusion of the service in the church nearly all remained kneeling for some moments, and the widow was one of the last to rise. She turned quickly towards the i coffin, and immediately averted her eyes, giving the Duke her arm, and waiting with peculiar fortitude the last partine , stroke. Since his death no one had been so often in Lord Frederick's death chamber as his widow, loth to tear herself away, and yet not willing to leave him in any other person's

hands. She had been with him night and day, and had kept vigil over his remains with great fortitude. As the coffin emerged from the Duke's portal it was seen that many had been weeping. Mrs. Gladstone, leaning on the arm of her daughter, had broken down, notwithstanding the strength she displayed when she first heard the dreadful tidings which brought grief to England, and put many households in mourning. The procession from the church porch was in the same sequence as that into the -church. The distance was over 100 yards and uphill. No service was read during this walk, but the silence reigning above was impressive in the extreme. Arrived at the grave. the Duke, with the widow and Lord Edward, took up their position on the right of the coffin, Lord Hartington, Lady Egerton, and her husband (Admiral Egerton) being opposite. The clergy were at the head, immediately behind whom were Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone. The former had his mouth hardpressed to keep the scalding tears from falling, while Mrs. Gladstone had given way completely. The members who had seen Lord Frederick only a week ago thick in his Parliamentary duties completed a circle round the grave. The banks around were crowded with the more honoured of the Duke's tenants, who occupied the outer circle. Then, in a loud but quivering voice, the Rev. Mr. Talbot con- tinued the service. The heartrending rattling sound of the earth cast by the sexton upon the coffin when Mr. Talbot read the words "earth to earth," sent a thrill of misery through every heart present, and the old Dike, whose fortitude had been apparent up to this time, now thoroughly broke down.

At the end of the service the choir, led by the school- master, sang the 142nd Hymn, "Brief life is here our portion," the air and words known to many was joined in, the Archdeacon of Derby lending Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone his hymn book. The cthers of the family seemed to know the laymr., and joined in when their choking sobs would allow them to do so. The widow stared at the grave the while, never raising her eyes, which were bedewed with painful tears. When the hymn had ceased, and the sweet vibration of the youthful voices had died away in the dis- tance, the benediction to bowed heads was delivered. With one last look upon the coffin that held all dear to her in the world, Lady Frederick Cavendish went down on her knees and placed the Queen's beautiful wreath at the head of the grave. Then turning as if she had steeled herself to the ordeal, she took the Duke's arm, and walked down the path on the opposite side of the churchyard to that the proces- sion had come up. Sympathy for one who in her widowhood bad borne up so well in the dreadful ordeal moved the people to crowd round her, and many were the whispers of condolence that struck upon her ear. She, with Lady Egerton and Lady Edward Cavendish occupied the first carriage that left the churchyard on the return to Chatsworth. Next carriage held the Duke of Devonshire, the Marquis of Harlington, Lord Edward Cavendish, and Admiral Egerton, the ministers following in carriages which brought them straight to Rowsley. The ceremony was not completed until twenty minutes past three o'clock. MANIFESTATIONS OF PUBLIC SYMPATHY.

At many towns in the United Kingdom Thursday was ob- served as a day of mourning, to mark the universal feeling of sorrow at the death of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke, while in many places, notably in Ireland, and where the late lord was well known and respected, church bells were tolled, and business was almost altogether suspended. At Penrith, where the Duke of Devonshire is lord of the manor, the shops were all closed,and the Union Jack floated at half-mast. The Yeomanry Band played the "Dead March," and the church bells tolled muffled peals. At Bar- row, and throughout North-East Lancashire, the day was also observed with marked respect, and tokens of mourning were everywhere displayed. At Middlesbrough business was suspended in the afternoon, flags being hung half-mast high from the public buildings, and muffled peals rung. THE ARRESTS.

Throughout the whole civilised world tidings are eagerly awaited of the arrest of the perpetrators of the Pho3nix.Park murders. In all quarters of the kingdom the police autho- rities are on the alert for any trace of the assassins, and in Ireland many arrests have been made, but there iq nothing yet to show that hands have been laid on any one of the actual cutthroats. A man na.ned Moore, believed to have landed from America, was seized at Maynooth on Monday night, but on being brought to Duqlin there appeared to be no evidence of identification against him. At Limerick a man with blood-stained trousers was arrested, but he was able to give a satisfactory account of himself. There is a man in gaol at Tuaam answering the description of the car- man. Two suspicious-looking characters have been brought before the Monaghan magistrates and remanded pending inquiries. In the Phcenix Park, on Tuesday, two men were taken into custody on suspicion, but afterwards released. The Chester police have made an arrest, acting on instruc- tions from Ireland. All the licensed carmen in Dublin were on Monday paraded before the witnesses at the inquest, but nothing came of it. A statement has been made to the police by a young man at Southport to the effect that he can identify the men who committed the crime. As the man adheres to his statement, and tells a story of having been asked to assist in the assassination, he has been tahen over to Dublin. At Preston a man named Quinn was arrested on suspicion; and on the statement of a detective officer that he had received important information, and had reason to believe that he could get such evidence as would connect the prisoner with the crime, he has been remanded. THE CAVENDIS HES.

Mr. R. H. Mason writes :—lt is worthy of note that the first distinguished member of this family, Chief Justice Sir John Cavendish, was murdered by rebels 500 years ago. When Wat Tyler's insurrection extended itself to Suffolk, the mob attacked his house in Bury St. Edmunds, and, having got hold of the venerable judge, they murdered him in the market-place. That was on the 15th of June, 1351." THE EXTENT OF THE PUBLIC FEELING.

Meetings continue to be held in all pas of the country at which resolutions are passed, as also by magistrates, boards of guardians, town councils, and other public bodies, ex- pressing indignation and abhorrence at the assassinations in Dublin, last Saturday. It may be mentioned that the Central News agency says that the number of telegrams of this kind that they have received is three times as many as the telegrams expressing condolence on the death of the Earl of Beaconsfield, and twice as many as the telegrams of resolutions paged in connection with the recent attempt on the life of the Queen. A large proportion of the messages on the present occasion are from Ireland, but to some of these resolu ions is added a clause condemning the action of the police in firing into the crowd during the late disturbances at Ballina.

div.head: STATESMAN.
div.p: STATESMAN.

It is a melancholy fact that almost the last official act of Lord Frederick Cavendish's life was to complete, in con- junction with Earl Spencer, the necessary arrangements for the release of every suspect in Ireland, except eighty who are confined on charges of committing crime or treason- felohy.

div.head: MR. BURKE'S SUCCESSOR.
div.p: MR. BURKE'S SUCCESSOR.

Mr. It. G. C. Hamilton, formerly Accauntant-General at the Admiralty, and recently Permanent Under-Secretary of that department, has been appointed to succeed the late Mr. Burke as Under Secretary for Ireland. Mr. Hamilton, who has for some time discharged responsible public duties in association with Mr. Trevelyan, left London on Monday night for Dublin.

div.head: MESSAGE FROM THE POPE.
div.p: MESSAGE FROM THE POPE.

A telegram from Rome, dated Monday, says :—The Pope, on hearing of the murders committed in Ireland, sent the most decided instructions to the Irish Bishops, in order that they should express their horror at the crime, and urge all Catholics to conform to the laws of the land, instead of corn- mitting acts of violence in the hope of bettering their condi- tion. All the papers express their horror at the murders in the most unmitigated terms. They fear that Mr. Gladstone will have to modify the more liberal policy he had just in- augurated. They, however, hope it will not produce a change of Government, as Mr. Gladstone's foreign policy is very popular in Italy.

div.head: NEW CHIEF SECRETARY.
div.p: THE NEW CHIEF SECRETARY.

Mr. George Otto Trevelyan M.P., who has been appointed to succeed Lord F. Cavendish as Chief Secretary for Ireland, was born July 20, 1838, at Rothley Temple, Leicestershire, is son of Sir Charles Edward Trevelyan, Bart., K.C.8., and Hannah More Macaulay, sister of Lord Macaulay. He was educated at Harrow School and Trinity College, Cambridge, where he was second in the first class in classics. He was elected member for Tynomouth in the Liberal interest in 1865; and for the Border burghs in 1868. Mr. Trevelyan was appointed Civil Lord of the Admiralty, in Mr. Glad- stone's Government, in Dec., 1868, but resigned office in July, 1870, on a point of conscience connected with the Government Education Bill. He advocated a sweeping re- form of the Army, including the abolition of the purchase of commissions both in and out of Parliament. He wrote

from India "Letters of a Competition Wallah," republished from Macmillan's Magazine in 1861; " Cawnpore," in 1865; "The Ladies in Parliament, and other pieces," collected and published in 1869; and "The Life and Letters of Lord Macaulay," 2 vols., 1876, 2nd edit, 1877. He has since written a life of Charles James Fox. The new Chief Secre-
tary came into office with the present Government as Secre- tary to the Admiralty.
REWARD.

A reward of £lO,OOO is offered by the Government for such information as will lead to the conviction of the murderers of Lord F. Cavendish and Ir. Burke, or £2,500 for that of any one of them. A free pardon will be granted to accomplices furnishing information who wet e not actually concerned in the commission of the crime. AN EXTRAORDINARY STATEMENT.

Two brassfitters named Macnee and Fry, in the employ of the Great Southern and Western Railway Company, have, it is stated, made a very important disclosure to the police. They state that they were actual witnesses of the assassina- tion of Lord Cavendish and Mr. Burke. According to their narrative it appears that on Saturday evening they had gone up the Park from Inchicore on bicycles. When they reached the Phoenix column they turned towards the town, and were going in that direction when they saw, close to them, Lord Cavendish and Mr. Burke. The attention of Macnee and Fry was almost wholly concentrated on their bicycles, but suddenly they observed two men attack the Chief Secre- tary and Under Secretary, while not far distant were two other men. They saw one man raise what appeared•to be a large knife and plunge it into the breast of Lord Cavendish, who had gone out on the roadway from off the pathway after he had, as is conjectured, received the first stroke. They heard his Lordship exclaim to his assailant, "Ah, you villain," and at the same moment the knife was again thrust into his breast. Lord Cavendish fell almost under the bicycle, which was going unsteadily, and which he touched in falling. The rider was dreadfully frightened, and made all possible speed to get away. It is stated that his com- panion, who was following at some yards' distance behind, when he saw what was being done was about to stop his bicycle and go to the assistance of the Chief Secretary, but the same murderer who bad stabbed his Lordship advanced towards him when he perceived his intention, holding the bloodstained knife uplifted, and made a dash at him. The bicycle rider terrified by what he had seen and the attack made upon his own life, made all possible haste to follow his comrade, leaving the unfortunate nobleman to his melancholy fate. But before he had gone far he says that he noticed that one of the assassins went back to the pros- trate body of the Chief Secretary, and again buried his knife in the body. Macnee and Fry appear to have had their attention so absorbingly attracted to what was occurring on the road that they did not observe the assassination of Mr. Burke, which took place on the pathway, and tbeir sole de- sire seems to have been to get away from the appaling scene as soon as possible, and to secure their own safety. They also state that at a distance of some twenty or thirty feet from where the murders were perpetrated, they observed a hackney car standing on the left hand side of the road, the driver sitting in the dickey, and the horse being towards the city. The car was empty. They did not see it start.

div.head: SUSPICIOUS CIRCUMSTANCE.
div.p: A SUSPICIOUS CIRCUMSTANCE.

A Chorley correspondent writes:—" An incident pointing to the Fenian origin of the murders in Dublin happined on Saturday night at Chorlev. An Irishman, aged about 30 years, called at Mr. Fowler's newspaper shop shortly after eight o'clock, and, asking for a Dublin paper, said that Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke had been shot, and that Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Parnell were dead. Mrs Fowler said she had not heard, when he assured her of the fact. The remark was questioned by a bystander, when the Irish- man replied warmly, but nothing was thought of the matter until the circumstances were so terribly confirmed."
FUNERAL OF LORD CAVENDISH.
VIEWING THE BODY FOR THE LAST TIME.

The body of Lord Frederick Cavendish, which was viewed by a considerable number of the tenantry on Wednesday, was seen for the last time by the members of the ducal family late on Wednesday evening, and the coffin was then screwed down. The Duke of Devonshire was completely overcome after the farewell view of his son's body, and quite broke down. The Marquis of Hartington was also deeply affected. The body is covered with beautiful wreaths and flowers, amongst them being a wreath sent by Her Majesty.

div.head: FUNERAL CEREMONY.
div.p: THE FUNERAL CEREMONY.

Early on Thursday morning the little hamlet of Edensor, within the Chatsworth domain, was astir. Messengers from the house to this village were going to and fro with the latest arrangements for the last obsequies of Lord Frederick Cavendish. The church, which is built upon the side of a knoll, was during the earlier hours decorated by ladies' hands, the gardens of the Duke's model village growing many of the floral decorations. The chancel window sill was covered with a deep carpet of wall moss or lichen, on which lay crosses of azaleas. In the centre a large cross of yew, studded with narcissus and edged with spires, was placed upright on either side of the window, with triangular devices of pritnroses and bluebells. Above the communion table there was an inscription in white flowers upon a black ground—"l am the resurrection and the life, saith the Lord." The round pillars that supported the roof of the church were decorated with American bamboo foliage entwined. The sills of all the windows in the nave were carpeted with wall moss and crosses of white flowers, surrounded by forget-me-nots upon it. The large grey granite font at the end of the church was made a bank of the most beautiful spring flowers, consisting of primroses, bluebells, forget-me-note, and arum lilies ; and the edge of the basin was covered with narcissus. Nothing could Le more lovely than the arrangements of the flowers. The graveyard in all its still religious beauty was not touched, except where the grave, at the highest point, was dug. Here two tombs setting forth the decease of some of the Duke's kinsmen hail been covered over with a temporary platform, in the middle of which the grave had been dug or rather cut, for the bottom for two feet is a bed of granite, lying upon which, previous to the body being lowered, were many wild flowers thrown in by children. They formed a pretty simile of death, for they had faded as they lay in bunches. The tenantry from all the Devonshire estates commenced to flow into the little village betimes. The Duke having given all the labourers a holiday, they were utilised by the steward in directing the tenants to their places along the line of route. The latter were in nearly every case dressed in black, with white silk ribbons tied on their left arms. It is believed that every holder of land under the Duke was present except the feeble people and children. They were so numerous that the road to the church from Chatsworth Hall, a winding way a. mile in length, was lined with them n three, and in good positions ten, deep. By noon over 20,000 people had assembled on the different parts of the slopes giving a view of the house, where all the in- terest at the time was centred. Some more thoughtful than others had ample lunch baskets spread out under the shade of the huge elms which dot the park at intervals. The sun was extremely hot, although ominous black clouds were on the horizon in the early part of the morning. A special service was held in the private chapel attached to Chats- worth, where the body of Lord Frederick then lay in the , centre of the aisle. The Duke of Devonshire, the Marquis of Hartington, Lord Edward Cavendish, Lady Frederick Cavendish. Lady Louisa Egerton, Colonel Cavendish, Admiral Egerton, Major Lyttleton, and Lady Ed-

div.head: RECEPTION OF THE NEWS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: RECEPTION OF THE NEWS AT WARRINGTON.

Never was so profound an impression produced in War- I rington as that created on Sunday morning by the intelli- gence that the new Chief Secretary for Ireland (Lord F. Cavendish) and the Under Secretary (Mr. Burke) had been assassinated on the previous evening in Dublin. At first the startling news was received with incredulity, which, how- ever, later in the day gave place to the utmost consterna- tion and feelings of intense indignation towards the perpe- trators of such awful and dastardly murders. Groups of persons were to be seen standing in the principal streets of the town throughout the day discussing the melancholy in- formation, and the political situation generally, and at many louses blinds were drawn as a mark of respect to the memory of the deceased nobleman. Allusion was made to the hor- rible tragedy at both morning and evenin, services at the Parish Church, where special hymns were sung, and the organist (Mr. C. E. Rcwley) played the Funeral March. At Wycliffe Church in the evening the Rev. John Yonge ' made referenc 3 to the terrible occurrence in his , prayer, asking that special wisdom might bs given to those who guide the affairs of State, and consolation to those who mourned. References were also made at Holy Trinity and St. Peters' Churches, Bold-street and Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapels, Legh-street Primitive Methodist, Golborns-street Baptist, and other chapels. When the details of the assassi- nations were posted at The Examiner office they were eagerly read by the large numbers of persons who col- lected round the windows; and so great was the demand for newspapers on Monday morning, that the newsvendors' supplies were exhausted a short-time after arrival. At the Borough Court on Monday reference was also made to the subject by the Ex-Mayor (Councillor Fairclough) who, on taking his seat, said: We cannot commencl the proceed- ings of the court this morning without expressing our utter abhorrence at the foul outrage perpetrated in Dublin on Sunday, and expressing our sympathy with the relatives of the murdered people. I am sure it will be a stain on this country if the murderers are not found out and brought to justice, as I hope they may be.—His worship the Mayor, who was late in appearing on the Bench, intimated that be had intended to make a few observations on the crime, and said he agreed with the remarks of the Ex-Mayor. WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION AND THE

div.head: ASSASSINATIONS.
div.p: ASSASSINATIONS.

With the object of passing resolutions of condolence with the bereaved relatives of the late Chief Secretary (Lord F. Cavendish) and Under Secretary (Mr. Bnrke), a special meeting of the General Council of the Warrington Liberal Association was held on Monday evening in the club. The John Yonge was voted to the chair, and amongst the numerous company present were Messrs. Councillor Barker, John Bonnell, M. 'Bowden, J. H. Gornall, W. Burn, T. Bir- chall7 J. Green, H. Roberts, S. Barlow, W. Roberts W. • Chappell, G. Wallington, jun., kc. The CHAIRMAN said he apprehended the meeting was not c died for much speaking,—(hear, hear)—but for the purpose of giving expression to the profound grief which he was sure dwelt in the heart of everyone present. (Hear. hear.) He thought it would be perfectly impossible for anyone to describe the emotions or the thoughts which were at work in all their minds at the receipt of the telegraphic intelligence on Sunday morning. It would, he supposed. he perfectly true to say that no event of (coal tenour and dreadfulness had occurred within the life of any person in that room. The whole affair was so full of circumstances of heartfelt grief and sorrow that words failed one in endeavouring to express any at-let-plate feeling in regard to it. They were simply appalled by the event which had come upon them like a struggle. And yet, although they v. ere powerless to say much, they would be altogether neglectful of their duty if they did not in some way or other put on record somewhat of the feelings which dwelt within their hearts on that occasion. (Hear, bear.) Those feelings. he took it, would run in two channels. First of all they would all feel perfectly full of sympathy with the farnilie, ' which had been so grievously and foully bereaved ; and secondly, they would desire to express in the strongest way they could to the chief of the Liberal party—(applause)— and his admirable body, the profound sense of grief with ' which they were filled by this event. I hey must be con- scious that the hands of Mr. Gladstone and his c4eagues of , !lie Ministry would need all the strength and all the sup- port—(hear, hear)—whicb. the Liberal party at present
could give. them; and he hoped as the result of their brief I
meeting they would be able to send to that noble old
_ chieftain an expression of sympathy with him in this grief, which not alone affected him on account of the well-being _
of the party, but on account of his personil affection for Lord F. Cavendish; and also an earnest desire that he _ _
might have the wisdom given. him to carry on the policy

which he had been bold -enough to indicate, and do what in him lay for the entire pacification of Ireland. (Hear, bear, and applause.) Of course they were well aware that the feelings which had been prevalent since the intelligence reached them had been very much, if not altogether those produced by anger, but he trusted the hours which had since elapsed would have begun to have a beneficial effect on the minds of the people, and that the somewhat wild and reck- less statements which might have been made in the earlier consciousness of this event, had given place to feelings of calmness and more intelligent judgment; and that when the position was able to be looked at calmly and intelligently the country would feel that the palm of righteousness was the same palm,. and the palm of justice and brotherhood
perhaps after all the wisest part. He hoped Her Majesty's Government would be upheld by the united voice of the Liberal party to pursue that policy which they had so

courageously entered into. (Applause.) He called upon Mr. GORNALL to move the first resolution :—" The General Council of the Warrington Liberal Association views with the most profound concern and grief the terrible calamity which has befallen Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke, and desires to assure the bereaved families of their sincere and deep svmplthy in this unlooked for season of _ _ .
indescribable sorrow."—Mr. Gornall said he did not know
that he could add anything to express his sympathy with that resolution, more than that having worked for 15 years

amongst the Irish of Warrington he -did not believe one of them sympathised with the terrible calamity which had taken place. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He did not intend to make any remarks to his political opponents, but there were two matters which came before his
notice on the previous day which compelled him to come to the conclusion that the Tory party had no . _

sympathy with Ireland. A prominent Tory on the previous day said the lives of ten thousand Irishmen were of less importance than that of one Englishman. Ho (Mr. Gornall) totally disagreed with that statement. He believed, and he

was taught so from the pulpit of the chapel he attended, that the soul of an Irishman was of as great value as the soul of an Englishman. (Hear, bear.) Whilst a few gentlemen were perusing the news of the outrage on Sunday, feeling in great trouble and anxiety, with not the slightest iota of party spirit in their breasts, they were accosted by a priest of the Church of England, who, pointing to the pla- card, said "There is your new departure." He (Mr. Gornall) wished that man had been at the ,Wesleyan Chapel, where he would have beard everyone of them, as it were, crying with emotion at the mournful expressions of the minister. He felt that the clergyman as an Englishman had disgraced

himself. (Hear, hear, and applause.j Councillor BARKER, in seconding the motion, said words failed to express the detestation with which they regarded the calamity which had befallen the houses of Cavendish and Burke.

The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. BOWDEN, who was received with applause, moved "That this meeting begs to offer to the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, and the other members of Her Majesty's Govern- ment, their sincere sympathy and support in the terrible loss which the country has sustained by the assassination of Lord F. Cavendish aod Mr. Burke, and trusts that they may be enabled adequately to cope with the present great crisis in the affairs of the United Kingdom, and to persevere in such policy as may be wise and righteous for the entire pacification of the Irish nation at large." He said he need hardly say that since he heard of the outrage be had not been himself at all. (Hear, hear.) In fact if he had sustained a family loos he did not think he could have realised it more keenly; and he must acknowledge that its effect upon him physically had been very great. (Hear, hear.) When he heard of the assassinations his mind re- verted in the first place to the widow and children of Lord F. Cavendish; he did not like to picture to himself the pro- found misery that that family must be.plunged in by this abominable act. (Hear, hear.) Then he thought of that great man at the head Of affairs in this country, a man that had been assailed not only by his enemies across the chan- nel but also by the Tory party of thie country at a time when the very life of the nation was at stake. When he thought of this he had said in his own mind that those men who'would try to harm Her Majesty's Government when such crises were taking place, if they were not as bad as assassins were a near approach to it. (Hear, -hear, and applause.) Any men that would try to bring into disrepute a Government which was coping with a se; ions difficulty, were the protectors and the inciters of those people who were committing outrages. He felt sure there was no right-minded person but who deplored these assassinations. (Hear, hear.) At the same time they must not be driven to the other extreme. He put it to them as Englishmen—and possibly there were Irishmen present— whether, if they knew a family, and there were such fami- lies, in which there was a son who was a disgrace to that family, they would denounce the whole of the family as a bad lot? (Cries of "No.") Would they say that they were all partakers of that man's sin? (".No.") Certainly not; and if there were a few people in the Irish nation that had forgotten themselves and run into that kind of desperation which took place on Saturday night, they must not brand all the Irish as villains. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) Because some of them had cast aside all teligious restraints and their love to God, they must not say that all the rest of the Irish had done so. (Hear, hear.) He did not believe it. (Hear,-hear.) Even that day some Irish people in Warrington had deplored the assassinations with tears in their eyes. He hoped the Government would be sustained at this great crisis; and he was glad to see that the Conser- vative party were showing a little sympathy, if it were not almost too late. (Hear, bear.) With reference to the per- petrators of the crime he had his own thoughts, and he could not bring himself to believe they were Land Leaguers. (Hear, hear.) Fenians in Ireland, Communists in France, Socialists in Germany' and Nihilists in Russia, were, in his opinion, all animated by the same spirit; and he thought the time had really come when all honest men, and all religious men—(hear, hear)—should endeavour by all pos- sible means not to speak harsh words, but to live according to the truth, for truth alone could save them. (Loud applause.) Mr. SAMUEL BARLOW cordially seconded the resolution. He had, he said, great sympathy for the Irish in this matter, and he did not believe that in this act the Irish had had a hand. • He was afraid this outrage would be a serious blow to Mr. Gladstone, and from what he could gather would injure his health more than anything that had occurred for years; and he trusted the whole English people would sympathise with the Government and the Irish people in this great crisis. (Applause.) Mr. THOMAS Bancmann, •in supporting the resolution, expressed the hope that out of this great evil some good would come, as often happened; that it would unite the Irish people with the Liberal party, and show them that if Ireland had ever to be pacified it must come from that party whose great chieftain was W. E. Gladstone. (Applause.) Mr. GEO. WALmtscrrox, jun., also supported the resolu- tion, which was carried unanimously. Mr. JOHN BONNELL proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding, which was seconded by Mr. HENRY WHITHAM, who Suggested that Mr. H. Roberts should use what influence he possessed to induce the Mayor to call a town's meeting. In supporting the resolution, Mr. H. ROBERTS, referring to the question of a town's meeting said he did not feel at liberty to take part in anything Of the kind and for this reason. He made it his business to spend a great portion of , Sunday in seeing Irishmen and Englishmen, and eliciting ( from them their opinions on this terrible misfortune. During the day he was brought into personal contact with more than one prominent Conservative in the town, and he was thoroughly disgusted to find that, at a time like the present when the whole nation was appalled at the terrible tragedy, they could not even put party feeling aside, but must point the finger of scorn at the grand old chief, and say the assas- sinations were the result of his policy' even whilst they were coming from the church where they had been worshipping God. He could not join in Oolva's meeting with men who had opinion.; of this kind. He was afraid a town's meeting would only lead to such evidences of differences of opinion on this question that instead of having a happy result it would have an unhappy one. (Hear, bear.) He was met on Sun- day by Father Feeny.and in a kinder and more sympathetic a manner no man could have expressed his grief at the foul murder ; and great numbers. of Irishmen told him (Mr. Roberts) with voices trembling with emotion and tears almost running down their faces, that they would give any- thing, make any sacrifice, if they could undo this terrible act. (Hear, hear.) As the hour before the dawn eras said to be the darkest, he hoped this calamity might be only the immediate precursor of the brightest future for Ireland,and the least they could do, as Radicals, because he was proud to call himself a Radical, was to persevere in the face of all .he taunts that were thrown at them, and stand shoulder to shoulder with Irishmen, who were as anxious for the honour of their country as they (Englishmen) possibly could be. (Hear, hear.) Let him say a word on behalf of the Irish. Be had seen a number of them that day and there did not seem to be one that did not hold his head down for very shame. Let them (the Liberals) stand by them wherever they were. (Hear, hear.) At work there would be found Englishmen who would taunt them about this thing, and it would be hard for them to bear with the insults which would be levelled at them, and the least they could do was to offer their sympathy and support. (Hear, hear.) In this new policy which Mr. Gladstone had inaugurated, a policy which they believed must be blessed with great benefits for Ireland —if he was to carry it out it could only be by the united support of the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) Immediately their horror at this outrage had passed, the Tories would renew their attempts to defeat his policy ; the moment decency would allow them they would be ‘Z hounding " Mr. Gladstone as/they had done for the past two years, and do everything they possibly could to weaken his power. (Hear, bear.) Although the Government were taking the wisest course' there had not been a policy which called upon every Liberal so earnestly and so determinedly as this one to stand hy and help the grandest minister which England had ever known to carry with all his power and all his mind what was nothing more nor less than a policy of justice and peace to our sister country. (Loud applause.) The vote was carried by acclamation, and the chairman having responded, the meeting separated. The Secretary (Mr. H. Roberts) has received the follow- ing reply to the resolution forwarded to the Marquis of Hartington :—"Sir,—l am desired by the Marquis of Hart- ng,toon to beg that you will convey to the members of the Warrington Liberal Association his lordship's incere acknowledgment of the sympathy for himself and family

of the expressed in the resolution forwarded in your letter Bth inst., passed at a meeting of the General Couacil. la" sir/ yours faithfully, R. H. HOBART." Dear Sir,—For almost twenty years I have been the victim to what my varicus (lectors called organic weakness, and through the whole course of their t, cab-trent I received little or no relief, though I spent at least £5O altogether, I therefori gave up all hope of getting better. 12,1Iargreaves-street, Oldham, Nov. 17th, 1881:

Dear Sir,—Ever since I was four yea's of age, my parents in- form me that I have suffered from great weakness. At the present time, I am 21 years of age, and if the pal ticulars of my ease will be ot any service to you, I shall be only too happy to give them to you. For a great many years I have been under differeut doctors, and the last doctor I visited told me he could do no more for me; so he sent me to the Soothport Hospital, but after remaining there some time wiihout findirq, any benefit, I returned home. I have been treated as a consump- tive tatinit. I have earned very little money for my parents, seldom being able to work through being so weak, and most of the time I hive been under the dcctor's treatment. About three weeks ago I commenced wearing your " Magnetaire," and in a week's time I felt so strong that I began work, and have never been off work one hour since. I assure you I should never have thought it p,ssible that I should feel so str,ng as I di now, and you may depend upon it both I and my parents shall always recommend your Appliances. Yours faithfully, Mr. Lonsdale, ELIZABETH HIILLEY.

INDIGESTION, DEBILITY, &C. 175, Middleton-road, Oldham, Oct. 14th, 1881. Dear Sir,—On your last visit to Oldham I purchased from you a " Magnetaire " Belt. At that time I had been suffering for many years from indigestion, debility, accompanied with severe headaches. I had tried all k'nds of medicine, and been under several d ctors, but instead of getting better I gradually got worse. Hearing of such a number of Oldham people who had warn your Appliances with such beneficial results, I resolved to purchase the" Tilagneteire," and lam very grateful in being able to say that after wearing your Appliance, I began to improve in a wonderful manner, and in a short time I was completely cured. It is now about two years since I purchased your " Magnetaire," and I never felt stronger, healthier, and more cheertul than I do at the present time; and when I look back to the tima when I was such a great sufferer from indigestion, weakness, Bzc., I cannot help thinking that your " Magnetaire " is a great ble.sing to suffering humanity.—Yours truly. - Mr. R. 11, Broom-street, Hanley, Jan. 4th. 1882.

Dear Sir—When I came to you four months ago, I had been paralysed in one leg for ten years, the limb being perfectly cold and stiffened. I also suffered from scrofula badly, and was troubled with a very severe cough. I have worn the belt and soles you recommended ever since' with the following result:— 1 eau now walk very well with the leg that was previously stiff and numb, and can bend the joints, the circulation too is quite restored through my body, have lost the cough entirely and my face is very much better, the skin now being dry and much lighter in colour than before. We are all very highly satisfied with what your Appliances have done, and shall al- ways rec3mmend them with confidence in any similar case. My spirits and appetite are also much better.—Yours truly, Mr. B. Lonsdale. JNO. OBIFFITIIB.

Church Eaton, Stafford, December 26th. 1861 Sir,—ln behalf of my fellow-sufferers, and in justice to you I give you my experience of your Magnetaire." Some seven years ago I had a severe p tralytie attack which had left me with a stiff shoulder and arm, with little use in my hand. I used the electric remedies, then invented, for three years with benefit, and after that time, as I was convinced that I could not exocct any further relief from them at my age (now 76), I discontinued them. Hearing from Mr. Clendinnen of your Appliances (though without mws:ll faith in them), I purchased one of your Invigorators, and, to my surprise, in tea days I found my arm much more supple and useful, but the benefit I have received is very marked, and I have but little doubt that my limb, though very weak, will continue to improve under your Appliances. I wish you to send me a Magrietaire Friction Glove, as I think friction win cimplete the cute,— Yours, &e. Mr. R. I:onsdale. A. C. TALBOT.
