div.p: IV IDNES LOCAL BOARD.
IMPORTANT MEETING.

The monthly meeting of the Widnes Local Board was held tea Tuesday afternoon, at the offices, Alforde Chambers. Mr. F. U. Gcssage, J.P., presided, and there were also present Messrs. O'Keeffe, Kershaw, Sadler, 13ooth, Webster, Johnson, Carey, Pankburst, Forster, Shuttleworth, Wright, Midwood, Medley, Al;en (clerk), Roberts (engineer), and Dickson (nuisance inspector). MIL MIDWOOD AND THE SEWERAGE SCHEME. Mr. MeDwooh asked if the contract for the sewerage works was let ; secondly, what was the amount of it; thirdly, whether wevleave had been applied for on behalf of the Hutchinson trustees; and fourthly, if any offer as to way- leave had been made by the Board. Mr. KERSTIAW said the contract had been let—"the second tender" haying been successful. The price of the contract was a little below £12,000. A tender was put in at Some- thing like £1.500 less, but the committee decided to take the one e. about '£12,000, after considering the references. The Board must not, however, forget that the expenditure of this sum would only carry the sewer as far as Moorfield- lane. He believed that a wayleave had been asked for by Hutchinson's trustees, but no offer had been made by the Board, and the matter was. at present in abeyance. The question was one which could be dealt with by the committee which had to be appointed. Mr. MeDwoon was anxious to understand this matter of wayleave a little more particularly, as he was not at all satisfied with the explanation offered by Mr. Kershaw. It was very important before the minutes relating to the way leave were passed that they should be furnished with further information. He believed that three names had been men- tioned as arbitrators. , The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Midwood will you pleaze bring us to the actual point to which you are referring? - Mr. KERSHAW replied that Mr. Midwood was entirely wrong in his supposition, for no arbitrators had yet been fixed upon. [Mr. Midwood: I did not say there had.] Cer- tainly a proposal on the subject had been submitted by Hutchinson's trustees, but no decision had been arrived at. The Crum-Auer : Mr. Midwood, you are referring to what took place at the meeting on the 11th April? Mr. MIDWOOD: Yes. The CHAIRMAN: Well, we cannot deal with anything so far back. In fact, the matter you refer to arises out of the minutes of April 3rl, and we cannot wake up April 3rd again. Mr. Mrnwoon said it looked to him as if the Board had Offered wayleave to Hutchinson's trustees. The CHAIRMAN; I have got the printed minutes before me, and I don't see anything of the kind. Mr. SADLER: They said that terms had been offered. Mr. CAREY remarked that if Mr. Midwood had any ques- tion to ask in relation to the names of the arbitrators, the committee would be. glad to give a reply. The names of those gentlemen were, however, recorded, and he therefore scarcely understood what it was which Mr. Midwood desired to know. Mr. MflawooD replied that the minutes certainly conveyed to him the idea that some offer had been made. The CHAIRMAN: Well, Mr. Kershaw has answered that question by stating that the Board has not made any offer. Mr. MIDWOOD: I didn't hear that. The CHAIRMAN: But he said so, and we cannot go over the matter half a dozn times. He answered your next ques- tion by saying that Hutchinson's trustees had approached the Board, who had not favourably received their proposi- tion; and he also said that the Board had not made a counter offer. Mr. MIDWOOD : Well, I wish to know what the offer was. 31c. WRIGHT (rising) : That is my question. Mr. KERSHAW said the trustees wished them to adopt Ditton-road and the new street down to that road. As to ' the latter matter, he could only presume, and not speak with authority upon the point. He objected to do anything of the kind, but would rather at once recommend that the Board make an offer to pay a certain sum, as he was quite aware they could obtain the wayleave by Act of Parliament. All they required was a reasonable arbitrator. Mr. s7A.DLF.It said he should like to know how it was that these terms had not been before the Board previously. How was it that they were not submitted to the Joint Committee who had to deal with the matter'? Mr. KERSHAW: We have dealt with the terms before. Mr. SADLER : But still you call upon a man to agree to a thing of which he does not know anything! Mr. KERSHAW : It is for the members of the Board to in- vestigate these things. Mr. CAREY observed that he might explain for the satis- faction of Mr. Midwood and Mr. Sadler, who did not appear to quite understand the position of affairs, that some cor- respondence had taken place with Messrs. Hutchinson and Co. about the wayleave, but whether the correspondence originated from the Health Committee, who had the sewer- age question in hand a little time ago, or from the Joint Committee, he did not quite remember. Whichever commit- tee it was, the fact still remained the same that the terms proposed were not considered such as it was advisable to accent without arbitration. They must understand with re- gard' to this particular sewerage scheme, that, so far as he knew, the matter was precisely the same as if the Board were dealing with a railway company, .for they possessed the power to go through the land belonging to the trustees, or, in fact, any other land, with the sewer they proposed to construct, and the amount of the payment they should make had to be settled by arbitration. It did not really matter to the Board whether the question of amount was settled now, or when the- sewer was completed. He bad been told that Hutchinson's trustees were lie this position— they were not able to make a bargain with the Board, as the Court of Chancery did not permit them to do so without going to arbitraVon. As far as he understood the question, Hutcnineon's trustees simply wished to place it before hon- ourable and reasonable arbitrators, and to be paid whatever

they might adjudicate, whether the amount be large or small. The Board had agreed that the question should go to arbitration, and the particular stage of the preliminary proceedings at which they had arrived at the moment was that the names of three gentlemen had been mentioned as arbitrators, which selection was approved at the meeting on the 11th ult. What was asked, in order to make the matter more simple, was that "they " should have one arbitrater, but the Hutchinson's trustees said they would rather have one en each side, and a referee. Mr. KERsraw : They asked us to name three gentlemen, and we did so, on which they turned ronnd and said, "No, we appoint Mr. Jones." Mr. CAREY said he believed the course proposed to be adopted by the trustees was the usual one. Mr. KERSHAW : Yes, but they withdrew from the position they had taken. The CHAIRMAN : Well, what it really comes to is, that tLe gentlemen named have not been accepted by anyone. Mr. WEBSTER : He says that the question of the sewer could not be settled without arbitration.. .

The CHAIRMAN (to Mr. Webster) :" You are quite mia- taker, sir. He said that the question of easement could not be settled without going to the Court of Chancery. Mr. WEBSTER : Well, if that is so, how is it that they have made this offer. They can settle that, and-why can- not they settle this? Perhaps if we go to arbitration, it will cost more than the wayleave. Mr. MnosvooD observed that the important roint,,in his opinion, was that the Board had not made the trustees any offer, as the result of this was that when the matter went to arbitration they would be liable for the expenses on both , sides. That was a very serious consideration indeed, as things were now going on in Widnes. He wished to know if the Board intended to make Hutchinson's trustees an offer. Certainly, it did not appear as if they did, because the three gentlemen to be engaged in the arbitration had been already selected. Mr. KERSHAW : You are really wrong; this is the offer of , the trustees to us. Mr. MIDWOOD: I quite understand that, but what I wish to know is why the Board have not made the trustees an offer, as those gentlemen do not appear to have the necessary power to come to any terms. Mr. KERSHAW : Tell me who is competent to make that offer. The CHAIRMAN did not see how Mr. Kershaw could answer Mr. Midwood's question ; but it would be perfectly competent for that gentleman to br:ng the matter forward arsain. -Mr. CARET said Mr. 3lidwood was quite right in suppos- ing that it might be to the advantage of the Board to make the trustees an offer. Though the members had had inter- views with the trustees, they had not made them any offer in writing. If Mr. Midwood's remarks amounted to this— that it would be best for the Board to make an offer in writ- ing, so as to nut themselves on the right side, he agreed with him. Perhaps it would be well if Mr. Midwood would put his ideas on the sublect into writing. Mr. KErtsuAw considered it would be more prudent to discuss the question in committee. Mr. MIDWOOD next referred to a case of arbitration which had come under his notice, where the land had previously been let out for building purposes. The price offered for it was is. per lineal yard; the amount of the award was £ll is. Gd., and the costs of the arbitratioa £l3O. The discussion then dropped. APPOINTMENT OF A SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. On the motion of Mr. PANSITCRST, seconded by Mr. MID- wool), it was resolved that the Sewerage Commi,See should comprise the members of the Joint Highway and Health C ommittees.

ASSOCIATION OF LOCAL BOARDS. On the proposition of Mr. CARES-, seconded by Dr. BOOTH, it was agreed that the chairman of the Board, and Mr. Handley, the chairman of the Finance. Committee, should form the deputations to the meetings of the Associa- tion of Local Boards.

div.head: LOCAL RATING.
div.p: LOCAL RATING.

The CHAIRMAN r:ad a communicatl-on from a Welsh Local &aid in favour of Boards taking united action sa that royalties and ground rents might be taxed pro rota with other revenues. The coal raised in the district referred to in 1880 was 4443,020 tons, realising a royalty of £160,000, of which sum not one penes:,' was paid to the local rates! Ttere were also during the same period 40,000 houses in the union which were paving a ground rent of about £50,000, and yet this large sum was entirely exempted from rating. In conclusion, the chairman (Mr. Gossage) said he con- sidered the subject a very proper one for their consideration,' and, upon his suggestion, the communication was referred to the General Purposes Committee. ECUNOMICAL PROSPECTS.—THE LE7EL CROSSING NUISANCE. The Highway Committee's minutes showed that a letter had been received from the London and North-Western Railway Co., stating that they contemplated laying down ' add tional "cross over roads," which they honed would, with . improved working arrangements,rnaterially reduce the amount

of shunting at Waterloo-road level crossing. The committee recommended that notice lie given the company that unless the gates be made the full width of the road, according to the Board's minutes of the 14th February, or wicket gates put at each side of the road, the Board should insist upon the shunting being discontinued. Mr. KERSHAW moved the adoption of the minutes, and re- marked that he was determined, as chairman of the commit- tee, that during the coming year the work should be done better and in a more economical manner, if the committee would support him. As to the level crossing matter, they would remember that in a previous communication with Mr. Shaw, the district manager, that gentleman stated that the company were laying down additional "shunts " near Carter- house bridge, and also shifting the water tank nearer Ditton; so that the long trains might not be stopped. Now the complaint of the Board was not in reference to the lone- trains, but as to the shunting. His advice was that if the railway company would not proceed to do the work, the Board should take other measures for the purpose of com- pelling them to do so. Mr. MIDWOOD seconded the proposition as to the minutes, and said he heartily joined in the observations which had fallen from Mr. Kershaw in respect to keeping the expenses down. He (the speaker) was certainly of opinion that a great amount of money was being spent in carrying out the work of tae Board, and some of the bills submitted for pay- ment were of a most unreasonable character. lie remem- bered one in which the repairs to a barrow were placed at 175., whereas a new one could not have cost much more. As to the Waterloo-road crossing, he considered it a terrible nuisance. The men connected with it were constantly opening and closing the gates. He remembered that when he was a member of that Board in previous years, he formed one of a deputation to the company in reference to this very matter, and they received a promise that the gates should never be shut more than four minutes at a time. This agreement the company had entirely failed to carry out, as the other night he waited eight minutes at the gates before he was allowed to pass. Mr. CAREY expressed a desire to know what was meant by the " cross over roads." He had understood that the company were going to put in some crossings on the Liver- pool side of the old station, which would materially diminish the difficulty which at present existed at the Waterloo-road croesing. He suggested that the Highway Committee should make some enquiries as to what the rail- way company proposed to do. MIDWOGD : We ought to insist upon the company giving us some answer as to what their intentions are. • The CHAIRMAN thought that if the company had "cross over roads " nearer Liverpool, they would be in a position • to deal with all the traffic without going near the Waterloo- road crossing. Mr. KERSHAW said the matter would not be remedied in the way suggested by Mr. Grossage. The CHAIRMAN : then the only way is either to put a bridge under or over. Mr. KE,RSHAW : Mr. Shaw acknowledged that our request was reasonable.

Mr. CAREY : Yes, and I believe that Mr. Shaw is ready to recommend the company to do what is right and reasenaLle ; but before you put the resolution, I should prefer to move an amendment, to the effect that we ask the London and North- Western for a tracing in order that we may know what they propose to do. Mr. MIDWOOD said that, as far as he was concerned, he did not think there was anything unreasonable in the minutes, and he should prefer that they be passed as they were.

div.head: UPTON QUARRY.
div.p: UPTON QUARRY.

Mr. CARRY asked if the surveyer had satisfied himself as to a remedy having been provided to meet the complaints of the Board in regard to Upton Quarry. Mr. HIGGINSON said the owner stated that the walls pro- tecting th 3 quarry had been their present height from time immemorial, and he did not see the necessity for raising them.

The CgmamAN : I do not see that the fact of the walls having been as they are from time immemorial meets the difficulty. That is rather a long time, certainly, but it does not deal with the present ! Dr. BOOTH considered the place in a very dangerous con- dition.

The minutes of the Highway Committee were then passed, with the exception of the one suggesting that the Board in- sist upon the railway company discontinuing the shunting, which was struck out. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE: MR. MIDWOOD AND THE

div.head: ENGINEER.
div.p: ENGINEER.

The Gee and Water Committee's minutes showed that the illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 16.63. It was proposed that the offer of Dr. Campbell Brown to test four samples of water per annum, at a cost of £l3, be accepted, the analysis to be according to Dr. Frankland's process. The offer of Messrs. Lea and Sons to supply slack for the two years ending 20th April, 1884, was accepted at the following rates :—Delivered at Netherley, 5.5. 3d. per ton; ditto a Steel's Well, ss. 9d. per ton. It was recom- mended that the pumping be discontinued on Sundays when there was an ample supply of water in the reservoir, and the men's wages reduced proportionately. Mr. MIDWOOD said he had seen a statement in the papers to the effect that the Board had been losing £375 yearly owing to slack being used instead of coal at the boilers. Mr. PANKIPORST stated that the matter referred to by Mr. Midwood had been already fully discussed by the commit.,:e and also by former committees. After referring to what Mr. Gaskell, jun., and Mr. Brown had said upon the subject in the past, he observed that the committee had decided to give the proposal to use slack a two years' trial. Mr. MinwooD considered that as they had an engineer to the Board, and paid large salaries to various officials, they onglat to do what they could to save the money of the rate- payers. It was not for the members of the Board to have to make such discoveries as these. He had been informed that the gentleman to find this matter out was a late member of the Board, and the question arose of where the engineer had been all these years not to discover it.
The discussion then dropped, and the recommendations of the committee were adopted, with the exception of the one proposing to accept the offer of £l3 .for an analysis on Dr. Frankland's process.

div.head: HOSPITAL.
div.p: THE HOSPITAL.
Mr. SADLER moved, and Mr. -MARTLEY seconded the motion for the adoption of the minutes of the Hospital Committee, which contained nothing of public importance, and the resolution was passed.

div.head: HEALTH CF THE DISTRICT.-VACCINATION RETURN'S.
div.p: THE HEALTH CF THE DISTRICT.-VACCINATION RETURN'S.

The minutes of the Health Committee contained the medi- cal officer's report, which showed that the births for the month had been 93, or at the rate of 44.6 per 1,000; deaths 48, or 23 04 per 1,000, including 13 of children under one year, 12 between one and five years; and two from zyrnotic disease. Mr. Dickson reported that several cases of scarlet fever and measles bad been reported throughout the district. Several of these were now convalescent, and the others were progressing favourably. The attention of the committee had been drawn to the question of street hawking; and it had been decided to defer the consideration of the subject until the fair question had been decided. Mr. CAREY, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said he wished to draw the attention of the Board to the vac- cination returns' which he thought very satisfactory. The number of births registered had been 549; successfully vac- cinated, 429; dead, unvaccinated, 51; postponed by medical certificate, 28; left the neighbourhood, or could not be found, 37; and defaulters, 4. Mr. IUIDWOOD made a complaint to the effect that the night-so;1 contractor's men were in the habit of damaging the brick work of water closets, &c. If they found one brick loose they managed to knock two or three others out. Mr. CAREY said the contract with the gentleman in ,1 question was a very strict one, and he was liable for such I injury. Particulars of any damage could be furnished to 1 the committee.

The minutes were passed. Mr. WRIGHT remarked that the committee were desirous that the Board should reconsider the desirability of con- tinuing the fair in Widnes. It bad been suggested that the various owners of open land in the town should be written to, asking whether they would promise not to let spaces for shop, s, &c., if the Board decided to discontinue the fair. He moved that this course be adopted. Mr. SADLER seconded the resolution, which was agreed to unanimously.

div.head: FINANCE.-TIIE DISCOUNT QUESTION.
div.p: FINANCE.-TIIE DISCOUNT QUESTION.

Mr. SHUTTLEWORTII moved, and Mr. WRIGHT secondedl the adoption of the minutes of the Finance Committee, wltich was agreed to. It appeared that several consumers had neglected to pay their gas and water accounts according to conditions; but they had made application for the dis- count. The committee's recommendation was that it be noti allowed, and the printed comditions, be strictly enforccd.

div.head: ELECTION EXPENSES.
div.p: THE ELECTION EXPENSES.

Mr. WEBSTER said he had seen a report in the local papers to the effect that the expenses of the late election were so high owing to so many persons being present on tilt Board's premises during its progress. Mr. Beasley's bill was seven guineas. Mr. KERSHAW did not remember having made a state- ment like that referred to by the last speaker. Mr. Webster must not forget that Mr. Beasley was paid for acting as a public official; and he (Mr. Kershaw) did not think he had been over remunerated for the services he rendered. They had the benefit of Mr. Beasley's advice and direction for an entire fortnight; one night he was with them until ten o'clock, and then there was the day of election. Mr. MtowooD suggested that the observatrons of Mr. Webster related more to the extra expenses .than to the charge made by Mr. Beasley. Mr. KERSHAW: You must not always take notice of news-, paper reports, for they are not invariably col rect. (Laugh- ter.) Mr. MARTLEY (humorously): They are always correct, Mr. Chairman.

div.head: PLEASANT INCIDENT.
div.p: A PLEASANT INCIDENT.

The CHAIRMAN referred to the. fact that the Board•room that day contained a good selection of beautiful pictures, and that these, together with a number of books, had been bought for the Hospital from the proceeds of one day's match by the Football Club. The hearty thanks of the Board were due to the members. (Cries of hear, hear.)

div.head: 'THE IRISH ASSASSINATION.
div.p: 'THE IRISH ASSASSINATION.

Mr. GOSSAGE said the Board ought not to separate, as one of the public bodies of the kingdom, without expressing the horror and detestation with which they had beard of the fearful murder in Ireland. He suggested that it was per- fectly competent for them to express to the survivors of the late Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke the assurance of their heartfelt sympathy with them. Those who were in favour of so doh3g would signify their assent in the usual way. .

The resolution was unanimously agreed to. Dr. O'KEEFFE said he was exceedingly anxious, as an Irishman, to give expression to the horror and detestation with which he regarded the dreadful crime; and he had been

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY MAY 13, 1882. WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY MAY 13, 1882. WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.

asked to do so on behalf of his countrymen in Widnes, who universally viewed the atrocious murder and assassination with feelings of loathing. A more cold-blooded and demoniacal outrage could not possibly have been committed; and he be- lieved there was nothing more horrible on record in the annals of history, even if they included the action of the Nihilists in Russia, or the excesses connected with the revolution in France. When he first heard the news on Sunday, he thought it was merely a hoax, and he, therefore, gave no credit to it ; but when ho found it con- firmed on Monday morning, he was stunned, and walked about like one who had received a most dreadful blow. He believed

this had been the feeling of every person who had keard of this assassination. The crime certainly assumed even a more heinous shape when it was remembered that the most amiable nobleman, Lord Frederick Cavendish, went to Ire • land as a messenger of peace from this country to that un- fortunate land which had been suffering for so long a time. He felt sure that he was expressing the feeling of every Irishman when he said that he sincerely hoped the perpetra- tors of this mast horrible crime would very soon be found and delivered up to justice. He was nearly certain that there was not a single person who would afford them shelter; and he had no doubt that if they were known they would be hunted down like wolves, or other wild Ceasts. He was thoroughly confident that they would not be left long at large, but be delivered up to justice. (Applause.) MR. MIDWOOD AND THE SEWAGE SCHEME.

Mr. Min'lT,ro-or. said he should like to know how the sewage scheme was going on? Mr. KERSHAW : There is no money being paid. Mr. MiDwooD made a remark as to a certain sum having been put down in the accounts, upon which Mr. KERSHAW replied that this was for the old sewer. Mr. INlmwooD : It will not do to put things in that way. It was £3OO and something, and it is for the sewer which is at present going on,—not for some other old sewer which was there when this work was commenced. Mr. KERSHAW : We cannot do the work without paying for it.

Mr. MlDwoop : That I quite understand, but it has been suggested that it was three hundred and odd pounds paid for some old sewe?. Mr. KERSHAW : That is a misunderstanding. Mr. MIDWOOD : Bless me! I cannot be always misun- derstanding. Mr. KERSHAW : Who said that it was for the old sewer? Mr. MIDWOOD: Mr. Pankhurst. _

_ Mr. KERSHAW : He is speaking off the book. I have made it my business to go down there, and I consider the job, as far as it has gone, one that cAnnot be beat. I have been " inside " the place. and I think there is every credit due to the engineer of the work, thus far. This termin ted the proceedings.

edge.—Dr. O'Keeffe deposed to visiting the prosecutor at his house' on the 17th ult. He was suffering from a frac- tured fibula of the left leg. There was a slight discoloura- tion and contusion immediately over the seat of the fracture. The fracture had been caused by direct violence, and rot from a fall. Kelly was under his care, and some time would elapse before he was able to walk.—P.S. Strickland gave evidence as to apprehending the prisoner on the night of the 20th ult., in the prosecutor's bedroom. When told upon what charge he was apprehended, he said Kelly and himself had " made it right." The fcllowing morning Kelly was formally charged, and he replied lam innocent. I did put Kelly and his wife to the door."—Mr. Moore then addressed the Bench why the prisoner should not be coin-1 mitted for trial, stating there was not a single tittle of evi- dence upon which the grand jury would return a true bill. —Mr. Gossage said the Bench had carefully considered the evidence, and they thought they would not be doing their duty if they did not give the grand jury a chance of cutting this Lii. He thought from the evidence which had been brought before them there was not the slightest chance. of this happening.—Prisoner was then formally committed for trial.—Mr. Moore applied for the prisoner to be released on bail, which the magistrates granted, the prisoner in £BO and two sureties of £4O.

ASSAULT ON A WORK'S FOREMAN.—John Malone, a labourer, was charged with unlawfully assaulting James Mullen.—The complainant is the foreman of the Atlas Chemical Works, and on Saturday at noon be paid the de- fendant his wages. During the evening of that day he had occasion to enter the yard of the works, where the defendant met him and demanded some money. This demand not being complied with, he attackea the complainant, struck him on the face with his fist and in other parts of the body. —Patrick Riley, a labourer, corroborated this statement.— Defendant stated the complainant struck him on the arm with a brick, and that, had it mot been for the witness Riley, he would have choked him.—A boy, John Murray, said he saw the complainant send a brick at the defendant.—The defen- dant was fined £1 and 10s. 6d, costs, or a month's hard labour.

THE SCHOOL BOAPD AT IiVORIC-Mr. Danby, clerk to the School Board, summoned seven persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school. There were no points of interest raised in the cases, and the usual fine of ss. in- cluding costs was imposed upon the following :—Catherine Howard, Peter Riley, Hugh Nixon, Thee. Welsh, Margaret Allen, Robert Hamilton, Pat Quinn.

THEFT OF A PAIR OF BOOTS.—Wm. Rothery, a tramp, was brought up charged with stealing a pair of lace-up boots, the property of John Cartwright, living at 8, Victoria-ter- race.—The prosecutor on the 15th inst. placed the boots in the saddle room of Mr. Barrington's premises. During that day they were abstracted, and until he was shown them by the police on Saturday; he had not seen them since. On Saturday, P.C. 991 found the prisoner asleep in a new house wearing the boots, and he took him into custody. Prisoner denied the theft, and stated he had purchased them in Liver- pool. He now pleaded guilty, and he was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour. AN UNCONTROLLABLE YOUTH.—A boy named WM. J. Hobley, 15 years of age, was charged with stealing a pair of driving reins, of the value of is., the property of Mr. Hy. Singleton, of Victoria-road, Widnes.—John Quinn, labourer for prosecutor, said he missed the reins on Friday, and on Tuesday the prisoner confessed to stealing them.—P.C. Timperley then apprehended the prisoner, who said he was paid to steal them.—The mother of the boy said her son was completely beyond her control, and she would be glad if the Bench would find him a place on the ship Clio. She was willing to pay for his maintenance.—The boy having been previously before the Bench, was committed to gaol for a month.

A FAILING FOR " TIN."—A. woman named Margaret Travis was charged with stealing a can of the value of is. 61 the property of Patrick Cavanagh, of Prescot,—The plisoner who pleaded guilty, was stated to b a dissolute character. The Bench sentenced her to two months' bard labour.

WORSITIPPERS.OF BACCHUS.—The following persons were each fined for drunkenness :—Betsy Connor, George Lynch, Patrick MeTartland, Julia Croyden, John Furber, John Marr, Bernard O'Rafferty. BREACHES OF THE HIGHWAY ACT.—Joseph Dagnall was summoned for a breach of the Highway Act. On the 3td inst. P.C. Almond found the defendant's horse walking in the highway without anyone in charge of it.—Defendant was fined is. and costs.

EXTENSIVE ROBBERIE3 FROM FLATS.—.Tohn Nash sen., John Nash jun., Mary Nash and Annie Nash, members of one family, were brought up on remand charged with steal- ing a quantity of clothing and wearing apparel worth £l, fromthe flat Carrie.—Tlie Superintendent withdrew the charge against Nash sen.—James Ward, the captain of the flat, said he lived at Runcorn. At six o'clock on the 27th ult, he left the flat in the canal at Widnes. The following morning when be returned he discovered the padlock bad been broken from the door of the cabin, which had been ransacked. In addition to clothing about Bs. worth of provisions had also been taken.—P.C. Coates stated that about three o'clock on Friday morning, the 28th ult., whilst in Mersey-road, he saw the prisoner John walking towards Runcorn bridge \with a large canvass bag over his shoulder. The officer intercepted him, and in answer to his inquiries the prisoner said he was taking his clothing from his flat.—John Wilkinson' assistant to J. B. Imison, pawnbroker, Runcorn deposed that on the 28th ult. the prisoner Annie Nash offered the blanket produced in pledge, and 23. Gd. was advanced upon the article. The girl said her mother or brother had sent her; he could not tell which.—P.C. Barker apprehended the prisoner Annie Nash on the Ist instant at her home. He told the prisoner Mary that be had found some stolen property pawned by her daughter, and said it was his intention to search the hcuse. She said he was welcome to do so' and he discovered some of the stolen property concealed. The following day he apprehended the prisoner Mary also on the charge of theft. The girl stated that she had pawned the articles for her brother, and the prisoner Mary denied any knowledge of the theft.—P.S. Robinson said he received the prisoner John into custody from the Rochdale police. When charged with the robbery he replied "all right."—The prisoners were committed to take their trial at next Liverpool Sessions. They were,then charged with breaking into the flat Garston between 6 o'clock p.m. on the 27th ult.'and 6 a.m, on the 28th ult., and stealing therefrom a quantity of wearing apparel, the property of the Captain Halloran, who resides at Penketh.—The evidence having been given, the prisoners were also committed for trial on this charge.

SATURDAY.—Before Mr. George Artingstall (chairman), and Alderman Chandley. HEARTLESS THEFT FROM AN OLD MAN.—Two young men, named James Sullivan and James Arnold, licensed hawkers, the former of Doncaster, and the latter of Man- chester, were charged with stealing from the person of John Cassidy, a silver verge watch of the value of 15s. Mr. Cassidy, who is an old man, 92 years of age, was, it appared, sitting on a chair placed on a footpath in Church-street near to his daughter's house, on the previous morning, when the two defendants who had been drinking in the Gladstone Arms, came up. They entered into cmversation with the old man, who thought they were standing unnecessarily near to him. Presently he felt Arnold's hands at his watch. The prisoners then quickly walked away, and the old man as best he could followed. A young man appeared in the street, and Mr. Cassidy called to him to stop the prisoners, which he did. They were subsequently taken into custody and the watch found in the street.—Both prisoners pleaded guilty, and in extenuation of the offence said they were drunk.—Mr. Artingstall said he considered the men had committed a cool and deliberate theft, and were no doubt adept thieves.---Each prisoner was sentenced to three months hard labour, and the pedlar's licenses were cancelled. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), and the Ex-Mayor (Councillor Fairclough.) ASSAULT WITH A BRlCK.—Patrick McCarty, a labourer, was charged with being drunk on Saturday evening, and also with assaulting Hannibal Loocock. Loocock said whilst he was standing in his own back yard, the prisoner sent a brick which struck him on the head.—Prisoner said he was "standing in his own defence," and the Bench fined him 103. and costs, or the alternative of 14 days' imprison- ment.

A VIOLENT PrusoNEß.—Peter Baguley, a young fellow, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Market- street, and also with assaulting P.C. Bruen whilst in the execution of his duty. In Market-street on Satuiday night, the prisoner was drunk and disorderly. The constable re- quested him to behave himself and go home, when he became very violent and kicked the officer many times.—The Chief Constable observed that it took six policemen to bring the prisoner to the Bridewell—four to carry him and two to keep the crowd away.—A fine of 103. and costs was inflicted. FAMILY DESERTION.—Martin Noon, a middle-aged man, was charged with ruening away from the borough, leaving his wife and four children chargeable to the common fund of the Union.—Mr. Harbourne, relieving officer, said on the 2nd inst. the prisoner's wife applied to him for relief. He visited the house and found the family in a most dee.titute condition and the children almost naked. They were on the verge of starvation. He informed the woman to apply to the Guardians, which she did, and was ordered into the workhouse. A warrant was issued against the prisoner, and P.C. Wheatley apprehended him in Buttermarket-street on Saturday.—ln defence, the prisoner said he went away to get work, and he had now got a place in Manchester. His reason for coming into the town on Saturday was to take his family away with him.—Mr. Harbeurne said the Guardians had expended 103.—Prisoner promised to pay the money and remove his family, and the Bench, to give him an opportunity of doing so, adjourned the case one month. DRUNKE.NNESS.—The following persons were charged with being drunk, and a penalty was imposed in each case: —Thomas Rabbitt, Ellen Frankland, Naylor Horrocks, John Noon (58th appearance), Thomas Kelly. Thomas Garrity, on a similar charge, was committed to gaol for a month. The prisoner, it was proved, had acted in a most obscene manner to several children. Before Alderman Holmes and Councillor Fairclough. Wm. Durkin, bricksetter, Town Hill, was summoned for not sending his children Thomas and William regularly to school. Mr. Riley, the attendance officer, said this case had been dealt with several times by the School Attendance Committee. With the exception of a very short period the school fees had been paid by the Board of Guardians since 1879, and the children did not attend half-time, and never passed an examination. William had attended school 135 times and Thomas 121 out of a possible 2130. The Bench inflicted a fine of 55., including costs, in each case.—Peter Baguley, a hawker, who had this morning been fined 103. and costs for assaulting the police, was summoned for not sending his son to school. Mr. Riley said it was a singular thing that the defendant had to be Jarought up every fort- night, and this was his seventh appearance on this charge. The boy was in the street mid-day and mid-night. A fine of ss. was imposed.—James Warburton, labourer, Turner's- fold, who had had free schooling for his children for three years, was brought up on a similar summons. Richard had attended 50 times out of a possible 160, and Daniel 95 out of a possible 200. Defendant was fined Sc. in each case.— Mr. Riley also summoned the following persons, and a fine of sa. was inflicted in each case :—Daniel Siasmith, glass works, Elizabeth-street; John Hardy, tanner, Dial-street; Cornelius Lennon, forgeman, Portland-street; John Town- ley, brewery labourer, Haydock-street ; Pat Hanlon, hawker, Sankey Green; Mary Ann Gerard, Eustace-street; Henry Aston, tanner, Dal lam-lane. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. George Artingstall and Alderman Davies. DRUNICENNESS.—James Cogham, an old man, was charged with being drunk in Irlam. street, on the previous night, and he was fined ss. and costs. ATTEMPT TO DEFRAUD THE CHESHIRE LINES COMPANY. —William Davies, a young man, was charged with riding from Liverpool to Warrington without paying his fare, with intent to defraud the Cheshire Lines Company.—Thomas Clegg, ticket collector, said the prisoner attempted to make his exit from the station, on the previous day, without pro- ducing his ticket. Witness stopped him, when the prisoner said he had paid his last is. Gd. in purchasing a ticket, which he had given up to a porter. Afterwards he offered to pay his fare; but the officials would not accept it. A telegram was despatched to Liverpool, and a reply was re- ceived stating no Warrington ticket had been issued by the train from which the prisoner alighted.—Prisoner told a pitiful tale of his father being on the point of death at Great Budworth, and he was ordered to pay costs, 43. Od., and the fare, Is. ed.

WEDNESDIY.—Before Alderman Davies. ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM THE PERSON.—James Butler (18) and John Murray (16), " forgehands," were charged with having, in company with John Millett and Thomas Garritty, on Saturday last, stolen from the person of Wil- liam Cleaver, in a passage between Bewsey and Froghall Bridges; the sum of 4s.—Remanded. COMMENCING HIS CAREER.—Andrew. Carney, aged nine, living with his parents at 3, Fennel-street, was charged with having, on the Ist inst., stolen from the shop of Joseph Lawless, bacon and cheese factor, Market Hall, about 3s. in coppd.—lt appears that the little fellow is the son of John Carney, a joiner, whose wife carries on the business of a second-hand clothes dealer at 3, Fennel-street. On Monday night, the Ist inst., about five minutes past ten, P.C. Seed was in Horsemarket-street when he received information that there was a little fellow under a grid at the Market Hall, in Golden Square. The constable went there and found the little prisoner who said he had been playinc, " henny " and the Market Hall keeper had locked him in. He was released, and afterwards taken home. Nothing further was heard until Friday, when Mr. Lawless reported to the police that 3s. in copper had been extracted from a drawer in his shop. Enquiries were then made and P.C. Seed said when young Carney was taken to the, police station he had 10d. in his hand, but he said it belonged to his parents. He was charged With the offence, and be said "I did not take 35., I only took 2s. and I went away and spent it." The following morning he went to Manchester where he remained until Monday.—Alderman Davies : How did he get to Man- chester ?,—P.S. Cox: He says he walked there.—The Chief Constable : But he had money to go with.—The mother, who said she could not manage her lads, as she had to be out too many days, consented to the lad being birched, and he was ordered to receive six strokes. THIIRSDIY.—Before Captain Litton. REMIND CASE.—Patrick Mannion and William Armstrong were charged with stealing 1871 b. of lead, the property of Messrs. Roberts, Dale and Co., Mersey-street; and also with receiving the same knowing it to have been stolen.—Man- pion is a marine store dealer of Higher Bank-street, and Armstrong a carter in the employ of Mr. Lunt. At nine o'clock this morning Joseph Heyes, a workman at Messrs. Roberts, Dale and Co., saw the prisoners in the yard engaged in loading a "donkey cart" with lead, which they covered over with bags. He informed the manager, Mr. McConville. In the meantime the prisoners had departed from the pre- mises, but the manager overtook them in Wharf-street, and finding the lead on the cart gave them in custody. In con- sequence of a chimney falling there a few months ago there were many tons of lead on the premises.—The prisoners were

remanded. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Mr. John White. THE FRUITS OF BAD COMPANY. John Millett (15), Thomas Garrity (17), James Butler (18), John Murray (17), were brought up, on remand, charged with having, on the 67.11 instant, stolen 4s. from the person of William Cleaver, a youth described as of weak intellect.-e—Mr. Moore appeared for Millett, and pleaded not guilty. The other boys stated they were guilty of " receiving, but not stealing."—lt appears the prosecutor and the prisoners work at the forge, and on Saturday moening the prosecutor received his wages and a 'gratuity from his master, Samuel Wakefield, which amounted to Gs. Gd. As he was walking home from his work between Bewsey Bridge and Frogball-lane, the four pri- soners went up to him. Millett entered into conversation with Cleaver, and whilst so engaged put his band in Cleaver's trousers pocket and abstracted 4s. They then left Cleaver, who went home and the money was equally divided amongst them. Afterwards the prisoners were apprehended, and made statements throwing the onus of the robbery on Millett.—Mr. Moore addressed the Bench on behalf of Millett, remarking on his previouS good character. —Mr. Hunt pointed cut that Millett was the youngest of the prisoners, tnd said he believed he was the tool of the other prisoners, than whom there were no more expert thieves in Warrington.—Millett, who bad not been before the court before, was fined 103. and 4s. costs ; but the other prisoners, who had been before the court several times'previously, were each sentenced to a month's hard labour. THE THEFT OF LEAD.—Patrick Mannion and William Armstrong were charged, on remand, with stealing 1871bs. of lead of the value of 233., the property of Messrs. -Roberts, Dale and Co.—Mr. Moore defended Mannion.—The facts of the case have been reported, and the evidence ha-ving been given, Mannion was committed to gaol for three months, and Armstrong was sentenced to a month's hard labour. PROVOKING LANGUAGE.—A married woman named Ellen Warburton was charged with having, on the Bth May, used to Elizabeth Meehan language calculated to provoke a breach of the peace, and she was bound over to be of good baaviour.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Brock (chairman) and F. H. Gossage.

INTERFERING WITH A POLICE OFFICER. —JAIN Hannon was charged with assaulting P.C. Skinner in the execution of his duty, and also with having been drunk and disorderly. The officer stated that on Saturday evening he was taking a prisoner named Sweeney in charge, in Waterloo-road, when Hannon, who was standing near Walker's vaults, rushed up and did his best to liberate the man. He continued this conduct as far as the police station, when he was taken away by some of his companions. Prisoner was drunk at the time.—P.C. Johnson gave evidence in corroboration.—Han- non, in reply to the Bench, admitted having been drunk, but denied having committed the assault.—lnspector Barnett said this was the prisoner's 19th appearance at the court. In 1880 he was sent to gaol two months, and during last year three months for a like offence.—Prisoner was committed to gaol one month, with hard labour. HEAVY SENTENCE FOR STEALING SCRAP IRON.-- John Erawley and Joseph Dawson, two men, were charged with stealing a quantity of scrap iron, the property of the Widnes Limestone Co., on the 26th ult. Thomas Roberts, foreman at the works, said he lived in John-street, and on the date mentioned missed the iron, now produced, from the works. Two days afterwards, he visited the shop of Mr. Forster, marine store dealer, with a policeman, and found the stolen iron.—A lad who lives on the Widnes Marsh was next called, and said that on the 26th ult. he was working for Alfred Dutton, innkeeper and marine store dealer. On that day, the prisoners came to the shop, at about half-past seven in the morning, and Dutton took newt of iron from them, but he did not see him pay them for it.—Dutton was now put in the witness box, and stated that on receiving the iron from the prisoners, they told him they got it from a flat. He paid them 4s. 101 d. for it.—ln reply to Mr. Lewin, magis- trates' clerk, witness said he was not aware that the prisoners were bad characters.—P.C. Anderson said he went to For- ster's marine store with the witness Roberts, when he (Roberts), picked up the piece of iron produced, and identi- fied it as having been stolen from the works. He afterwards saw Dutton, who told him he had not bought any, but his boy had.—Dutton was recalled, and admitted having sold the iron to the dealer Forster.—Prisoners pleaded guilty ; and Inspector Barnett said that Brawley was an old offender. —Each of the prisoners was sent to gaol three months, with hard labonr.—Dutton was then recalled, and the Chairman said the Bench thought his conduct unsatisfactory. He ought to be exceedingly careful in purchasing goods of this description from anyone, and he should ascertain that they were come by honestly before he did so. If there were not so many ways of getting rid of stolen property, there would be fewer offences.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. F. H. Gossage, and G. Pilkington.

THE ALLEGED SAVAGE ASAULT.—llichael Donelan, of 10, Carlile-street, was brought up on ;remand charged with having on the let inst., unlawfully wounded Frederick Beck, of Moss-street, employed on the Cheshire Lines Rail- way as a signalman—Jr. Husband appeared to defend the prisoner. The case was reported at length in the last issue of The Examiner. The evieence given on Friday was repeated, and Mr. Hus- band having addressed the Bench for the defence, the prisoner was committed to the sessions for trial. THE SERIOUS CASE OF UNLAWFULLY WOLNDING. —A man named John Fitzbarris was brought up on remand from Friday, charged- with having on the loth ult„ unlawfully wounded William Myers. The plisoner was defended by Mr Husband. The prosecutor, who is a labourer, Living in Enfield-street, said he was at the Ship Inn beer- house about five o'clock on the 15th ult. In a passage off the Place were the prisoner and his brother playing skittles and he had a game with them. The prisoner and his bro- ther won, and they demanded 6d. from him in consequence. He refused to pay it as 31. was the only amount they could claim. When he went out of the house, the prisoner " set on" him and caught hold of him by the coat collar. Wit- ness pushed him off, when the prisoner struck him with his fist. A fight then commenced with the prisoner's brother and witness. Whilst this was going on the prisoner went to witness and struck him in the mouth; and in a few seconds he fell to the ground. He was not aware that anyone struck him when on the ground. Prisoner's brother was the first to strike him, and during the struggle kicked him on the right breast. He believed the prisoner's brother NV3S wearing shoes. Immediately after he was kicked he did not feel much pain, and he went to his work. In two hours he was obliged to go home, and the following morning he called in Dr. O'Keeffe. For three weeks he was confined Ito bed When his declaration was taken by the magistrates at his bedside, he believed he was going to die. He com- menced work on Monday morning.—Mr. Husband, who defended, put in a paper written bj the prosecutor, in which he said he thought the prisoner had done him no harm.--Dr. O'Keeffe stated that on Monday, the 17th April, he was sent for to the house of the prosecutor, who he found in bed. He examined him, and found he was injured on the right side of the chest internally and externally. He examined him with the stethescope, and discovered that his lungs were not in a perfect state. He prescribed for him, but inflammation of the right lung set in, and he gradually became worse. He (witness) was present when the prosecutor's "dying declara- tion" was taken. The injuries which he found Myers suffer- ing from were such as might have been caused by a kick. On the 21st ult. the prisoner was going from bad to worse, and he had faint hopes of his recovery. Myers had been under his care for three weeks. A few weeks before the 17th ult, he examined the prosecutor for an assurance company, and he was then in a healthy state.—A witness named Mary Maddocks, whose evidence was necessary to corn- plete the case for the prosecution, had. absconded, and Superintedent Barker applied for a remand Mr. Husband said he could not of course oppose a remand, but there was really nothing against his client; he only gave the prosecutor a " slap " in the mouth, which would not hurt a man much if he did not loose his teeth, which the prosecutor had not. His wife had told him that if the prisoner woe detained in gaol she would have to go to the werkhouss.—The prisoner was again remanded for a week, the Bench agreeing to release the prisoner en bail, himself in £4O and two sureties of £2O each.

THE CHARGE OF BREAKING A MAN'S LEG.—Paul Ker- ley, a marine store dealer, who has only recently been dis- charged from gaol, after undergoing 15 months; imprison- ment, was charged on remand with unlawfully wounding a rag gatherer, named Luke Kelly, living at -64, INlidwood- street.--Mr. G. Moore, of Warrington, appeared for the pri- soner.—With great reluctance the prosecutor took the oath, and it was only by very close question big the following facts were elicited from him. Prosecutor said on Monday after- noon, the 17th ult., he was having some drink with the prisoner in his own house in Victoria-road. He was sitting on a chair. The prisoner knocked him off with his hand, and when he attempted to rise from the floor be discovered his leg was injured. He was unable to tell why the prisoner had knocked him off the chair; he had never given him any provocation. He did not know his leg was broken until he was examined by the doctor. After he was knocked off the chair he walked home with the assistance of his wife. He "walked from the prisoner's house without assistance, but he was drunk and did not know whether tie was pushed'out or not." When he was knocked off the chair he cried out that his leg was broken ; but he did not know whether it was broken or sprained.—Cross-examined by Mr. Moore : He had known Kerley from boyhood, and had been on good terms with him. Drinking in the house with him on the 17th ultimo were three other mm. On that day the pri- s2ner had only been released from Kirkdale, and unfortu- nately for them they luid a lot of whiskey, of which seven persons were drinking. He thought they consumed about three quarts. He did not know whether the prisoner knocked him off the chair with his open hand or his fist. It was not his wish to press the -case. Since this occurrence it was a fact that the prisoner's wife had allowed him LI per week, and was willing to pay the doctor's fees.—By Super- intendent : He could not tell whether prisoner had thrown his wife out of the house before he knocked witness off the chair. There was no disturbance in the house to his Rnow-

div.head: ONE POUND NOTES.
div.p: ONE POUND NOTES.

A correspondent at Newton favours us with the follow- ing :—When a friend of ours in Scotland wants at any time to send us two or three pounds in payment of what he may want to buy in England, he sends two or three of those very handy pound notes of which he is so proud. But, unfortunately, no one here will take them for twenty shil- lings a-piece, so we have to hand them to some money dealer in Liverpool, and pay him from fourpence to sixpence for each pound sterling, and so we lose from two to two and a half per cent. because our friend has such a preference for pound notes, instead of paying one-half per cent, for a postal order for the same amount, and which 13 really a bank note that can be passed from hand to hand indefinitely if the name of the first person paid be omitted from the postal order by the person paying; but this, if not exactly Use majeste, is, according to Mr. Fawcett ::at any rate, not en regle. It will at least be a doubtful gain even if Mr. Fowler does carry his resolution in the Rouse of Commons declaring "that the prohibition of the issue of bank notes of £1 each in England and Wales is unreasonable and ought to be removed." People to whom pound notes might be most useful here are, as a rule, very suspicious of paper money of any sort, and prefer hard cash in Victoria sovereigns, and those not of Australian origin, as they sometimes look very like brass (nevertheless we wish we had a bushel of them) ; and the fortunate possessor of a twenty pound note finds it difficult to get it cashed even iu a bank, without finding " godfathers " for his identity and character, the rule being to look with distrust at all notes but their own unless you have an account with them, and then, if you happen to get a draft on Warrington say, and present it in Wigan, you must trust to Providence to find a friend in Wigan who knows you. But this is the beauty of banking and bank notes. Any further complication will be studiously avoided by the average Englishman if he be wise. It is enough to look at such countries as Austria and Russia to be warned against the introduction of small notes instead of gold. In neither of these countries can you hardly-find a gold ducat although nominally a geld standard. They may do for poor countries like Sweden and Norway, where you cm get a bank note for twopence halfpenny. England's gold is England's greatness in the main. To be sure our friend aforesaid saved the half per cent. like a thrifty Scot, and kept within the law, leaving us to make the best bargain we ce.uld with the money dealer. But if we mutt have £1 notes why not legalize the Scotch notes? and ate ;1 a march on Sandy by making him print them for us ! But softly, this might be too much to trust his exchequer, as a pound means a sovereign. Contrari- wise the Portuguese have cooly adopted our sovereign as their standard coin and thus saved themselves the trouble 'and expense of coining. English bank notes are not looked upon with special favour abroad although we are accustomed to say "I'. is as 'safe as the Bank of England," the same bank being only a corporation like others with some special favour granted by the state, it wculd be a long time be- fore English £1 notes would be appreciated there except by bankers, and people going to the Continent would need larger notes and no silver whatever, as it might be given away but could not be paid, not even at a dealer's, unless at a heavy discount. The only redeeming part is that an Eng- lish note is nearly always cashed at par (in English gold) when a sovereign is not so, invariably—as for example, in Spain. although the standard coin of the adjoining country, Portugal, as before said, is the English sovereign, and long may it be ours. The relation 'between Spain and Portugal is exactly similar to that between England and Scotland, even to the slight difference in race, but Portugal. unlike Scatland, has Chosen the better current coin we think. But usage is•secend nature, and the Scot is ever faithful to his pound note, and was in our boyhood averse to English sovereigns as we well remember. Being in the city of Perth, (the very mention of its name, by the law of association of ideas, brings before us the figure of a local celebrity making his tirumphal entrance there, and exit thence) as we did a penny the richer or poorer as you may think for we left it in debt to that extent. We took gold if not " money "in our puree, and nothing else had we. A fair maid of Perth, dark. stark, lovesome and lithe, and blithe as the morning, went far and wide to get a sovereign changed, for banks were closed, and the coin came back again, and we are her debtor to this day, which would not have been:the case if we had bad one of those useful pound notes, or they had had . less prejudice, not to say suspicion, of the English standard coin. •

div.head: DARESBURY HIGIT WAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBURY HIGIT WAY BOARD.

On Thursday the first meeting of the newly appointed , Board was held in the Sessions House, Daresbury, and there ; were present Messrs. E. Greenall, Major W. Fox, Joseph Cliffe, James Cooper, James Knowles, William Wilkinson, John Hopkins, Thomas J. Rigby, Philip Darbyshire, H. Houghton, W. Salt, R. L. Fryer, Thomas S. Burgess, John Weir, James Handley, Rev. A. Kenworthy, H. Linaker (clerk), and J. Derbyshire (surveyor).—Mr. HOPKINS had great pleasure in proposing the re-election of Mr. Greenall as chairman, for he was sure they could not do better than re-elect him.—Mr, RIGBY seconded the proposition, which was unanimously agreed to.—Mr. GREENALL, on taking the chair, said he was extremely obliged to them. As he had said on previous occasions, whatever he could do to help the interests of the Board, he should be glad to do. (hear, hear) ; but he thought the time had come when they ought to appoint a younger man (" No, no,") with more energy, as the. years were creeping on him fast, and after this year he must ask them to excuse him. However, during this year he would do his best for them. The work hitherto had been very pleasant, and he hoped it would continue so in the ensuing year.—On the proposition of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. JAMES BARBER, Mr. Joseph Cliffe was re-appointed vice-chairman. —The Finance Committee, consisting of the chairman, vice- chairman, Messrs. W. Salt, W. Bradford, Philip Derbyshire, Peter Percival, James Knowles, Thomas Bennett, and James Parr, were re-elected on the motion of Mr. norm/is, seconded by Mr. WEIR; and the usual resolution empower- ing the committee to sign precepts and cheques was passed. —The CLERIC read a letter from the Local Government Board enclosing copy of a letter which they had received from the Surveyor against the disallowance of £1 Bs. and 83. paid for stationery, and from which it appeared the amounts had been surcharged by the auditor because no minute of the Board or order in the order cheque book, authorising the Surveyor to purchase or pay for the stationery.—The CLERK explained that the stationery was obtained before the now order books came into force. Everything now passed through the order cheque book, but previously that was not the case, and Mr. Darbyshire got what he required, and the Board sanctioned the payment.—lt was decided that the Clerk write to the Local Government Board giving this ex- planation.—The SURVEYOR asked for instructins as to taking legal proceedings against persons who had horses pasturing upon the highways of the district. His inquiry had reference more especially to persons who bad travelling vans upon the road side.—The CHAIRMAN said the surveyor would find instructions in the Act of Parliament. The SURVEYOR reported that about noon on Wednesday eportion of the road at Stockton Heath over the sewer, which had recently been constructed there, fell to a depth of about 21- feet. He had the place, which was very dangerous, im- mediately restored, at a cost of 4s. or 55., and as this sort of thing had frequently happened, he asked for instructions as to charging the costs to the Sanitary Authority, to whom the sewer belongs. Mr. PERCIVAL : I think we closed with the contractor.—The CHAIRMAN: They paid a certain sum of money down for repairing the road.—Mr. CLIFFE : We have finished with them.—The ' CHAIRMAN: My impression is that having received a sum of money for putting these roads in proper order we really have taken upon ourselves all liability. We have nothing to do with the sewer. If the pipes had broken they had nothing to do with that, but our duty is to fill up the holes. —The CLERK: And if the Sanitary Authority ever break up the road to repair the sewer they must put it in order.—This mcluded the business.

div.head: RUNCORN FERTYMAN'S GRATE,
div.p: THE RUNCORN FERTYMAN'S GRATE,

Lines on the death of John Harrison, the well-known ferrymln, of Runcorn, whose death was recorded in The Examiner, last Saturday. For years he has bravely and carefully crossed The Mersey, when foaming and angrily tossed. Like the boat be was stout, and like her was broad set. He always stood ready, nor feared wind or wet. His eye was ever watchful, his voice firm and kind; He would pilot his passengers safely, and find Tho handiest landing for mother and child. From ebb to high water he manfully toiled, At day dawn, or midnight, if signalled to go, His boat he made ready to sail or to row; And many a traveller sounded the horn When belated at night or hard pressed in the morn. The thousands and thousands whom he ferried o'er Will grieve that he never will pilot them more. Respected whilst living, regretted tow gone. Of all he has carried he never lost one. His crossings are over, his sail laid aside. His oar lies unshipp'd, ebb'd out is his tide ; There down by the ferry, his anchor is cast In the deep silent grave, and his spirit at last Has cross'd the cold fl iod to the heavenl7 shore— The Ferryman Death rowed him quietly o'er. Runcorn, May Ist, 1882.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. John Brundrit (chairman) and S. B. Chadwick. •
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. John Brundrit (chairman) and S. B. Chadwick. •

QUARRELSOME NEIGUBOURS.—Ann Farrell, an old woman, was charged with assaulting Martha Walley, widow, No. 11, Vicar-street.—Complainant said she lived with her parents, and defendant was her next door neighbour. On the morn- ing of the 30th ult., she went into the yard to fill the kettle, when the defendant, whose house was in .the next yard, managed to hit her on the wrist, and next threw a bucket of water over her. Some angry words then passed between them, and defendant threatened that if she could only get hold of her, she would take her life. She went to close the yard door, when Farrell ran at her with a hatchet, aLd also threw a pint pot. Her (complainant's) father then went for a policeman.—Louis Done, father of complainant, said de- fendant threw a pint pot, which narrowly missed striking him upon the temple.—Mary Ann Marjury said she heard defendant come out with some terrible oaths and threatened to tear her liver out.—Defendant stated she was cleaning the yard of her house, when complainant told her to " keep her dirt" to herself. Walley was in the habit of harbouring her (defendant's) son, and since the new year came in " she had been killed by inches" through the conduct of the two. —Mary Ellen Brannon, a young woman, said she saw the bucket of water thrown.—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace six months, herself in £5 and one surety in a like sum. She had also 14s. 6d. costs to pay. NEW BATE FOR NORTON.—The Bench sanctioned a new rate of 10d. in the E for Norton, to realise £278 6s. 7d. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. S. B. Chadwick.

QUARREL BETWEEN VICAR-STREET WOMEN.—Ann Bos- tock was charged by Martha Whalley, of Vicar-street, with assaulting her on the 3rd inst.—Complainaut said that about four o'clock in the afternoon she was sweeping the dust off a carpet, and opened the yard door, when defendant rushed upon her, threw her down, and threatened to pull out her vitals, as she had taken a Summons out against her mother. She shouted out "Murder," on which defendant's mother and some of her other relatives dragged her off. This was about the seventh time that Bostock had been guilty of such conduct.—Two witnesses were called by complainant, and also one by defendant.—Bo:stock said that complainant's relatives were beating her boy, and on running out to chas- tise them, defendant set upon her.—Defendant was ordered to enter into sureties to keep the peace, herself in £5, and one surety in a like sum.

ALLEGED ROBBERY BY A LODGER.—AIice Highfield, who stated that she came from Bedford Leigh, was charged with having, on the 21st ult., stolen a velvet dress, a necktie, and a necklace, the property of Mary Barnett, a married woman, living with Mrs. Carter, of St. John-street.—Prosecutris said she was the wife of Richard Barnett, but was at present liv- ing apart from him. On the 20th ult. she went to Carter's to lodge, and was wearing the stolen articles. When she rose on the following morning, she asked the prisoner to lend her a scarf in which to go out for the purpose of- buying some bedstocks. She agreed to do so, and prosecutrix left the house about a quarter-past nine, and returned between ten and eleven, when she found that the prisoner had gone and taken the things she warcharged with stealing.—Ser- geant Walley said he received the prisoner into custody from the police at Liverpool on the sth inst., and she was wearing the stolen dress and necktie. On being charged she replied, "Yes, they do belong to her, but she has got my shawl, apron, jacket, and skirt."—The Chairman said the prisoner would be committed to take her trial at Knutsford Quarter Sessions.—Hightield then rushed out of the dock at the prosecutrix, and was about to strike her, when she was seized by Superintendent Williamson, and carried by him and Ser- geant Walley into the cells, shouting and cursing at the top of her voice. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Brun drit.

DRUNK ON LICENSED PREMISES—John Gallagher, for having been drunk on the licnsed premises known as the Greenway Vaults, on the 9th inst. was fined ss. and ss. 4(.1. costs.—The case was proved by P.C. Devenport.
THIIRSDAY.—Before Messrs. John Brundrit and C. W. Hazlehurst.

A POACHER'S CAREER.—Wm. Snaps, a tall muscular- looking man, was charged with having, on the 26th ult., at Sutton, trespassed with fcur other persons, during the day- time, upon land in the occupation of Mr. George Gorst ; and also with having at the same time and place used certain nets for the purpose of gaming without having an excise license.—George Hargreaves, gamekeeper to Sir Richard Brooke, said that on Sunday, the 26th of March last, about half-past ten in the morning, he saw the prisoner with John Wilkinson, Joseph Rowlands, Joseph Bailey, and Wm. Cooke, trespassing upon the land. He observed them "set" a bare in the prosecutor's field and do their best to catch it. As soon as they saw him Snape and Cooke went in the direction of Halton-road, and he (witness) picked up three or four nets. He summoned the prisoner at the time, but he absconded,and the.magistrates granted a warrant for him. The others were likewise summoned, but only Cooke and Bailey put in an appearance. Wilkinson was apprehended on another charge, and sent to gaol.—Prisoner now denied his guilt, though he admitted having been with the other men.—The Chairman said that ever since the year 1866 the prisoner had been busy game trespassing; and there were three charges of that nature brought against him last year. The life was a disgraceful one to lead, and he should have thought that by this time Snape would have seen the sense- less folly of the course he was pursuing. As he did not ap- pear to do so, the magistrates would have to inflict a penalty which they hoped would cause him to see the error of his way. He would be fined £4 and 183. costs in each case, or in default one month's imprisonment.
The Cleveland ironmasters decided on Tuesday to damp down the furnaces if the strike was not euded this week. The Sunderland ironr:orkers resolved on Tuesday to con- tinue the strike,

Bold-street Chambers, Warrington, April 17th 1882. NOTICE.—I beg most respectfully to inform the public of Warrington and the surrounding neighbourhood that since the recent dissolution with my son, T. C Pierpoint, I have concluded arrangements to take in as partner Hr. James Adams, who for a period of eight years has been engaged as managing assistant with W. Owen, Esq., Architect, &c., of Cairo- street Chambers, Warrington. Our firm will therefore from this date be carried on at the above address as Architects, Sur- veyors, Estate Agents. and Valuers, under the style or title of PIERPOINT & ADAMS. JOHN PI ERPOINT.

The CREDITOrs of the above-named company are required, on or before the sth day of June, 1881, to send their names and addresses, and the particu- lars of their DEBTS or CLAIMS, and the names and addresses of their solicitors (if any), to WILLIS It RICHARDSON, of Strand- road. Preston, in the county of Lancaster, Accountant, the official liquidator of the said company; and it is so required by notic,s in wtiting from the said official liquidator, are by their solicitors to come in and prove their said debts or claims at the Chainbers of the Honourable Mr. Justioe Chitty, in the Royal Courts of Justice, Strand, in the county of Middlesex, at such time as shall be specified in such notice, or in default thereof they will be excluded from the benefit of any distribution made before such debts are proved. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE SOUTH WEST WARD. LADIES AND G-ENTLEMEN, —At the request of an influential deputation, I have this day consented to become a Candidate for the representation of the South-West Ward in the Town Council. For a considerable time past I have been of opinion that our Rates are very excessive, and that most energetic action will be necessary to ensure their reduction. Should you honour me with your confidence, I shall endeavour as your ep, sentative, to carry out these views, and will on all occasions do what lies in my power to secure the best Munieiral Government at the least possible cost to the Ratepayers. I am, your obedient Servant, MATTHEW BOWDEN. 43, Wilson-Patten-street, May 3rd, 1882.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE SOUTH-WEST WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,--9, vacancy having oc- curred in the representation of the South-West Ward owing to the resignation, through ill-health, of Mr. Josiah Pemberton' Williams, I have consented, at the urgent request of a large number of influential Bur- gesses, to be:ome a candidate for the vacant seat lit the Town 0 ouncil 1 am, as most of you know, a large employer of labour, and a considerable ratepayer, and must conse- quently have the strongest personal interest in check- ing and keeping down the ever-increasing rates of the Borough, the payment of which has become in- tolerably oppressive. Let me therefore assure you that, if you •do me the honour of electing me as your representative, I will do everything I possibly can, compatible with the welfare of my fellow-townsmen, and with an in- telligent recognition cf our local requirements, to re- duce the expenditure in every department controlled by the Town Council. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, JOHN ED. WRIGHT.

(Runcorn) —School boards and school attendance com- mittees have no direct authority to inspect private adventure schools, but they are entitled to be satisfied of the efficiency of the education which children are receiving who are attend- ing other than public elementary schools. T. B. (Widnes).—" A Roland for an Oliver" means a blow for a blow or tit for tat. The origin of the phrase is in dispute. The best ecc!ount is that which refers it to Roland and Oliver, two paladins of Charlemagne, who were always endeavour- ing to outdo each other in chivalrous exploits. At length, says the legend, the two men met to,ether in single combat and fought for five consecutive days on an island in the Rhine, but neither gained tice least alvantage I FINANCE (Latchford).—The first sinking fund was established by Sir Robert Walpole in 1716, the second by Mr. Pitt in 1786. The latter, however, although designed to gradually relieve us of our liabilities, in reality sunk us rapidly deeper Into debt. In other words, we wenton clearing off 41,000,000 a year Of loans borrowed at a low rate of interest, while, to meet the expenses of our wars, we went on contracting fresh loans to a far larger amount at a higher rate. "POOR OLD JUMBO" (St. Heiens).-1. Baines' History of Lan- cashire, describing Et. Helens, says: "In this hamlet is situated the Episcopal Obapel of St. Helens, originally St. Ellen, which has given name to the town." On the right of the porch of the town hall is a niche which eontains a figure of Saint Helen, the ancient patron saint of the borough. 9. Sir Robert Peel was a Conservative. 3. Only peers are allowed to sit in the House of Lords; Mr. Gladstone, there- fore, is unable to do so.
